#5731. SpaceX Starship Will Need To Re-Fuel 22 Times In Space To Make It To The Moon

As NASA plans to send astronauts back to the surface of the Moon in 2028, there's still the small matter of figuring out how to get them there. While the Artemis II mission proved that we can send people around the Moon and bring them safely home, the space agency needs a way to take astronauts out of the Orion capsule and down to the actual ground. The original plan was for a SpaceX Starship to fulfill this duty, and that could still be the case. But delays in the development of that ambitious rocket caused NASA to re-open the contract, which allowed Blue Origin to toss its hat in the ring. Still, SpaceX insists it will fend off this challenge from a rival billionaire-owned space company and win the contract all over again. The only thing standing in its way: the minor fact that it has to refuel the Starship in-orbit, something never done before and that SpaceX hasn't even attempted yet. Oh, and it has to do it many, many times. How many? Great question.

The NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel recently announced that, by their calculations, a Starship would require fully 22 in-orbit refuelings to get that one single rocket to the Moon's surface, per Ars Technica. Again, the total number of times that any rocket has ever done this is zero. Specifically, the plan from SpaceX is to launch one Starship into orbit to act as a fuel depot; then launch many other Starships to load up that first one with fuel; then launch a final Starship to take on that fuel from the depot and head out to the Moon.

If 22 sounds like an insane number to you, you're not alone: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on the social media platform X, which SpaceX owns, "Actual number will be more like 6 to 8." That makes for quite a broad range of estimates. The reason this is so fuzzy is because the fuel we're talking about here isn't gasoline, but rather a mixture of liquid oxygen and methane. This actually boils off in the vacuum of space, so how much fuel can be transferred depends on the efficiency of the technology involved. Technology that has never actually been tested in orbit.

Currently, SpaceX plans to perform its first test of orbital refueling in early 2027, just a little over a year before it will theoretically do it for the Moon landing. If that doesn't work, well, SpaceX's lunar ambitions are in trouble. Even if it does go well, and there are absolutely no issues whatsoever with this unprecedented capability, there's still the small matter of actually launching all of these rockets. Right now, the still-in-development Starship only launches once every few months. Musk claims it will be launching weekly by early 2027, just months away. And then he further claims it will launch twice a week by the end of 2027. Let's just say that would be, ah, truly remarkable if it happened.

For once, let us be optimistic, and believe in words. If these words be true, and Starship truly is launching twice-weekly, then launching 22 refueling Starships (plus launching the initial "depot" Starship) would take... three months. And that is assuming no failures, either of the rockets or of the fuel transfer process. That's reduced to three weeks if you also believe Musk's figure of six launches. At least Musk has never once lied about his companies capabilities! If for some reason you don't believe in that launch cadence, then total refueling will take potentially years. Either way, that would amount to the most complicated endeavor NASA, or any space entity, has ever attempted.

By contrast, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin has a much simpler plan to get to the Moon. It's still complicated, let's be clear, but less so than SpaceX. The company's proposal calls for a mere four launches of its New Glenn rocket, assuming it doesn't explode and destroy its entire launchpad, again. The first three would park a booster stage in orbit; the fourth would put a Blue Moon lunar lander into orbit, where it will collect all the booster stages, stack them together, and then blast off towards the Moon. That is a wild dance all its own, but it doesn't require figuring out how to transfer any fuel.

If you're wondering where the actual astronauts are, don't you worry: they're on a completely different rocket altogether. The Space Launch System (SLS) rocket carries the Orion capsule into orbit with all the astronauts on board. The capsule then continues on from Earth orbit to lunar orbit on its own, as the Artemis II mission demonstrated. Somewhere along that path — whether in high-Earth orbit, high-lunar orbit, or low-lunar orbit (this part still isn't nailed down) — the Orion capsule will have to dock with either the Starship or the Blue Moon, depending on who wins the contract. The lander will then land, the astronauts will enjoy a nice walk around another world, and then the lander will return to lunar orbit. Then it's back aboard the Orion capsule and then back to Earth.

Sounds easy! Basically, a lot has to go right for NASA to make that 2028 landing date. How it shakes out in practice depends on how well a lot of untested equipment and procedures work. Then again, if you were to go back to the 1960s, the Apollo program wasn't exactly any more precedented, or safer. In that decade, though, NASA did have a lot more testing demonstrations before going for the Moon. This time around, the agency wants to get there faster.

#5729. 1976 Pontiac Trans Am For Sale With 7 Miles After Restoration Pairs 4-Speed Stick And 455 V8

For those looking to channel your inner Burt Reynolds from "Smokey and the Bandit," WeBe Autos (via Hemmings) has this lovely black-and-gold Trans Am for sale that's nearly the perfect match. Except, it's a 1976, not a 1978, so it doesn't feature the quad-headlight front-end that the movie car had. If that's what you want, however, this 1978 example or this 1979 one that's done roughly 22,000 miles should be of interest. Neither of them, mind you, is in black, nor do they feature a 455-cubic-inch V8 or offer the three-pedal experience like the '76 example we have here.

Unlike the movie car, though, this Trans Am is a hardtop coupé. But it has undergone extensive restoration and has only done seven miles since. And yes, it has the Screaming Chicken hood decal, or the "Rising Phoenix" if you're part of that camp. So what's the asking price for this 1970s muscle-car goodness? That'd be $72,495. Although it may not be as sophisticated as the latest BMW iX3 (also a $70,000 ballpark proposition), the 455 V8 and four-speed combo has enough personality and aura to challenge whatever these modern-day "computers on wheels" can offer.

Character assessment aside, what you get for your money is a well-finished exterior, a beautifully detailed engine compartment, an exceptionally clean underbody, and a beautifully restored all-black interior. While the Endura-style bumpers and Honeycomb wheels stand out as exterior highlights, the classic Trans Am instrumentation, custom Autosound audio system, and factory-style dashboard come across as some of the notable attractions on the inside. Sure, it might not be a T-top nor feature the movie car's front fascia, but then again, Bandit's companion was actually a 1976 Trans Am with a '77 front end.

Classic Industries and Hemmings reckon there were four cars used in total, while Autoweek counts five, but the important thing is that all Trans Ams used in the movie started out as '76 Special Edition 50th Anniversary cars with the updated '77 front end. Pontiac had to get creative because the movie's production began before 1977 models were actually available. And the engines you saw (or rather heard) on screen weren't part of the 1977 lineup at all. While Classic Industries reported the stunt cars retaining the 455 V8, in reality, you could not have optioned the motor in a 1977 car — it was retired after the 1976 model year.

Setting aside this bit of "Smokey and the Bandit" trivia, you can probably already tell how the Trans Am listing we have ties in with all this. It's a 1976 car in the right paint scheme, with the 455 and a four-speed manual thrown in for good measure. More importantly, there's no deception here, and it looks nothing like a 50-year-old hunk of metal.

Is the near-$73,000 asking price too much? That depends on whom you ask. It's a lot of money for something that old. Despite the restoration, that 455 was part of the Malaise Era lineup, which famously neutered a lot of high-performance V8s. Given that the listing mentions "emissions equipment present," it's unlikely that things are any different here. Still, for someone who likes '70s Americana, is an ardent fan of movies, or, above all, a true-blue Pontiac enthusiast, this Trans Am should hold plenty of appeal. Assuming, of course, they have the means to afford it.

#5727. Ferrari Luce Sold Out Through 2027 In Another Win For The Liberal Agenda

November 3 was a historic night for the liberal agenda as Democrats won just about every single major election across the country in a massively convincing fashion, leading many to declare that woke is indeed back. Perhaps then, it is no surprise that sales of the Ferrari Luce, the wokest vehicle Maranello has ever produced, are off to a roaring start with the order books now full through the end of 2027. As it turns out, internet haters who cannot afford a Ferrari aren't the tastemakers one would think.

Ferrari made the announcement that its first all-electric vehicle was sold out through '27 during its earnings call earlier this week, according to InsideEVs. The news comes after a July announcement from the automaker that the $560,800 EV had already hit its 2026 sales target after being available for purchase for just a couple of months. People want this thing, and people want pronouns in email signatures again. It's morning again in America.

"The Luce that we plan to sell next year basically are all allocated," Benedetto Vigna, Ferrari CEO, said in the earnings call, according to InsideEVs, adding that customers who placed an order now would have to wait a year to actually take delivery. Hopefully this isn't an empty promise, like "gas prices are going to come down after the midterms." Anyway, Ferrari hasn't said how many Luces it plans to sell, and it hasn't provided any sort of regional breakdown of orders so far.

Like Jon Ossoff and his lightning-fast election night, Ferrari made quick work of its 2026 sales goal. Two unnamed sources told the Financial Times that the automaker planned to sell just under 500 examples of the Jony Ive-designed EV this year, and doing it in such a quick fashion is quite the indictment on what the average internet car enthusiast thinks a popular car should be. Long term, Ferrari says it wants to sell about 2,500 Luces by 2030, or roughly 600 per year, though the exact ramp-up numbers haven't been released yet.

When the Luce first launched, you'd be hard-pressed to find a fan. Folks didn't like its looks, the fact it was a sedan, or the EV-ness of it all. People who never thought about cars were letting the takes fly, but Ferrari has remained steadfast. It has defended the Luce, attempting to showcase its new tech while also reaching the next generation of wealthy buyers in China and other tech hubs like Silicon Valley. Basically, they're targeting folks who are already driving EVs but are looking for something more premium.

Still, this hasn't stopped people, even though with close ties to Ferrari, from throwing hissy fits over the Luce. When the car first launched, we reported that Ferrari's former longtime CEO, Luca di Montezemolo, told reporters that if he were to say what he really thought about the Luce, he'd "be doing Ferrari a disservice" and it risked "destroying a legend." He even said that he hoped Ferrari would "at least remove the prancing horse from that car."

In any case, it's time to jump in the Luce, crank up "Fight Song" and blast down the highway, because we're libbing out in this bih.

#5725. Scandal-Ridden Cadillac F1 Owner Putting Team Up For Sale After Just One Year

The long-awaited entry of an American factory team was viewed as a coup for Formula 1. Billionaire financier Mark Walter is now looking to sell the Cadillac F1 Team after a single F1 season. While the team has failed to score a point in its maiden campaign so far, the sale would help him dodge scrutiny amid federal investigations into alleged self-dealing. Walter's TWG Group is in negotiations to sell a significant team stake at a $3 billion valuation.

Walter amassed a sports empire over the past 15 years. His investment firm Guggenheim Partners purchased the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2012 for $2.15 billion. Walter personally owns 27% of the MLB franchise. Since the acquisition, the Dodgers have alarmingly amassed over $1 billion in deferred payroll obligations on their way to three World Series titles. TWG would expand into racing in 2024, purchasing Andretti Global and its F1 entry bid. The company spent over $1 billion on the Cadillac F1 Team before its debut race in Australia earlier this year, nearly half that total was an anti-dilution fee.

How could Walter afford to do all of this? According to The Wall Street Journal, the U.S. Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission are investigating how TWG-owned insurance companies lent billions of dollars to Walter's other enterprises. IndyCar fans are familiar with these insurance companies, seeing Delaware Life and Gainbridge logos plastered on Andretti's cars. An internal review found that $20 billion in loans weren't disclosed to financial regulators. Walter presumably needs to repay said $20 billion as soon as possible.

The TWG firesale began in August. Walter sold the Los Angeles Lakers for $12.5 billion to Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital. The deal was negotiated over a weekend. He added the NBA team to his sports empire just last year for $10 billion. After the Lakers deal, TWG denied that the Cadillac F1 Team was for sale. Despite the denial, Fenway Sports Group is the favorite among several bidders to buy the F1 team. The company currently owns the Boston Red Sox, Liverpool F.C. and RFK Racing in the NASCAR Cup Series.

The Cadillac F1 Team's sudden sale could be viewed as an opportunity for another automaker to enter Grand Prix racing, but General Motors also owns a stake in the team. With that constraint, FSG is the most logical choice to keep the team on its current course as GM develops its in-house F1 power unit program. Even without the federal investigations, Cadillac has had a rough start. The team has yet to score its first point. Team principal Graeme Lowdon was replaced in August. American F1 hopeful Colton Herta has yet to secure a Super License, partly due to the team misreporting Herta's past results to the FIA after believing an error on the IndyCar website.

Voters delivered a stunning rebuke of Republicans and everything they stand for Tuesday night, taking control of both the House and the Senate in a wave of wins that just kept coming. Democrats kept winning, again and again, wave after wave. A bluekkake, if you will. And while that's great news for the stock market, the Middle East, healthcare, trans kids' safety, and so many other hugely important issues, voters also rejected Elon Musk and his billionaire meddling. We won't be able to get rid of him overnight, but at least Musk's dreams of a Tesla-SpaceX-Twitter-xAI merger are probably dead.

If you remember, Musk has long been reported to want his companies all under one roof to complete Tesla's tranformation into an AI/robotics company (or stop making cars without crashing the stock price). xAI already merged with Twitter and stuck Musk's antisemitism-spewing, CSAM-generating chatbot in Teslas, then merged with Spacex ahead of its IPO. Musk also floated the possibility with investors, and one of the Trump administration's lasting legacies will be its love of corporate mergers, so it sounded plausible.

With Democrats winning control of both the House and the Senate, likely finishing with 258 Representatives and 55 (or 56!) Senators, the left doesn't just have power, it has a mandate from the voters to put a stop to everything the Trump administration is doing. Raskin will chair the House Judiciary Committee, Garcia will chair the House Oversight Committee, and both have promised investigations into any criminal activity that's taken place. That's not exactly fertile ground for a major corporate merger, especially after Musk attempted to inflame a race riot in Ireland, campaigned for Germany's Nazi-adjacent AfD party, and blew hundreds of millions of dollars trying to elect Republicans.

Yes, our friends over at the Tesla Takedown kept a running thread going last night, highlighting every race Musk lost and how much money he wasted. Nearly two dozen races, all won by Dems, even though a Republican billionaire tried to buy their elections. Per Vanity Fair, Musk dumped an eye-watering $474 million into this election, and he still got kicked in the nards. He could have given $50,000 to 9,400 people and still wasted less of his money.

Democrats who haven't been bought off by the crypto and AI lobbies have been sounding the alarm in recent months about the dangers of any one person having as much power as Elon does. The man has the power to slow down Ukraine's military's internet, and the prospect of combining SpaceXAI with the most valuable car company in the world makes a lot of regulators nervous. Expect it to be a fight with the centrists in the party, but Dems are more likely to try to weaken Musk's power, not hand him a win.

Because our election system is weird, Republicans won't lose power until January and could theoretically rush the merger through. But even the Motley Fool — a website that published "Prediction: SpaceX Stock Will Go Parabolic After Nov. 6" the day both Tesla and SpaceX shares plunged — doesn't think that's likely. In an article foolishly calling the merger "inevitable," the MFers timeline is still "within the next 12 months" not "before January." They also admit many factors, including antitrust enforcement could be a problem for the merger.

With Dems winning a huge mandate to govern, Republican politicians should be less willing to stick their necks out for that eternally sticky loser, too, so calling it "inevitable" is certainly a take. More importantly, Republicans have a much more important activity on their agenda than facilitating this merger. #5719. FDA Panel Largely Pans Trial Data for Myopia Eye Drops

— Atropine slowed progression but clinical meaningfulness, robustness of data questioned

The regulatory status of a low-dose atropine eye drop formulation for myopia remained unresolved following a day-long FDA advisory committee meeting, but closing comments did not bode well for SYD-101.

The Dermatologic and Ophthalmic Drugs Advisory Committee (DODAC) did not vote to recommend for or against approval of the eye drops, but panelists' responses to key questions posed by the FDA suggested the evidence from a phase III trial of SYD-101 did not meet standards for approval.

"Basically, the summary is that, although the clinical trial is positive, it's not a robust outcome that would meet the standard presented to us as the reason for approval by the FDA," said DODAC Acting Chair Michael X. Repka, MD, of the Johns Hopkins Wilmer Eye Institute in Baltimore. "The issue of missing data remains sort of difficult for this committee to manage."

Primary support for the approval application came from the SYD-101-001 randomized trial (also known as the STAR trial) comparing two doses of atropine sulfate ophthalmic solution versus vehicle to slow myopia progression in 852 pediatric patients 3 years or older. The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients with myopia progression exceeding 0.75 diopters at 36 months.

The primary analysis showed that 39.5% of patients randomized to the 0.01% solution met the primary endpoint as compared with 49.3% of patients randomized to the control group (P=0.0452). The 0.03% treatment arm did not achieve statistical significance versus the control group.

The difference between the 0.01% arm and vehicle translated into progression slowing of 0.079 diopters per year or a cumulative difference of 0.21 diopters versus control. In a briefing document prepared for the meeting, FDA staff said the difference, though statistically significant, was not clinically meaningful and that the magnitude of benefit decreased over time.

Additionally, primary endpoint data were missing for 26% of patients in the 0.01% treatment arm and 23% of the control group. Sensitivity analyses showed the outcome data were influenced by different assumptions about the statistical impact of missing data.

The staff report also noted that the trial failed to show a significant reduction in axial length, which raised questions about the treatment's potential to alter myopia-related structural changes. Half of the participating centers did not measure axial length, and measurement was not uniform at the centers that did. Additionally, "external evidence from other randomized controlled trials conducted in non-Asian Western populations has generally been unsupportive of the efficacy of 0.01% atropine."

Summarizing the panel's comments regarding the clinical meaningfulness of the differences observed in the trial, Repka said, "The [committee] basically considered the clinical meaningfulness of the observed efficacy profile uncertain, both because of the magnitude, the question of just a shift or delay in myopia progression by the 6-month or 1-year cycle, and also the lack of corroboration on axial length in those centers that were able to perform it. [The committee] would recommend to manufacturers in the future to consider including axial length as a primary or key outcome measure."

The panel also appeared to agree with FDA staff that the published literature did not provide confirmatory evidence, beyond the SYD-101-001 trial, that would rise to the standards necessary for approval.

"When I look at the other studies, they were not as well performed or designed as the [SYD-101-001] study we're discussing," said panelist Timothy G. Murray, MD, of the University of Miami Bascom Palmer Eye Institute. "The size, stratification, and randomization that was done was a plus. The way that the data was looked at is a plus. The other studies fall far below that standard, and therefore, I wouldn't consider that substantial evidence or a standard for approval."

In a separate report for DODAC, representatives of Sydnexis noted that the SYD-101-001 trial was designed with input from the FDA. They emphasized that the trial met the prespecified primary endpoint and that the levels of statistical significance increased in a multiple-adjusted analysis (P=0.0226). Data for the key secondary endpoint also achieved statistical significance for the 0.01% solution versus vehicle (P=0.0002).

Though acknowledging missing data, Sydnexis stated that "missing efficacy data and discontinuations were not meaningfully imbalanced across groups. All prespecified missing-data sensitivity estimates favored SYD-101 0.01%, with treatment estimates generally consistent with the primary result."

DODAC panelists did not dispute the statistical significance of the primary endpoint but rather questioned the robustness and clinical meaningfulness of the results. Murray said the lack of robustness "calls into question our ability to interpret the data further."

Alex Kaizer, PhD, a biostatistician at the University of Colorado Anschutz in Aurora, noted that confidence intervals for efficacy data approached 0%, making the results susceptible to small changes.

"I think what this means to me, with the discussion around the potential clinical significance and the heterogeneity of the patient population, is that it feels like more data is truly needed to understand, especially in younger ages and fast progressors, what the benefit would be," he said.

Acknowledging that the treatment seems promising and is approved elsewhere in the world, Kaizer added, "These borderline results do make it challenging, because if just a few people change their outcome, it could change the result suddenly to a very different discussion than the one we're having today."

Throughout the meeting, several speakers noted that dozens of studies have demonstrated atropine eye drops' efficacy in myopia and that low-dose formulations are available in many nations, but not the U.S. Clinicians in the U.S. can and do prescribe low-dose atropine eye drops, but the medication is available only through compounding pharmacies.

The DODAC meeting had its genesis in a complete response letter the FDA sent to Sydnexis in October 2025.

"The FDA acknowledged in the complete response letter that this primary endpoint was met but stated its view that the data do not support the effectiveness of low-dose atropine in children with myopia," company officials stated in a press release. "No deficiencies were noted related to safety or product quality."

In response, Sydnexis submitted a formal dispute resolution request to the FDA, which subsequently scheduled the DODAC meeting to consider the evidence in separate presentations by FDA staff and speakers representing Sydnexis, including several pediatric ophthalmologists.

The next step is up to the FDA, and no timetable for a decision was announced at the conclusion of the DODAC meeting.

#5717. GM Recalls Over 67,000 Chevy Blazer EVs And Cadillac Lyriqs, Vistiqs, And Even Celestiqs For Temporary Loss Of Braking

General Motors is recalling 67,380 Chevrolet Blazer EVs And Cadillac Lyriqs, Vistiqs, and even Celestiqs because under specific circumstances, a software defect can cause a temporary loss of braking ability. According to the NHTSA recall report, GM is aware of 20 minor accidents due to the fault, two of which resulted in minor injuries. Fortunately, the condition only arises at low speeds, but any loss of braking is a deeply concerning and dangerous occurrence. Two-wheel-drive Cadillac Lyriqs are not included in the recall, and the only Blazer EV trims involved are SS and Police Pursuit Vehicles.

Cadillac Lyriqs are hit hardest by the recall, which includes 474 2023 Lyriqs, 22,819 2024 Lyriqs, 11,926 2025 Lyriqs, 9,322 2026 Lyriqs, and 44 2027 Lyriqs. The recall also includes 13,627 2026 Vistiqs and 5,175 2027 Vistiqs, as well as 51 2025 Celestiqs, and 31 2026 Celestiqs. (This is one of our best glimpses yet into how many Celestiqs have been sold.) The only Chevrolets included in the recall are 562 2024 Blazer EVs, 2012 2025 Blazer EVs, 1,314 2026 Blazer EVs, and 23 2027 Blazer EVs. VINs are already searchable on NHTSA's website, and the remedy comes in the form of an over-the-air update for owners who have opted in to those, otherwise owners will have to take their vehicles to dealerships to have the software update downloaded.

The conditions that lead to the temporary loss of brake function are very specific. According to the recall report and GM's testing, "when the brakes are lightly applied at low speeds during a sharp turn and the vehicle encounters a bump or depression – such as at the end of a driveway – a momentary release and reapplication of the brakes may cause the software's slip calculation to misinterpret wheel movement. In some instances, this may result in a temporary loss of braking. The phenomenon is unique to certain vehicles equipped with performance all-wheel drive (pAWD, RPO X0E) and is resolved when the brakes are applied again."

GM already recalled 21,469 all-wheel-drive Lyriqs for a similar issue in 2024, but it found that vehicles built with the software changes following that recall and vehicles that already received the software update from that recall are still susceptible to the conditions described in the new recall, and they need the latest update. The latest software update corrects the slip calculation in the vehicle's brake system control module that causes the temporary loss of braking, which coincidentally is the same claim made on the 2024 recall. Hopefully this time it actually fixes the problem.

If you drive one of the cars included in the recall, be aware of the possibility of braking loss, and remember that if you experience braking loss, normal brake function should return on the next brake press. Dealers should already be notified of the recall, but owner notification is estimated to begin on December 14.

#5715. Upfront TAVR May Be the Way Forward in Moderate Aortic Stenosis, Trial Suggests

— First randomized study to evaluate TAVR versus clinical surveillance in moderate AS

Upfront transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) was more protective against death and heart failure events compared with clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis (AS) with at least one at-risk feature, the randomized PROGRESS trial showed.

At 2 years, a composite endpoint of death from any cause or a heart failure event occurred in 16.7% of patients in the upfront TAVR group versus 23.9% of those in the clinical surveillance group (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.93, P=0.02 for superiority), reported Philippe Généreux, MD, of the Gagnon Cardiovascular Institute at Morristown Medical Center in New Jersey, during the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics annual conference, hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation.

In addition, TAVR with the balloon-expandable Sapien 3 platform had a safety event rate of 5.9% at 30 days, which was well under the prespecified 13.7% performance goal, and the bulk of events were hospitalizations for device- or procedure-related complications (5.6%).

The study was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

"Moderate AS is not benign, and these patients would benefit from earlier referral to a valve clinic for comprehensive evaluation to establish the optimal management strategy," Généreux concluded. "Rather than waiting for progression to severe AS, PROGRESS supports TAVR for patients with moderate AS and at-risk features."

Importantly, the trial has follow-up planned for 10 years. In the meantime, Généreux said that the PROGRESS trial has already identified the "optimal time" for intervention in AS considering the balance of safety and efficacy.

Among the clinical surveillance patients who started out with moderate AS, 57.4% eventually underwent a delayed aortic valve replacement (AVR) by 24 months. Of these patients, over 80% had progressed to severe AS.

Meanwhile, the TAVR arm showed the "best hemodynamics that we ever saw" with the Sapien valve, Généreux reported, citing the effective orifice areas, mean gradients, and minimal paravalvular leaks achieved. "The future will tell, but I strongly believe based on the data today ... [that] this is the optimal timing of intervention to ensure optimal treatment for a patient given that we can treat a second time."

"This disease progressed faster than [we] expected," he stressed. "You need to follow these patients. You cannot abandon them."

During a press conference, panelist Pinak Shah, MD, of Mass General Brigham in Boston, called the trial a "truly practice-changing study" that "really underscores the importance of close follow-up and the fact that AS is not a benign disease."

The results also suggest a drastic widening of the pool of TAVR candidates.

A large registry study, also by Généreux and colleagues, recently showed that patients with moderate AS outnumber those with severe AS by nearly 2:1, and over a quarter of those with moderate AS in this study progressed to severe AS by 2 years.

Ultimately, Généreux argued for doing away with the dichotomy of moderate versus severe AS altogether and moving towards intervention on "clinically significant" AS instead.

For their trial, the investigators sought participants who were at least 65 years old with moderate AS plus at least one at-risk feature. The majority were recruited from the U.S. (87.1%), with a minority coming from sites in Japan, Australia, the Netherlands, Canada, and Switzerland.

Out of 1,294 patients screened, 744 were randomized 1:1 to transfemoral TAVR or once-yearly clinical surveillance from October 2021 to January 2024. Mean age was 78 years, and 39% were women. The Society of Thoracic Surgery risk score was about 3.0%, and fewer than half of patients were deemed low risk per the heart team. New York Heart Association class III/IV symptoms were observed in about 35% at baseline. The Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) score was about 64 on average.

The top at-risk features that qualified people for the study were valve-related symptoms (96.4%) and diastolic dysfunction (43.8%).

Généreux reported that 91% of enrolled patients had moderate AS in terms of both moderate aortic valve area (AVA) criteria and peak velocity/mean gradients. The mean AVA was 1.2 cm2, the mean gradient was just over 25 mm Hg, and the peak velocity was 3.3 m/s. About one in four people had an elevated aortic valve calcium score.

The effectiveness endpoint was a composite of death (8.4% vs 7.3%, HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.67-1.93) and heart failure events (10.8% vs 19.0%, HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.37-0.81). Of note, a heart failure event had to meet all three criteria: new or worsening heart failure symptoms, two or more objective indications of new or worsening heart failure (physical, laboratory, imaging, and/or invasive findings), and escalation of heart failure treatment.

Altogether, the number needed to treat for benefit at 2 years was 14 in the trial.

Separately, as a standalone endpoint, heart failure hospitalizations were fewer in the TAVR arm (7.4% vs 14.9%, HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.30-0.77). However, the composite of death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization did not statistically give TAVR an edge (17.7% vs 23.3%, P=0.07).

As for health status improvement, the mean KCCQ score was 79.6 points in the TAVR arm at 30 days. The proportion of patients alive with an improvement of 10+ points in KCCQ score at 1 and 2 years favored TAVR (39.0% vs 23.2%, P<0.001).

Généreux noted that when it came to delayed AVR in the control arm of the study, KCCQ scores generally dipped before the delayed procedure, followed by a substantial improvement 30 days later.

The incidence rate of new permanent pacemakers was 13.0% with upfront TAVR versus 10.4% with clinical surveillance.

Of note, limiting wider generalizability, PROGRESS had notable exclusion criteria that barred people with unsuitable anatomy for transfemoral TAVR, significant clinical comorbidities, very low ejection fractions, or prior aortic valve replacement or valvuloplasty, among others.

"Certainly, we have to be very careful with patient selection," commented Shah. "For most, the lifetime management is going to be important ... A lot of these patients are probably going to come back for repeat procedures."

#5714. “War” Secretary Pete Hegseth Endorses 15 Minute City Model

You just can’t make this stuff up. While conservatives around the world are waging holy war against the “15 Minute City” concept, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has gone all-in on the idea. His newly announced “Fortress America” military resilience plan includes a new vision for military bases that embraces walkability and quality of life. If that sounds like the 15 Minute City plan in action, it is. Oh, lordy…

Walkable communities are as old as the hills. That’s what people did before automobiles hit the scene and cities were organized around cars. Credit for applying the walkability model to 21st century urban planning goes to the Franco-Colombian scientist Carlos Moreno, who formalized the 15 Minute City concept in 2016. The idea got a further boost of attention when the Mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, pitched walkable, bike-able neighborhoods as part of her successful re-election campaign in 2020.

The COVID-19 lockdown of 2020 was also a pivotal moment, with a surge in work-from-home households drawing attention to the need for local resources as a matter of survival and resiliency in case of a widespread emergency.

The 15 Minute City model covers a lot of ground, but the basic idea is that people should be able to do their shopping, recreation, socializing, and other essential routines within walking or biking distance from their homes, making cars largely optional within the neighborhood. Walkable access to schools and health care is also part of the plan.

The argument for 15-minute cities (also called 15-minute neighborhoods or 15-minute communities) is also pretty straightforward. Walking is healthier than sitting in a car. Avoiding injury or death from car accidents is another plus. Walking also reduces carbon emissions, and it saves money on gas.

In addition, walkability levels the playing field, so to speak. Everyone in the 15-minute zone has walkable access to basic resources, regardless of whether or not they can afford a car. In other words, there is a significant equity and inclusion element to the concept…

…and, that’s where the trouble kicks in. In 2022 the World Economic Forum posted an article by Lisa Chamberlain, the founder of the urban communications and business firm Strategies for City Builders. Chamberlain describes a 15 Minute City as characterized by diversified, mixed-use neighborhoods built to withstand shocks like COVID-19 and climate change.

“As climate change and global conflict cause shocks and stresses at faster intervals and increasing severity, the 15-minute city will become even more critical,” Chamberlain emphasized, with a further emphasis on equity and inclusion:

“Specifically, communities that foster and maintain social and economic relationships don’t have to be wealthy, but they do need to be walkable and safe, with both residential and commercial buildings intact. And, I would add, for 15-Minute Cities to thrive, not just survive crises—and this cannot be stressed enough—they must also have plenty of mixed-income and equitable housing, as well as digital access.”

It didn’t take long for the conspiracy machine to kick into action around the globe. In February of 2023, for example, the Australian news organization ABC radio summed up the 15 Minute City conspiracy theory thusly:

“To some, it’s an urban planning concept that promotes sustainable and healthy living.

“To a small group of others, it’s a plot by ‘tyrannical bureaucrats’ to take our cars and control our lives, which could lead to a real-life Hunger Games scenario.”

“Limiting cars and promoting pedestrian or bike access is framed as a slippery slope to government-run, open-air prisons,” ABC continued.

Yikes! ABC also cites the Canadian psychologist Jordan Peterson. who railed against “idiot tyrannical bureaucrats” who “decide by fiat where you’re ‘allowed’ to drive…and, make no mistake, it’s part of a well-documented plan” (emphasis added).

Ohfergawdsakes, of course there is a well documented plan, and it’s called urban planning. And, that’s where the US Department of Defense comes in.

On September, in a move that sailed under the CleanTechnica radar, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the new “FORTRESS America” plan, with FORTRESS representing “Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability.”

Stripping away Secretary Hegseth’s testosterone-fueled purple prose in the September 30 announcement, FORTRESS AMERICA applies the 15 Minute City urban planning model to major Defense Department bases in the US, ensuring they can operate independently of civilian infrastructure for a sustained period of time. That includes everything needed to support community life in addition to the supplies needed to sustain military operations.

FORTRESS America even goes beyond the initial 15 Minute City concept. As envisioned under the “Next Great American Base” element of the program, a central feature of the plan consists of access to a reliable source of on-site energy.

Don’t just take my word for it. “The program aligns basing and infrastructure projects to ensure they are collectively advancing toward greater independence,” Hegseth stated in the official order, with independence referring to the capability to sustain operations within a facility that is cut off from civilian resources. In other words, sustainable urban planning for military facilities.

Hegseth tasked the Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment to carry out the new order. The base design part of the order was passed along to Dale Marks, the Assistant Secretary for Energy, Installations, and Environment.

Marks did not let the 15 Minute City grass grow under his feet. In a public presentation on October 29, he emphasized the importance of building quality of life into a sustainable model for military facilities in the US.

“Let us build installations worthy of the warriors who call them home,” Marks emphasized. “The nation shouldn’t expect warfighters to focus on high stakes, multidomain operations when they come home to base housing with black mold, failing plumbing and leaky roofs.”

“Substandard living conditions are not minor inconveniences. They are an active drain on morale, combat readiness and our retention of top-tier talent,” Marks elaborated.

It’s not just a matter of rehabbing military housing. In the presentation, Marks made the case for a full blown 15 Minute City model. “The Next Great American Base will include a compact, walkable concept with premier schools, advanced healthcare and town centers that foster community,” Marks continued, neatly summing up the fundamentals of 15 Minute Cities in a nutshell.

Marks anticipates that state governors and other stakeholders will compete to see where the first “Next Great American Base” will be constructed. Once complete, the new facility, and its 15 Minute City, will serve as a model for future projects.

As for the on-site power generation angle, nuclear energy gets the pole position — for now. As Marks and Hegseth both emphasize, though, speed is of the essence. Results are demanded within months, if not weeks. That leaves plenty of room for solar-enabled microgrids to throw their hat into the FORTRESS America ring. After all, if speed-to-power is the name, solar and batteries are the game…

That means it can't be activated on the car. Soon, the complaint will be filed with the Korean Fair Trade Commission, a consumer protection agency, according to Reuters. Tesla will have to answer for why it marketed FSD to prospective buyers for years, even collecting the $6,726 lump-sum payment required for activation, even though it couldn't legally be used.

Currently, just 20% of Teslas registered in South Korea can legally use FSD because they're built in the U.S., according to a preliminary testimony given by Tesla Korea country manager Seo Young-deuk last month. Those specific cars meet U.S. vehicle-safety standards that South Korea recognizes as part of a free trade agreement. The thing is, most Teslas on the road in South Korea are manufactured in China, where no such agreement exists. It was only recently that Tesla started the process of obtaining FSD certification on China-made vehicles, even though it has been charging customers for the software for over three years.

Right now, it's not totally clear how many customers in South Korea bought FSD subscriptions on ineligible vehicles, but the automaker has sold over 170,000 China-made vehicles in the country since 2023, Reuters reports. The company continued to market FSD as sales of ineligible China-manufactured vehicles surged in South Korea in recent years, and last year, 99% of new Teslas sold in the country couldn't legally use FSD.

The complaint alleges that last year, Tesla promoted FSD as "coming soon" and posted a demonstration video filmed in South Korea without clearly disclosing that the tech could only be used in a tiny fraction of the vehicles it was selling, according to Reuters. The consumer advocacy group accused Tesla Korea of deceptive marketing and has asked the KFTC to issue a temporary cease-and-desist order on marketing FSD for ineligible vehicles, impose fines and refer the case to state investigators.

It may be an uphill battle, though. Just last month, a court in Seoul dismissed a lawsuit filed by Tesla owners seeking refunds for the FSD option, Reuters reports. The court rejected the claim that Tesla had failed to deliver the driver-assistance system. Instead, it put the onus of the issue on regulatory and legal restrictions that had limited the company's ability to roll out future functions.

#5711. Nabrawind’s Crane-Free Wind Towers Face a Supplier Test

Spain’s Nabrawind has developed a way to install exceptionally tall wind turbine towers without bringing an enormous crawler crane to the site. Its Nabralift system uses a tubular upper tower supported by a three-legged steel structure. Hydraulic equipment raises the assembled turbine while modular sections are inserted below it near ground level. The lifting frame can then be removed and used on another installation. This addresses genuine logistical and construction problems, particularly at remote sites where specialist cranes are expensive to transport and where wind can interrupt conventional lifting operations.

The company has progressed beyond demonstration-scale hardware. In September 2026, UL Solutions issued type certification for Envision’s 7.8 MW turbine on Nabrawind’s 188-meter tower. Fortescue is using 17 of those tower configurations at the 133 MW Nullagine wind project in Western Australia’s Pilbara region, where construction is underway. Nabrawind previously erected a 160-meter prototype in Spain in under two weeks and has supplied smaller commercial towers in Morocco and France.

The engineering benefits are credible. Nabrawind reports using roughly 20% less tower steel than comparable conventional tubular designs and reducing foundation concrete by as much as 80%, depending on the design and site. Those are supplier claims rather than independently established savings across all wind farms. The potential to avoid large cranes, simplify transport and raise turbines in windier conditions could also matter substantially to total installed cost and construction schedules. High hub heights only earn their keep when those costs are justified by the electricity generated over the project’s life.

The current deployment has an unusual commercial structure. Fortescue acquired Nabrawind in September 2025 and is building Nullagine to serve its own mining operations. Fortescue has the capital, internal electricity demand and industrial incentive to support a technology it owns. Successful installation in that context would be important evidence of construction performance, but it would not establish that an unrelated wind developer can finance and maintain the same system under ordinary third-party commercial arrangements.

Nabralift’s proprietary construction approach creates a procurement issue. Conventional tubular towers can be sourced from several qualified manufacturers, and experienced contractors can compete for much of their construction work. A developer selecting Nabralift currently depends on one supplier for the core tower system, specialist lifting knowledge and associated support. Wind turbine original-equipment manufacturers also create supplier dependencies, but concentrating another critical part of the project in a proprietary installation system requires its own contract and risk assessment.

A type certificate provides valuable technical assurance about the certified turbine-and-tower configuration. A lender or insurer still needs enforceable delivery schedules, long-term warranties, repair and maintenance provisions, clarity on replacement parts, and a workable remedy if the supplier’s capacity or commercial priorities change. These questions become more important when a wind farm must operate for 25 years or longer and there is no qualified alternative provider of the same system.

Nabrawind’s next important proof point is an independently developed and financed large wind farm that accepts those risks on commercial terms. Qualified installation partners, credible long-term service arrangements and greater competitive capacity could make its engineering advantages easier for developers to buy. The 188-meter tower has earned technical attention; its broader market depends on financing and procurement confidence catching up with the machinery.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Nabrawind’s self-erecting design, Fortescue’s Nullagine deployment and the supplier concentration that independent wind developers would have to manage. It follows my earlier assessment of 300-meter wind towers, where construction economics were the central challenge.

#5710. NASA's Swift Space Telescope Re-Enters Atmosphere With Five Times More Risk Of Casualties Than Anticipated

On Wednesday, NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a space telescope that's been in orbit since 2004, finally re-entered Earth's atmosphere above Indonesia. However, it appears to have done so with a risk of casualties five times beyond what NASA technical standards mandate. How and why this happened isn't immediately clear; NASA Public Affairs Specialist Alise Fisher told Jalopnik, "In the leadup to Swift's Nov. 20, 2004, launch, NASA determined the risk was consistent with mission requirements as allowed by agency policy." Somewhere between launch and reentry, that risk assessment shifted. It's unlikely that anybody made a specific mistake; this is probably the result of, well, space being hard. Still, it does highlight that our main defense against the detritus of astronomical ambitions is pure luck.

Swift is only crashing to Earth because it ran out of fuel to stay in orbit or adjust its trajectory. To NASA's credit, it did throw $30 million at a private company in an unprecedented attempt to rescue Swift with another satellite that would pull it back up into safe orbit. Sadly, the rescue satellite itself failed, dooming Swift to this fate.

In formal terms, Swift suffered an "uncontrolled reentry," which basically means it had no propulsion and just fell from space. NASA's own requirements, most recently updated in 2021 but going all the way back to 2001, state: "For uncontrolled reentry, the risk of human casualty from surviving debris shall be less than 0.0001 (1:10,000)." If you're not aware, there's no actual law requiring that satellites de-orbit in some sort of safe way that won't, you know, crash into a city or kill anyone. So our shield against the skies is just statistics. This is the threshold at which NASA feels the risk is acceptable. For reference, in all of history, just about 10,000 satellites have de-orbited, so... statistically we're due. And that was before we were putting tens of thousands of satellites up every few years.

In Swift's instance, however, NASA played its cards a little close to its chest. For one thing, it did not put out a risk assessment for the reentry, which is unusual. Then, in the middle of a longer announcement, the agency mentioned that Swift's risk of human casualties was actually "1 in 2,100." That's a risk of human injury or death five times beyond what it was meant to be.

Fortunately, the odds appear to have resolved in our favor. There are no reports of anyone being struck by space debris from Swift. Most of the satellite was expected to burn up during reentry; the trouble would come from whatever survived, likely dense pieces like the telescope lens or the reaction wheels. If any of those made it to the surface, there doesn't appear to have been a person around it.

That's a roll of the dice, though. At some point, as thousands of satellites de-orbit per year in our new megaconstellation era, laws should be passed to manage this formally. That would likely mean requiring controlled reentries, when the satellite still has a little fuel left to navigate to a safe spot out in the ocean. The other option, which companies like SpaceX have been pursuing, is to design the satellite to burn up entirely on reentry. The issue there is what effect all that vaporized metal might have on the atmosphere. Scientists don't yet know the answer, for the simple reason that there was never a reason to ask that question before. Now, the health of our planet may depend on it.

As space gets busier and busier, more and more will fall to us down here from up there. Up until now, the power of statistics has kept us safe. But eventually, a 1 in 10,000 chance is going to happen. Especially if some of those chances turn out to be riskier than intended.

#5707. Darolutamide Improves Metastasis-Free Survival in Very High-Risk Prostate Cancer

— Phase III DASL-HiCaP trial showed a 58% reduction in the risk of metastasis or death

Adding darolutamide (Nubeqa) to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and radiation therapy significantly improved metastasis-free survival in patients with very high-risk prostate cancer, according to findings from the phase III DASL-HiCaP trial presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology congress. At 4 years, the metastasis-free survival rate was 95% with darolutamide versus 88% with placebo.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, investigator Tamim Niazi, MDCM, of McGill University in Montreal, discusses the findings, including which patients may benefit most from treatment intensification, the safety results, and why he considers the data practice-changing.

Following is a transcript of his remarks:

So DASL-HiCaP, it was a phase III randomized trial assessing the role of the additional darolutamide to 24 months of androgen deprivation therapy plus a locoregional radiation therapy for patients who are at DASL very high risk, so specifically selected patients who are very high risk based on DASL criteria. We'll talk about this in a minute or two.

But what this study actually showed for these patients who are at a very high risk of recurrence and relapse is that adding darolutamide increased the metastasis-free survival by conventional imaging. It's important, it's not by PSMA [prostate-specific membrane antigen], it's by conventional imaging at 4 years, from 88% in the placebo arm to 95% in the darolutamide arm, with a hazard ratio of 0.48. That is a 58% risk reduction in favor of darolutamide.

So how we define very high risk in DASL-HiCaP is not the usual high risk and not the same thing as STAMPEDE very high risk.

For patients who had prostate in place for primary radiation therapy, the very high risk was defined as either grade group 5, Gleason 9-10, or pelvic lymph node disease. Any of those would've made participants eligible. And for participants who had a grade group 4, meaning Gleason 8, they had to have an additional risk factor, either a clinical T2b or higher, a PSA [prostate-specific antigen] more than 20, or radiological T3a or higher.

On the other hand, for patients who had salvage radiation therapy after radical prostatectomy, those patients had to have their PSA either persistent after surgery, meaning having not gone to zero or rising within 12 months to a 0.1 or higher. They would've been eligible to participate as long as they met the eligibility criteria, either a grade group 5 with a Gleason 9 or 10 of course, or pathological or clinical pelvic lymph node positive. Similar to primary radiation therapy, patients in salvage were also eligible if they had grade group 4, and were also eligible if they had an additional risk of pathological T3a or higher.

But to us, it is a more higher-risk patient population compared to other studies, for example, ENZARAD, but not STAMPEDE.

Both groups received the contemporary doses of radiation therapy and hormonal therapy, higher doses of 78 Gy and higher in primary setting, 64 Gy and higher in salvage setting. And of course the pelvic radiation therapy was mandated in the study.

So the standard treatment was given very well to the contemporary stage, and then it was for darolutamide to show an improvement. So it did. It decreased the risk of metastasis by 58%. To me, I think it is practice-changing and it definitely defines a new path for patients who are at a very high risk of recurrence.

Not only did it significantly improve metastasis-free survival, the adverse events were pretty similar between the two groups. Specifically, there was no additional cardiovascular toxicity by adding darolutamide. It was almost identical between the two groups. And furthermore, the addition of darolutamide to locoregional radiation therapy did not cause new emergent toxicity when it comes into a combination of treatment in this investigation.

#5704. Shorter Days and Dark Afternoons Can Trigger Depression

— Scientists are trying to understand what causes SAD

As winter approaches and daylight hours grow shorter, people prone to seasonal depression can feel it in their bodies and brains.

The millions of people estimated to have seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, typically have episodes of depression that begin in the fall and ease in the spring or summer. One trigger for SAD is when clocks revert to standard time, which happened Sunday across much of the U.S., bringing darker afternoons. A milder form, subsyndromal SAD, is recognized by medical experts, and there's also a summer variety of seasonal depression, though less is known about it.

In 1984, a team led by Norman Rosenthal, MD, then a researcher at the NIH, first described SAD and coined the term. "I believe that because it is easy to remember, the acronym has stuck," he said.

Scientists Are Trying to Understand What Causes SAD

No single cause for seasonal affective disorder has been identified. The disorder affects many more women than men, according to the NIH. Symptoms can be similar to depression, and can include persistent feelings of hopelessness or pessimism and difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions.

In one effort to better understand what's going on, scientists are learning how specialized cells in our eyes turn the blue wavelength part of the light spectrum into neural signals affecting mood and alertness.

Sunlight is loaded with the blue light, so when the cells absorb it, our brains' alertness centers are activated and we feel more wakeful and possibly even happier.

Researcher Kathryn Roecklein, PhD, at the University of Pittsburgh, tested people with and without SAD to see how their eyes reacted to blue light. As a group, people with SAD were less sensitive to blue light than others, especially during winter months. That suggests one possible cause for wintertime depression.

When Days Get Shorter, Powerful Light Can Help

Many people with SAD respond to light therapy, said Paul Desan, MD, PhD, of Yale University's Winter Depression Research Clinic in New Haven, Connecticut. The therapy can involve exposure to bright light for about a half hour in the morning, powered by devices that emit light about 20 times brighter than regular indoor light.

Research supports using a light that's about 10,000 lux, a measure of brightness. You need to use it for 30 minutes every morning, according to the research. Desan said this can help not only people with SAD but also those with less-severe winter blahs.

Special lights run from $50 to more than $400. Some products marketed for SAD are too dim to do much good, Desan said.

Yale has tested products and offers a list of recommendations, and the nonprofit Center for Environmental Therapeutics has a consumer guide to selecting a light.

If your doctor diagnosed you with SAD, check with your insurance company to see if the cost of a light might be covered.

Talk Therapy and Medication Can Also Help Some With SAD

Antidepressant medications are a first-line treatment for SAD, along with light therapy. Doctors also recommend keeping a regular sleep schedule and walking outside, even on cloudy days.

Light therapy's benefits can fade when people stop using it. Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, has been shown in studies to have more durable effects, said Kelly Rohan, PhD, of the University of Vermont in Burlington.

Working with a therapist can help people take small steps toward having fun again, Rohan said. Those with SAD should try planning undemanding but enjoyable activities to break out of hibernation mode, including getting out and seeing a friend for coffee.

Tribeca took the crown for the hottest neighborhood in Manhattan luxury sales last week, nabbing the top two priciest sales in the borough.

The lower West Side neighborhood, which John F. Kennedy Jr. and his bride, Carolyn Bessette, did much to make famous, has continued to push toward the Hudson River with new luxury residential skyscapers.

Last week's top two sales were coincidentally on the same street, with contracts signed at 111 Murray St. and 71 Murray St. Both were penthouse condos.

"I like to call it 'Tribeca lite,'" says Brown Harris Stevens agent Lisa K. Lippman, who has long represented real estate in the neighborhood. "It's not prime Tribeca."

The broker says "prime" Tribeca would be around the the area of Duane and North Moore Street. (JFK Jr. and Carolyn lived in 20 North Moore St.)

But as prime Tribeca filled up, development spread east and west—with the western edge closer to sweeping river views, as well as the Hudson River Greenway bike path and all of the riverfront parks and piers.

"The area feels less residential," she tells Realtor.com of Murray Street and the surrounding streets, which are packed with glass skyscrapers. "There's always people who want to be on a higher floor, have a lot of amenities, but pay a little less."

The top sale for the week ending Nov. 1 was Penthouse One at 111 Murray St., with an asking price of $33.95 million. The penthouse, inside a 64-story tower built in 2018 and designed by architect David Mann, was a sponsor sale.

The sprawling, extra-large unit—at 7,675 square feet with five bedrooms and 6.5 bedrooms—was snapped up by Richard Saghian, the founder and chief executive of Fashion Nova, for $31 million, according to multiple reports.

According to Forbes, the 45-year-old fashion mogul is worth $2.1 billion and is the No. 1,900–ranked richest person in the world.

The penthouse will be added to his growing property portfolio, which includes a $141 million Bel-Air mansion and two Miami Beach properties: a $30 million double lot and a $32 million estate.

His latest acquisition offers 360-degree views of New York Harbor, as well as 233 square feet of private terraces with which to enjoy them.

The sweeping river views really helped move the property, says listing agent Emily Sertic of Douglas Elliman, who has headed up sales in the building since its launch.

"You'll capture a glimpse of Central Park, the Empire State Building, all the historic bridges, the rivers, and the harbor," she says. "From its view line only, it really encompasses an incredible experience of New York. Everywhere you turn, there are these astonishing view lines that just go on and on."

"The view line and the grandeur of the space for entertaining was really important," she says of what helped attract the billionaire buyer, who was represented by Ryan and Emilia Serhant of Serhant.

The great room alone is over 2,000 square feet, says the broker, and boasts an eat-in kitchen, butler's pantry, and private terrace.

"Whether it's for work, entertainment, guests, or family, the bedrooms were a huge draw to the space," she says.

Saghian, the college dropout son of Iranian immigrants, is reportedly single with no children.

The fast-fashion mogul appears to appreciate a real estate deal—creditors of his Bel-Air mansion originally wanted $295 million at auction and a judge had to approve the sale because of the relatively low price it ended up fetching. And the Tribeca penthouse originally asked for $50 million back in September 2025.

"It has all the features that any trophy buyer is looking for," says Sertic.

Some of those features fit for a billionaire include a chef's kitchen with Wolf, Miele, and Sub-Zero appliances, dual fridges and dishwashers, a 60-inch custom gas cooktop, multiple ovens, and a full-height wine refrigerator.

The full-service luxury building contains the usual array of amenities one would expect at this price point.

There is a 24/7 door attendant, concierge service, and valet team; a full-service wellness center and spa complete with hammam, treatment rooms, and a 75-foot lap pool with private cabanas; a fitness center; a children's playroom with splash pad, and a teen arcade room. There's also a private dining room, screening room, and landscaped garden.

The penthouse comes with a $36,000 monthly fee, including HOA dues and taxes.

The second top sale of last week was also on Murray Street. The glass-walled triplex penthouse at 71 Murray St. is a four-bedroom, 4.5-bath unit with a price tag of $18.5 million.

Listed by Jeremy V. Stein of Sotheby's International Realty, the sprawling 6,700-square-foot condo included an astonishing 3,148-square feet of terraces, including two roof terraces decked out for entertaining with a full Viking kitchen, fire pit, and dining area. There is also a floating glass staircase and 36-foot climbing wall.

Topping a boutique building with only 12 residences, the penthouse has monthly common charges and taxes totaling $17,232.

The two downtown top sales aren't that unusual—the former warehouse district has been trendy since the late Kennedy scion took up residence there in the early 1990s. (Actor Robert DeNiro—who moved there in 1981—can truly claim pioneer status.)

Sertic says the typical neighborhood buyers tend to be "youngish buyers and their families" who work in the surrounding neighborhoods, especially the Financial District.

"A lot of our buyers walk to work," she says. "They are high-performing and fast-moving, so convenience is huge."

Despite Tribeca nabbing the top two sales, it was the Upper East Side that pulled the most luxury (over $4 million) contracts again this week. Of the 34 contracts signed, the UES dominated with the highest amount of sales for the 10th time this year.

As is usual, condos outsold co-ops, 17 to 12. However, with only five sales between them, co-ops are holding their own.

The upward sales trajectory of co-ops—where buyers tend to be subject to a rigorous board approval process—is likely the effect of luxury inventory being so slim, say experts.

It also probably helps that co-ops often trade lower than condos, with an average ask of $6.48 million versus $10.44 million for condos, according to Olshan Realty.

The most expensive co-op of the week was a new build, constructed in 2023. The Lenox Hill penthouse at 200 East 75th St. had an asking price of $16.85 million.

Kiri Blakeley writes about trending news at Realtor.com. She has also worked at Forbes Magazine, Forbes.com, CafeMom, and DailyMail.com, covering everything from billionaires to celebrities to crime. Her work can be found in news outlets worldwide, including Yahoo, SF Gate, New York Post, Seattle-Post Intelligencer, Marie Claire, She Knows, Huffington Post, and New York Magazine. She has an M.A. in journalism from Columbia University. In her spare time, she writes psychological thrillers under a pen name. She lives in Brooklyn, and her cat foster Instagram account has over 4 million views.

#5702. Pascal Tricuspid TEER Handed Soft Victory in 'Hamstrung' CLASP II TR Trial

— Pascal Precision device was recently approved by the FDA

The Pascal Precision transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) system eked out a win in symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) in its pivotal randomized trial.

In CLASP II TR, there was significant clinical improvement among patients randomized to tricuspid valve TEER plus optimal medical therapy, as opposed to medical therapy alone, in a hierarchical analysis counting all-cause death, right ventricular assist device implantation or heart transplant, tricuspid valve intervention, number of heart failure (HF) hospitalizations, and overall health status.

This primary endpoint produced a win ratio of 1.98 favoring the Pascal Precision (95% CI 1.47-2.67), reported Charles Davidson, MD, of Northwestern Memorial Hospital in Chicago, at the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics (TCT) annual conference hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation.

The TEER benefit was driven by 6-month health status improvement alone: Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) scores were on average over 10 points higher in the device group compared with controls, according to co-trialist Suzanne Arnold, MD, MHA, of Saint Luke's Mid America Heart Institute in Kansas City, Missouri, speaking alongside Davidson.

"The CLASP II TR trial demonstrates safety and efficacy of the Pascal system to improve health status in symptomatic patients with [severe or greater] TR," the study authors concluded.

The efficacy results were not what the authors had originally hoped for, however, as CLASP II TR was initially designed for a 24-month primary endpoint -- only later revised to 6 months due to control group attrition to commercial therapy following FDA approval of the Evoque tricuspid valve replacement system and the TriClip G4 TEER device in 2024.

Still, it was on the basis of this study that the Pascal Precision recently got FDA approval for tricuspid valve repair. Initially, the device had entered the market for mitral TEER in 2022.

Co-investigator and TCT panelist Rebecca Hahn, MD, of NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center in New York City, maintained that despite the "hamstrung" analyses in CLASP II TR, "it does in the end add to the literature supporting the treatment of these patients with [tricuspid] TEER."

Indeed, CLASP II TR marks the fourth trial (after TRILUMINATE, Tri.Fr, and TRIC-I-HF) to show superiority of tricuspid valve repair over medical therapy, especially concerning patient-reported outcomes, noted Jörg Hausleiter, MD, of Klinikum Der Universitat Munchen in Germany, the study discussant at TCT.

In fact, Hausleiter's TRIC-I-HF study had the distinction of being the landmark study showing that, among the selected population of sicker people with severe TR at high risk for future HF events, transcatheter tricuspid intervention reduced all-cause death and HF hospitalization while improving quality of life.

Davidson and Arnold reported that their trial was also able to give tricuspid TEER the edge for proportion of patients alive with ≥20-point improvements in the KCCQ overall score at 6 months (38.8% vs 12.3%, P<0.001), as well as the proportion alive with more modest ≥10-point improvements in KCCQ (57.1% vs 25.4%, P<0.001). Additionally, those achieving moderate or better TR at 1 year came out to 80% with the device versus 30% with only medical therapy.

For the TEER recipients, the composite safety event rate reached 6.9% at 30 days and 20.1% at 1 year. Among the most frequent events were single leaflet device attachment (3.4% and 4.8%, respectively), severe bleeding (3.1% and 8.5%), and cardiovascular mortality (0.3% and 5.4%).

"I think it's important to help people feel better," said Patrick O'Gara, MD, of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston, also a panelist at TCT. "If patients are feeling better, it's a good outcome provided the procedure is safe and is provided by people who are expert in its implementation."

"In some ways, we should be cautious, we need to temper expectations ... There are huge gaps between expectations and the reality of what we're able to achieve," O'Gara told the audience.

The CLASP II TR trial, conducted in the U.S. and Canada, had participants with severe-or-worse TR randomized to Pascal Precision TEER with medical therapy (n=294) or medical therapy alone (n=148).

The cohort averaged about 80 years old, with just under half being women. Nearly 60% had New York Heart Association class III-IV symptoms. STS-PROM (for mitral valve repair) scores were about 7.5%. Approximately one in four people had a HF hospitalization in the past 12 months.

TR etiology was largely secondary (over 75%) and most commonly graded as severe (58%) as opposed to massive or torrential.

The authors reported that 92.5% of the treatment arm got the device implanted successfully. This group was roughly split between those who got one and two devices.

Davidson and Arnold noted that their open-label trial left room for a placebo effect. Participating centers and operators also generally had limited prior experience with the Pascal system, they added.

One important remaining question is when operators should intervene on TR.

During a press conference, Roxana Mehran, MD, of Mount Sinai Hospital in New York City, stressed the importance of the heart team and the fact that in the U.S., tricuspid TEER is still covered with evidence development. The expectation is that TVT registry data will continue to accrue to show who is the right patient at the right time for tricuspid TEER, she suggested.

The TVT registry has the downside of being single-arm, Arnold noted, but she agreed that it will still be helpful for providing long-term data.

#5701. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.
