#5700. Post-midterms, hospitals still face a long road to policy relief, advisers warn

Post-midterms, hospitals still face a long road to policy relief, advisers warn" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hospitals facing major policy headwinds won’t be able to sustain operations through cost cutting or revenue protections alone, and they shouldn’t bank on immediate political relief following this week’s midterm results, BRG policy and health system operations consultants warn.

Health systems across the country have been gearing up for the years-long rollout of Medicare and Medicaid policy changes from 2025’s H.R. 1, whose standout changes, such as Medicaid work requirements and state-directed payment restrictions, will begin in earnest on Jan. 1. The implementation is expected to reduce the number of patients with coverage and limit supplemental payments to providers, compounding challenges they’re already facing this year after expired Affordable Care Act subsidies pushed many patients off marketplace coverage.

“I’m generally an optimist as [my] personality, but the quote that comes to me is ‘It can never be so bad that it can’t get worse,” David Wildebrandt, a managing director in BRG’s healthcare practice, said during a Thursday media roundtable on federal policy takeaways for healthcare providers. “It’s really very troubling, the cumulative toll of everything that’s happening, because health systems have an incredibly difficult ecosystem in general in terms of capacity constraints, payer mix, softer volumes.”

Those headwinds will land amid a midterm election in which healthcare issues are top items for voters. Reversing or hobbling H.R. 1 has emerged as a priority for Democratic candidates and party leaders, promises that would have no small impact on hospitals hoping for a financial lifeline.

“I do think the biggest ticket item here for the next couple of years is how One Big Beautiful Bill Act implementation goes, how states respond and whether or not Congress tries to have a say by potentially trying to amend that bill in the first couple of years,” John Barkett, managing director in BRG’s Healthcare Transactions and Strategy practice, and formerly an advisor on the White House Domestic Policy Council, said. “It's not uncommon for big bills, including Obamacare or Medicare or any other big bill, to be amended within a couple of years of passage.”

In a scenario where Democrats take both the House (currently considered very likely by pollsters) and the Senate (more of a toss-up), BRG’s healthcare practice advisors said they anticipate a slew of new congressional oversight and investigations into health agencies and some of the organizations they’d cut deals with in recent years. And even if they can’t get a partisan health bill signed into law, there’s still room to write and pass bills that could become new policy in a future majority, as was the case with Medicaid work requirements pushed by Republicans during the end of the Biden administration but ultimately codified last year.

As for the OBBBA, the BRG consultants acknowledged that revisions to the sweeping Medicaid changes are possible, but pointed out the steep hill they’d need to climb.

“President Trump will still be president, and he will view a policy that amends the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in favor of hospitals as a concession to Democrats—and therefore, he’ll be looking for something in return,” Barkett said. “And so the question will be—how big is the ask for what the Trump administration would want in return for amending a signature law … and what he’s asking for would have to be palatable for Democrats. And that’s where I think there’s a lot of uncertainty right now.”

“Providers shouldn’t really plan on relief coming from Washington in that way,” Dave Brueggeman, another managing director in BRG’s healthcare practice, said of an OBBBA amendment and a potential swift return of marketplace subsidies.

Barkett noted that second-term, lame duck presidents tend to look at their legacy as lawmaking grinds to a halt. That could make Trump and his administration “even more emboldened to take action through [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid] rulemaking,” he said.

“The question I’m thinking about is—what signals is the president giving about what he wants his legacy to be on healthcare in the last couple of years,” he said. “I’m not sure that anyone who’s saying they know what that is necessarily has the mind of the president. I think it could go in several directions, and it’s particularly interesting given that the Supreme Court … has been constricting what an executive branch can do when they’re thinking creatively about how to interpret statutes.”

Should Republicans maintain control of The Hill, Barkett said the industry should expect a continuation of the policy agenda from the past two years—reduced coverage, lower spending and deference to regulatory agencies—with “maybe some bipartisan work going on,” such as pharmacy benefit manager reforms from earlier this year.

“The bottom line here is that revenue pressure from the OBBBA isn't a one-year problem,” said Brueggeman. “It builds over the next decade, and the systems that come out of it in best shape will be the ones that start adjusting the revenue and cost strategies now.”

The policy landscape is unprecedented ground for management teams that, likely for the first time in their careers, are facing a year in which overall health insurance coverage isn't increasing.

Wildebrandt's chief advice, based on best practices BRG is seeing among big names like HCA Healthcare and Tenet Healthcare, is to cut through the unknowns and develop a financial exposure plan with “very sophisticated predictions of what's going to happen with charity care, uncompensated care, the amount of uninsured, EBITDA forecasts."

“The one thing I would certainly want to impress upon everyone is [that] it is different for every hospital. You cannot use a blanket statement,” he said of the policy impacts going into effect. Such predictions “really create a true north for everyone to look at. […] Some of the systems that are doing that, it’s been very much an awakening event.”

The immediate next priority, Wildebrandt said, is for systems to model and protect enrollment among patients who will still be eligible for coverage after January’s work requirements implementation deadline, for instance by “standing up outreach centers to help with the documentation and the education of the work requirements.” Brueggeman similarly raised red flags over yet-to-be-shared state guidance on how the changes could impact Medicaid presumptive eligibility, and noted that many BRG hospital clients are reviewing their collections and self-pay and charity care policies amid an expectation of increased payment difficulties.

From there, health systems will need to begin ramping up their cost optimization and strategic realignment, likely to a greater extent than what they’ve already pursued over the past year.

“What we share with our clients and folks that are really getting ahead of this is another 5% to 7% of cost reduction on top of what they're already doing,” he said. “And that really gets you into deeper areas beyond labor, beyond supply chain. What we're working on mostly is a transformational roadmap.”

The chief opportunities here, he said, involve integrated care models and leaning into many of the skills systems developed under risk-based arrangements to direct patients to community providers or other lower-cost settings when possible.

“We’ll likely see an explosion of growth in partnerships with FQHCs and other community organizations to get folks into the right care setting and reduce unnecessary utilization,” he said. “And another important area, one we’ve honestly given some lip service to over time, is partnering to expand ambulatory access and, again, reduce preventable hospital use.”

Wildebrandt described these efforts as requiring “structural changes” addressing “fixed costs, and not just working into variable costs.” That means taking a hard look at what’s currently on offer.

“We see many organizations assessing their portfolio, looking at service rationalization—especially big systems that have integrated and have redundant OB units within the same perimeter,” he said. “You'll see more Centers of Excellence coming out of this, which will decrease access, but consolidating services, OB, pediatric intensive care units, and other non-core programs like post-acute rehab. … You’re seeing folks also spinning things off, spinning hospitals off, spinning service lines off. So definitely a lot of activity in this space.”

Leaders from major nonprofit health systems who were on the panel agreed. Matt Brown, president of CommonSpirit Health’s South Region, said it’s become more routine to hear of cost-conscious systems targeting stiffer benchmarks for their labor spending—salary, wages and benefits expenses below 45% of patient service revenue, “when 15 years ago under 60% was appropriate."

He and Gail Kosyla, chief financial officer at AtlantiCare, also acknowledged that nonprofits are already weighing options on service lines that are losing money for the system, noting that providers could mitigate the impact on patient access by partnering with another community provider already offering the same services.

“Those are difficult decisions, and they really go to patient need, community need, as well as that financial component,” Kosyla said during the roundtable.

With the scope of headwinds to come, panelists agreed that cost management alone won't close the gap without corresponding efforts to protect revenue.

Brueggeman said his team has been working “every day” on an “explosive growth” in termination planning, as providers negotiating new network agreements with payers are increasingly willing to play chicken in order to maximize revenue. Should those disputes come to a head, a hospital’s network exit could mean reduced access to care for local patients.

Brueggeman noted that the contentious negotiations have recently lost a natural common ground. Risk-based arrangements with shared upsides and downsides have become less appealing to providers due to a “lack of ability to specifically predict what those outcomes would look like,” with the policy changes, he said. “That creates a significant tension against what was, at one time, considered an outlet in these negotiations of creating a shared responsibility around risk. It's creating a little bit of a dam in that process.”

CommonSpirit’s Brown was up front about the need to go toe-to-toe, and the benefits for doing so.

“We’re doing everything we can with payers to understand how we maximize our reimbursement,” he said. “That means draconian things at times. We’ve had markets go out of network with Medicare Advantage providers. And we’ve gotten back in recently—specifically a community in Texas. We went out for a while and then came back in as a national player.”

“We have to do everything we can to leverage our scale in negotiations with payers—and with states to ensure that we don't get hit with provider fee problems in places like Kentucky, Colorado and California to the level that H.R. 1 projects,” he added.

#5699. Abdakibart Shows Strong Early Efficacy in Hidradenitis Suppurativa

— Phase II LOTUS data suggest IL-1 beta inhibition could become an important new approach

Phase II findings presented at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology meeting in Vienna showed promising early efficacy with abdakibart, an investigational interleukin (IL)-1 beta inhibitor, in patients with hidradenitis suppurativa (HS).

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Martina J. Porter, MD, of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, discusses the week-16 LOTUS trial results, including Hidradenitis Suppurativa Clinical Response 75 (HiSCR75) rates, early separation from placebo, the study's safety profile, and what the findings may mean as the drug moves into phase III.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

I was fortunate to present the phase II findings for the abdakibart study, which was by Avalo Therapeutics. Abdakibart is an IL-1 beta inhibitor. And what we showed was the week-16 or the primary endpoint results for the study. And this was one of the largest studies that we've seen for phase II to date. There were over 240 patients, about 80 in each arm, and there were two different abdakibart doses and then a placebo group.

The key point here was that HiSCR75, which is our higher depth of response, it was about 43% of patients in both of the dosing arms that achieved HiSCR75 compared to about 25% of placebo patients. And this is one of the highest, I would say, efficacy endpoints that we've seen to date for any HS phase II study. And I think it really validates that this is a novel mechanism that will probably be involved in treating HS going forward.

And I think some of the other important things, too, that we found were that there was actually quite an early split between the drug arms and the placebo group. So even as early as week 4, there was a difference in almost all the endpoints that we were talking about for the study.

Also for the 16 weeks, there were almost no safety findings at all for this IL-1 beta, which is actually very promising. A lot of times we get really concerned about HS patients, who have so many comorbidities, but there weren't any increased infection risks, for example. There were some injection site reactions, but they happened across all the groups, both the placebo and the abdakibart arms, to the same degree. And the most common side effects that we saw were things that are probably unlikely related to the drug, like headaches. So I think in terms of safety profiles, which are really important to dermatologists, this was quite clean for the 16 weeks.

So I think the important implications of this is that we'll see this molecule move into phase III and we'll also be able to see over a longer-term period -- so not just 16 weeks -- how it performs. And historically for all of our drugs in HS, we really like to see key differentiation and efficacy endpoints and clean safety profiles at week 16. But as we know for HS in general, it's also a lot about how these patients do long term at 6 months and 12 months and even longer because a lot of the times what we see is continued improvement in their disease severity over these periods, especially after we move out of the placebo response.

#5697. How MRD is powering the next wave of precision oncology

How MRD is powering the next wave of precision oncology" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cancer care is shifting beyond the detection of visible disease. A new generation of molecular residual disease, or MRD, testing can detect tiny traces of ctDNA that may remain during or after treatment, offering an additional way to identify disease when traditional approaches may not yet reveal it. Dr. Rick Baehner, Divisional Vice President, Chief Medical Officer, Precision Oncology, Abbott cancer diagnostics, explores why MRD represents the next chapter of precision oncology and how the next-generation Oncodetect® test could help move cancer care from reactive treatment toward more proactive monitoring.In this video interview with Kelly Hogan of Fierce Healthcare, Baehner explains how MRD testing can provide molecular insights into some of oncology's most pressing questions: Is treatment working? Is cancer truly gone? Has disease returned? He also explores why sensitivity is critical, particularly when tumor burden is low, including in low-shedding cancers and as ctDNA levels fall during and after treatment. Baehner explores the science behind whole-genome sequencing-based MRD tests and looks ahead to what broader adoption could mean for oncology workflows, clinical decision-making and patient outcomes. As MRD testing becomes more integrated into everyday care, he argues that cancer monitoring may become as individualized as cancer treatment itself. Watch the interview to learn why the next era of oncology may be defined not only by how we treat cancer, but by how quickly and intelligently we anticipate its return.

#5696. Justin Baldoni Discreetly Sells Former Los Angeles Home for $2.1 Million After Making a ‘Fresh Start’ in Nashville

Actor Justin Baldoni discreetly offloaded his former Los Angeles home months after relocating to Nashville, TN, for a “fresh start.”

The three-bedroom, three-bathroom Culver City abode went for $2.1 million in an off-market transaction in August, according to Page Six. The 1,992-square-foot house was built in 1952 and sits on a 5,736-square-foot lot.

“He hasn’t lived there in years,” a People magazine source said. “The family has been living in Nashville for a bit now, but they moved to Ojai before that.”

The “It Ends With Us” director and his wife, Emily Baldoni, reportedly bought the home in 2017.

In an October 2020 People magazine interview, the couple opened up about life in the “urban farmhouse.”

The Baldonis said they invited loved ones to visit the home to write prayers and affirmations on its exposed wooden beams after completing a nine-month renovation.

“In the beams of the house is literally love,” Justin said.

The home had a host of interesting features, including a climbing wall in the garage for their children, Maiya and Maxwell.

There was also a built-in Wolf coffee machine and a top-of-the line Kohler toilet the actor compared to a “Transformer.”

While Emily shared that the plumbing feature “takes care of everything,” Justin noted that the family “didn’t panic as much as some others when all the toilet paper disappeared.”

The sale of the Los Angeles property isn’t the only quiet real estate move Justin, 42, has made this year.

Property records indicate that he listed his sprawling Ojai, CA, compound for $8.88 million on Feb. 5. The listing came just days after a rental listing for the same property—which was asking $40,000 a month—was taken down.

The estate, which the couple purchased for $2.2 million in 2020, has since been taken off the market.

The five-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom dwelling on a 10-acre lot in the picturesque neighborhood of Santa Paula was described by Emily as a “magical place” in a 2023 Architectural Digest interview.

Inspired by their trips abroad, the couple went to lengths to design “the whole house with feng shui in mind,” a practice inspired by his mother, “who’s done it for 30 years.”

“When we went to Tulum and parts of Mexico, we would take pictures of lamps or couches—just as inspiration—and then we started to put together a Pinterest board of things that we liked,” he said.

The couple made a series of upgrades to the home to create a “sanctuary.” According to the since-removed listing, the home was outfitted with “a state-of-the-art medical-grade air filtration system,” electromagnetic frequency shielding around the primary bedroom, a saltwater pool, and a “regenerative orchard.”

It also included a hot tub, sport court, custom-designed gym, LED-lit in-ground trampoline, koi pond with waterfall, fire pit, and walking paths.

Additional technological amenities included EV charging stations, a state-of-the-art security system, and fire mitigation systems.

The family packed their bags for Tennessee in December 2025, amid the highly publicized legal drama Justin was involved in after actress Blake Lively sued in 2024, claiming he had sexually harassed her during the filming of “It Ends with Us.”

“It’s obviously been an incredibly difficult time for the whole family, but Nashville has given them a fresh start,” a People magazine source previously shared.

After denying the allegations, Justin filed a $400 million countersuit against Lively and her husband, Ryan Reynolds, her publicist Leslie Sloane, and Sloane’s PR firm, citing defamation and breach of contract.

The suit was later dismissed by a judge, as were Lively’s sexual harassment claims. The actress later pursued allegations of retaliation against Justin, as well as his production company and publicity team.

Justin and Lively reached a private settlement days before the case was due to go to trial in May 2026.

However, the dispute continued when Lively sought $8 million in legal fees from Justin. She was awarded a total of $407,451.75 in an Aug. 26 order.

In July, when the dispute was still ongoing, the Baldonis posted an Instagram Reel to address the situation for the first time.

“We have not spoken publicly for the better part of the last two years, and it’s not because we haven’t had anything to say,” Justin said. “It just felt like every time we went to make a video like this, we wanted to speak, something was telling us not to. It just didn’t feel like the right time, and we were talking about it and feeling into it and praying about it.”

While Justin kept his statement fairly vague and never named Lively, the couple did share that they had experienced a lot of “trauma.”

"What I will say is that there have been so many painful things that have been spoken into existence over the last couple of years,” he said. “That created so much noise, and we didn’t want to add to the noise. So we just wanted to let the justice system run its course."

The couple noted that they had “so much more to say,” but that they were “going to focus on continuing the healing” and “hanging out” with their “kiddos and enjoying life.”

According to the New York Post, the family’s new Nashville home is a $3.4 million newly built abode. The six-bedroom, six-bathroom property spans 7,000 square feet and is situated on an acre lot.

Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5694. Cancer Vaccines Show Promise. But We Have More Work to Do.

— A look at how individualized cancer vaccines may fit into a complex treatment landscape

The controversy surrounding the premature disclosure of Moderna and Merck's mRNA melanoma vaccine results risks overshadowing a more consequential clinical discussion: how individualized cancer vaccines might fit into an increasingly effective and increasingly complex treatment landscape.

The results are very encouraging. Reducing recurrence and distant metastases by adding a treatment with a new mechanism to an effective checkpoint inhibitor represent meaningful progress. Our work now is to determine which patients benefit, how vaccination should be sequenced with other treatments, and whether its promise extends beyond melanoma.

In INTerpath-001, which randomized 1,137 patients with completely resected stage IIB–IV melanoma, results presented at ESMO showed 2-year recurrence-free survival of 82.2% with the mRNA-based cancer vaccine intismeran autogene plus pembrolizumab (Keytruda) versus 70% with placebo plus pembrolizumab. The absolute difference was 12.2 percentage points; the hazard ratio was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.45-0.75). At a median follow-up of 24.6 months, an overall survival benefit had not been demonstrated.

Preventing recurrence has clinical value. It can spare patients further treatment and morbidity. But not all patients benefited from the intervention, and these findings do not establish efficacy across other cancers.

The biological rationale behind intismeran autogene is compelling. Personalized mRNA vaccines encode tumor-specific neoantigens that antigen-presenting cells process and present to prime and expand tumor-reactive T cells. PD-1 blockade complements this response by reducing inhibitory signaling that limits T-cell activity. Vaccination may therefore broaden tumor-directed immunity while checkpoint inhibition supports its function. INTerpath-001 demonstrates the benefit of adding vaccination to pembrolizumab; without a vaccine-only arm, it cannot formally establish synergy.

This approach brings together tumor sequencing, computational antigen selection, mRNA delivery, and immunotherapy. Yet a predicted neoantigen is not necessarily an effective immune target. Translational studies must clarify which responses control the cancer clones responsible for recurrence.

The vaccine discussion also needs to account for progress in neoadjuvant immunotherapy. In SWOG S1801, beginning pembrolizumab before surgery improved event-free survival compared with administering it entirely afterward. In NADINA, neoadjuvant nivolumab-ipilimumab followed by surgery and response-directed postoperative therapy improved event-free survival compared with surgery followed by nivolumab (Opdivo).

These advances make sequencing a central research question. Could vaccination improve outcomes after neoadjuvant immunotherapy? Might patients without a major pathological response have the greatest need? Conversely, could patients with a major response avoid additional treatment?

INTerpath-001 does not answer these questions. Nor can cross-trial comparisons, as populations, endpoints, and treatment strategies differ. The neoadjuvant question is particularly relevant to patients with clinically apparent, resectable stage III disease; it should not obscure the vaccine findings in other patients represented in the trial.

We need studies that integrate advances in treatment rather than simply accumulate postoperative therapies. Residual disease after checkpoint inhibition also does not necessarily imply vaccine sensitivity. That hypothesis requires testing.

Beyond melanoma, our optimism must remain tempered by the evidence. Tumors differ in antigen availability, antigen presentation, immune infiltration, and mechanisms of immune suppression. Still, early findings justify investigation and enthusiasm. A phase I pancreatic cancer study demonstrated persistent vaccine-induced T-cell responses in some patients receiving an individualized mRNA vaccine alongside atezolizumab and chemotherapy. Immune responders had longer recurrence-free survival than nonresponders.

This establishes biological activity, not that vaccination improves outcomes in pancreatic cancer. The study was small, lacked a randomized control group, and compared patients according to their immune response. A randomized trial is evaluating the combination more rigorously.

Patient selection deserves similar discipline. Pathological response and circulating tumor DNA are attractive candidates for refining postoperative decisions. But identifying patients at higher risk of recurrence is different from identifying those more likely to benefit from vaccination. Biomarker-guided treatment strategies require prospective evaluation.

Delivery is another clinical endpoint in practice. In INTerpath-001, vaccine production was successful for more than 99% of patients assigned to intismeran, an encouraging feasibility result. Median time to the first vaccine dose was 64 days. That interval is not simply a manufacturing-time estimate, but it makes treatment coordination -- and the feasibility of preoperative vaccination -- important research questions.

Safety also requires attention. Grade 3-5 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 14.2% of patients receiving intismeran plus pembrolizumab versus 13.4% of those receiving pembrolizumab alone. However, all-cause adverse events led to discontinuation of any study drug in 16.6% versus 9.5%, respectively. Similar rates of severe treatment-related toxicity do not establish an identical treatment burden.

Regulators must evaluate manufacturing consistency alongside efficacy and safety. Clinicians need durable outcomes, patient-reported quality of life, and practical delivery data. Health systems must determine whether treatment is feasible and affordable beyond specialized centers.

As an oncologist working in clinical development and global cancer care, I would place access within the development agenda from the beginning. Adequate tissue, sequencing capacity, production infrastructure, and coverage and reimbursement will determine who benefits.

Personalized cancer vaccines could become an important component of perioperative treatment. Their greatest contribution may come through careful integration with checkpoint inhibition, response assessment, and better patient selection. Our responsibility is to translate an encouraging result into longer and better lives, while avoiding unnecessary treatment, toxicity, and financial burden.

#5693. The Confidence Trap: What a New Survey Reveals About AI and Health Decisions

The Confidence Trap: What a New Survey Reveals About AI and Health Decisions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Healthcare remains difficult to navigate. People often must piece together information from providers, benefits, pharmacy, digital tools and care teams while trying to understand costs and what to do next.

Increasingly, they’re turning to consumer AI chatbots for answers. The appeal is understandable: they’re available anytime, respond instantly and can make complex information more digestible.

But healthcare decisions require more than quick answers. The quality of guidance depends on context. General-purpose AI tools typically don't have access to a person's medical history, benefits, costs, care team or broader health circumstances, and they aren't designed to provide clinically governed guidance.

According to a new survey commissioned by MD Live, 37%  of people surveyed turn to AI chatbots for health questions because they're available any time; 31% because they're faster than seeing a doctor; and 30% because AI is reassuring when people are worried about a health concern.

Most people don’t realize how much what they say, or don’t say, impacts the answer they get. The survey findings reveal just how often people reframe questions to elicit a preferred  response, or how much influence these tools have on site-of-care decisions.

Fifty-three percent of respondents admit to rewording questions until an AI tool gives them the answer they were hoping for. Nearly three-quarters leave out relevant medical history when they ask, and this gap can go unnoticed: 22% believe AI factors in their personal medical history even if they’ve never shared it.

The same trust carries over to their children, too, with 71% comfortable relying solely on AI to determine what kind of care their child needs, and 68% to decide whether their child needs care at all.

The behavior is understandable. People often seek reassurance when they're uncertain or worried about a health concern. But in healthcare, reassurance alone isn't always what's needed. Decisions are strongest when they are informed by relevant context, clinical expertise and an understanding of what happens next.

What we’re seeing is a growing number of people making site-of-care decisions with tools that may lack important clinical context. When guidance is generated without a complete understanding of the individual, recommendations may feel personalized while remaining fundamentally generic.

The issue isn't whether AI has a role in healthcare. It does. In fact, AI's capabilities are advancing quickly. The more important question isn’t whether AI can generate an answer. It’s whether that answer reflects the individual’s unique health situation, care needs, benefits, costs, and available care options. Without that context, even sophisticated tools can produce guidance that doesn't reflect a person's real circumstances.

As a result, healthcare organizations may increasingly face a challenge where generic guidance drives highly personal healthcare decisions, with downstream implications for utilization, costs, and patient outcomes.

AI models can prioritize agreeableness in ways that complicate health decisions. A Stanford study published in Science in March 2026 found that large language models endorsed a person's position 49% more often than a human would and affirmed harmful or clearly wrong choices 47% of the time.

That mechanism explains why rewording works so well: the models adjust to please their users. People have learned to reword their questions because the system is built to reward persistence with reassurance, whether that reassurance is warranted.

The impact of this behavior is not theoretical. The survey found that 59% of respondents say they've received AI health information that they later realized didn't fully apply to their personal situation, and 49% acted on it anyway before finding out.

This is also backed by independent research: Oxford researchers, publishing in Nature Medicine in February 2026, ran the largest user study to date on LLMs assisting the public with medical decisions and found that people using AI made no better choices in real triage scenarios than those relying on a search engine or their own judgment.

A separate BMJ Open study from April 2026 audited five popular chatbots across common health topics and rated nearly half of all responses as problematic, while also finding that the tools consistently responded with confidence and certainty.

Studies show that AI’s clinical capabilities are advancing quickly. But healthcare is different from many other consumer use cases. The quality of the response depends not only on the technology itself, but on how well it understands the person behind the question. In healthcare, broadly correct information is not always the same as clinically appropriate guidance. Not to mention, this isn't a fringe behavior. Pew Research found that a quarter of Americans now use AI chatbots to self-diagnose symptoms, and KFF's tracking poll puts overall AI use for health information at 32%, on par with social media.

The consumer need for fast answers and on-demand access is real and isn't going away. The question is how healthcare leaders meet consumers where they are while helping them make informed care decisions.

At MD Live, we believe the future of healthcare AI isn't simply about delivering answers. It's about helping people make informed decisions with appropriate clinical support and a clear path to care when the situation calls for it. People are already using AI to determine where to go for care. The opportunity now is to ensure those decisions are supported by experiences that combine technology with clinical expertise, helping people move from information to informed action.

#5691. From Transparency to Defensibility: The Standard Mid–Revenue Cycle AI Requires

From Transparency to Defensibility: The Standard Mid–Revenue Cycle AI Requires" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Written by: Hani Judeh, MD, CMO and CMIO, Accuity Healthcare and Stephanie Smith, MD, Vice President, Clinical Intelligence, Accuity

Healthcare AI is moving from enthusiasm to accountability.

The Health AI Partnership's AI Vendor Disclosure Framework, described in NEJM AI, gives health systems a structured way to evaluate AI vendors across intended use, system performance and compliance, data stewardship, integration, and lifecycle management. That transparency matters — it gives buyers a better way to ask what an AI system actually does before it's purchased and implemented.

For mid–revenue cycle vendors, though, disclosure is only the starting point. The more important question is whether the recommendation can be defended.

That distinction matters because mid–revenue cycle AI doesn't operate at a distance from consequence. It sits inside decisions that affect documentation integrity, coding pathways, reimbursement, denials, payer scrutiny, reviewer burden, and provider trust. A single recommendation may influence whether an opportunity is surfaced, escalated, deprioritized, or acted upon — and hospitals and physicians remain accountable for the decisions they make using vendor AI outputs.

At Accuity, we believe that responsibility requires a higher standard: clinical and coding integrity.

Clinical and coding integrity means an AI-supported recommendation should be clinically meaningful, documentation-supported, coding-relevant, and defensible under review. It should be clear why the recommendation was made, what evidence supports it, what uncertainty remains, and whether the case is appropriate for automation or expert review. That is the difference between AI that can be described and AI that can be defended.

Health systems are operating on thin margins, which means they need automation that stays reliable after launch — not automation that creates new volatility. Missed clinically valid findings become revenue leakage. Unsupported recommendations create rework, denials exposure, and payer clawback risk. Prioritization pathways without monitoring can make work disappear from view while risk quietly accumulates.

Stable automation doesn't happen by accident. It requires evidence standards, decision boundaries, monitoring, change control, and rollback criteria. Governance isn't administrative drag. It's how automation stays reliable as documentation patterns, payer behavior, coding guidance, and client workflows shift over time. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework identifies these same measures as core functions of trustworthy AI systems.¹

This is why mid–revenue cycle automation can't be judged by throughput alone. A clinically plausible finding isn't automatically a coding-supported opportunity. A documentation phrase isn't automatically evidence of an active, reportable, reimbursable condition. The work requires careful translation across medicine, documentation, coding guidance, payer scrutiny, and operational workflow — and that translation cannot be left to automation alone.

Accuity's approach combines physician-led clinical logic development, physician-coder adjudication, governance controls, and downstream appeals management for the cases we touch. Physicians and coders bring different but complementary expertise: physicians contribute clinical context, disease understanding, plausibility assessment, and judgment under uncertainty, while coders bring documentation standards, coding guidance, reimbursement logic, and defensibility discipline. Together, they determine whether an AI-supported opportunity is valid and appropriate for action — giving automation both structure and restraint.

Physician-authored logic defines the clinical intent of the technology. Expert judgment determines when evidence is strong enough to act, when uncertainty should stop automation, and when human review is required. That is the Accuity value proposition: not automation for throughput only, but automation governed by the people who understand the clinical and coding consequences of being wrong.

Lineage is where defensibility becomes real

A vendor AI output doesn't remove accountability. The hospital still has to act and respond to scrutiny. The physician still has to stand behind the clinical record. The coding and revenue cycle teams still have to defend the resulting claim.

That's why evidence lineage matters. A recommendation should be traceable from the output back to the record evidence, diagnosis or procedure, coding rationale, and logic or model version that produced it. Mid–revenue cycle decisions don't rest on isolated words — they depend on source, timing, attribution, clinical context, documentation sufficiency, and coding relevance. Lineage allows reviewers and governance teams to understand where the evidence came from, why it mattered, and whether it was strong enough to support action. It also creates the path for error review, drift detection, recurrence tracking, and logic correction.

Accuity extends that defensibility downstream. For the cases we touch, appeals management connects the original recommendation to the evidence, clinical rationale, coding rationale, and payer-facing defense. That matters because defensibility isn't proven when an AI output is generated — it's proven when the recommendation can withstand denial and audit scrutiny. Without lineage, an AI output is an assertion. With lineage and downstream defense, it becomes part of an operating model that can stand behind the work.

The HAIP framework is an important step toward more disciplined AI evaluation and procurement in healthcare. But in the mid–revenue cycle, transparency is the floor. Clinical and coding integrity is the standard.

Defensible automation means AI-supported work shaped by physician-authored logic, physician-coder judgment, evidence lineage, lifecycle governance, and appeals support for the cases we touch. That's how automation can reduce burden without hiding risk, support efficiency without sacrificing defensibility, and help protect financial stability in an environment where margins are thin and volatility is costly.

The future of mid–revenue cycle AI won't belong to the largest model or the loudest automation claim. It will belong to systems that can be trusted at the point of use. More defensible AI. Not just more confident AI.

Less than two weeks after Mass General Brigham said it had begun laying off workers, the head of the health care system has sent employees a cryptic email saying MGB faces urgent financial challenges and needed to make improvements but provided no specifics.

#5689. Midstream Health nabs $20M series A to help hospitals recover lost margin

Midstream Health nabs $20M series A to help hospitals recover lost margin" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Health systems are losing margins they’ve already earned, according to Sumit Kadakia, CEO and co-founder of Midstream Health. The startup bets that artificial intelligence can improve hospital margins by finding money that is already embedded in contracts and transactions.

Midstream Health, an autonomous financial operations platform for health systems, picked up $20 million in series A funding to expand its AI financial platform. The company is expanding across a customer network representing more than $100 billion in annual operating expenses and over 250 hospitals nationwide.

Valtruis led the financing round with continued participation from Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Foundry and CommonSpirit Ventures, bringing Midstream’s total funding to $29.2 million. Fairview Health Services and Keck Medicine of USC are among the newest health systems to join the platform, alongside CommonSpirit Health, Mount Sinai Health System and Houston Methodist.

Midstream says its AI financial platform helps health systems find and recover margin across revenue and cost, strengthening the financial capacity needed to keep investing in care and serving their communities.

"We bring all of a health system’s data together, across pharmacy, supply chain, managed care, revenue and cost, into a single source of truth, and then put AI agents on top of it to find and recover money the system is owed. We call it the 'second financial brain' for a health system," Kadakia said in an interview.

He added, "That’s a lot of technical talk for a pretty shocking problem: hospitals are multibillion-dollar enterprises, and most of them don’t have any form of managerial finance."

With that data foundation in place, Midstream Health's domain-trained agents proactively flag and prioritize cost-saving and margin opportunities such as missed rebates, pricing errors, payer underpayments and policy-driven denials.

Kadakia describes the platform as "an army of agents that runs alongside a health system’s finance and supply chain teams, never sleeps, and is constantly finding and recovering margin."

The company plans to use the fresh funding to expand its product and engineering capabilities, particularly as it moves into new verticals. It also plans to continue formalizing its sales and marketing functions and building a dedicated research function that owns its underlying data connections, Kadakia said.

Health systems are facing a financial sustainability crisis, fighting to protect razor-thin margins. More than 110 rural hospitals have closed over the past 20 years, and another 720—representing roughly a third of all rural hospitals—are at risk of closure. Much of what’s slipping away is money health systems have already earned, buried in their own contracts and spend.

According to Kadakia, one system can have thousands of contracts across supply chain, pharmacy and managed care, each with its own pricing tiers, rebate triggers and amendments. "Nobody has time to check every one against what the system actually buys and pays, so a six-figure rebate can disappear because one form was missed. Meanwhile, most healthcare AI money has gone into the claims fight between hospitals and insurers. Every dollar one side wins, the other side loses, and the total cost of care goes up. Deflationary AI will make care cheaper to deliver, and the most direct way to do that is making sure [that] health systems collect what their contracts already say they’re owed. Margin that stays buried in a contract never reaches patients," he said.

Kadakia says he has a personal perspective on the issue—his father practiced at two rural West Virginia hospitals that have since closed.

"In today's challenging healthcare environment, we have to be thoughtful about how we manage our resources and continually look for opportunities to operate more efficiently," said James Hereford, CEO of Fairview Health Services, in a statement. "By leveraging AI-driven financial operations, we can improve financial performance, allowing us to focus more resources on delivering care to our patients and communities."

CommonSpirit Health, one of the largest nonprofit health systems in the U.S., was an initial investor in Midstream and became one of the first healthcare partners chosen to implement and validate the platform through integration with supply chain operations. After implementation, Midstream's AI agents provided "measurable gains within days, surfacing opportunities like missed rebates and underpayments," according to Daniel Barchi, CommonSpirit Health's chief information officer.

"It is a closed-loop AI system that transforms financial intelligence into real-time action, delivering a data foundation, visibility and execution capability," Barchi said in a statement.

Across its customer base, Midstream claims it has identified more than 1,500 financial recovery opportunities this year, from six-figure rebates buried by a single missed form to systemic payer underpayments. Early Midstream partners are projecting more than 5x ROI this year. The platform is on pace to reach $100 million in client savings by the end of 2026, the company claims.

In the near term, Midstream is on pace to reach $100 million in client savings by the end of 2026.

"The longer-term piece is what I’m most excited about, because I think this enables a renaissance in value-based care. Value-based care was built on an unstable foundation. To take on risk, a hospital needs a clear view of what care is actually costing it and why, and the systems to give hospitals that view were never built. If we give them that foundation, they can take on more risk, and that’s how you start to deflate the arms race between payers and providers," Kadakia said.

In the current financial environment, health systems need solutions that can improve their financial position quickly, noted Mike Spadafore, managing director of Valtruis. "We’re backing Midstream because it’s built first-of-its-kind infrastructure to turn complex financial data into action. Where enterprise healthcare technology can take years to demonstrate value, Midstream delivers within the quarter," he said.

AI is intensifying an ongoing financial battle between health systems and insurers, and data shows that this AI "arms race" is driving up short-term healthcare costs. The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association estimates hospitals’ AI coding tools added nearly $1 billion in costs over two years, and insurers are answering with AI of their own.

"Patients, employers and taxpayers pay for that arms race. The next decade should be judged by a simpler test: does the technology bring total cost down? That’s the standard we hold ourselves to," Kadakia said.

The French pharma Servier said Tuesday that an experimental drug it purchased in June for $1.55 billion in cash, plus about $1 billion more in potential milestones, failed to slow a rare form of muscular dystrophy in a long placebo-controlled trial.

It’s a surprising setback for both Servier and the patients with Becker muscular dystrophy, who currently have no approved treatments. The drug, called sevasemten and originally developed by Edgewise Therapeutics, had previously shown promising results in a smaller, randomized study.

“The results of the pivotal GRAND CANYON study are not aligned with certain findings observed in prior clinical studies,” Servier said in a statement, using the company’s name for the Phase 2 trial. “Servier is conducting a comprehensive analysis of the GRAND CANYON study dataset, together with relevant prior clinical data, to better understand and further characterize the study findings.”

#5687. Why Are Medical Students Learning About Physician Unions?

— Brian Muthyala, MD, MPH, weighs the promise and pitfalls of collective action

Medical students are taught how poverty, access to care, and other systemic factors affect patients' health, but many struggle with a fundamental question: What can one physician realistically do about problems that extend far beyond the exam room?

At the University of Minnesota Medical School in Minneapolis, Brian Muthyala, MD, MPH, teaches second-year students about building collective power -- including physician unionization -- as one potential approach to addressing systemic challenges in healthcare.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Muthyala discusses why he introduced the course, how physicians can advocate for patients beyond individual clinical encounters, and why he believes unionization holds promise but is not without risks.

The following is a transcript of this video:

I don't think unionization is a panacea. I don't think it's a silver bullet, and it has its own risks.

So I started teaching this course and it's built on the idea that collective problems require collective solutions. So I'm the director of our social medicine thread in the medical school at the University of Minnesota. And so what I teach is around all of the nonbiological reasons that one person might be sick.

And in the context of many conversations over the medical students' first 2 years, they get to this point where they recognize that poverty, low socioeconomic status, a history of experiencing structural racism, you name it, all of these are sort of large collective problems. And many students say, "Well, what am I supposed to do about that? I'm just one person and I need to learn how to take care of pneumonia and heart attacks and rheumatologic conditions. I need to learn all these things, and I've got to deal with this too. What am I supposed to do?"

And the session is really two parts. And so the first is a webinar that's sort of a conversation around what are different ways historically that physicians have built collective power. We talk about things like mutual aid. We talk about things like community-based participation. And then one of the things we talk about is the history of unionization by physicians historically. The second part of that series is I brought a panel of mostly physicians, but also labor organizers as well, to talk about the issue of physician unionization -- challenges, pitfalls, all of those things as one approach that's imperfect certainly, but one approach to building the collective voice of physicians to try to solve large societal or collective problems that exist.

Historically, the way I was taught physician advocacy was, well, if you've got a problem with something, write a letter to your senator, go testify at the Capitol. And that feels unreachable to a lot of students. They're like, "I'm really busy right now. And then when I'm a physician, I have 20-minute appointments. I've got all this paperwork. I've got all this stuff to do. That feels really inaccessible."

We don't get to ignore it as physicians. As physicians, we're sort of stewards of a community trust and it's our responsibility to understand these issues to the best of our ability and address them to the best of our ability -- and that doesn't mean quitting our day job and going to the Capitol or whatever. And so I give them this sort of pyramid of approach and the first level is understanding the problem. So reading about it, understanding the history, learning.

The second is how do I start to communicate interpersonally with patients around these issues as they impact? How does access to care affect the patient that I'm sitting in front of? The next is how do I understand my own institution's support around these issues? What does my clinic do to help somebody sign up for insurance if they just lost Medicaid, whatever that may be. Because every system is going to be different in terms of what resources they have. And the last is a policy level. You get to choose which level you want to approach these issues.

We've seen a corporatization of healthcare delivery in the last 25 years. If you want to have a seat at the table, we have to build a system that will allow you to operate against and oftentimes push against large corporate interests, which I and others, and I think many students identify as something that puts patients at risk. And ultimately that's what this comes down to is I think unionization can be -- I don't know if it has always been -- can be one way to elevate the needs of patients to a level in which they can be advocated for. And I think physicians are responding to the corporatization of medical care.

I say this in the class: I am nervous about physician unionization. Historically, physician groups have not been unions, but physician groups have been professional societies, so like the American Medical Association [AMA] as an example. My worry about physician unions are the same worries that I have around historical physician groups. The AMA was against the initial legislation that brought forward Medicare and Medicaid in this country. The AMA, again, historically at its inception did not allow for nonwhite physicians to join its ranks.

And so the history of physicians joining their collective voice is complicated and physicians are not a homogeneous group. In fact, I think we're a very heterogeneous group. Will unions be able to focus a large heterogeneous group's energies, privilege, power towards the betterment of patients is a question that I don't think has been answered. And I think rightfully should be questioned if it's possible.

I'm an optimist by my nature and I think that the more voices that are at a table that are not representative of corporate entities is a good one. And so I think physician unions have the potential and possibility of really advocating for significant change for the betterment of patients, but that remains to be seen at this point.

#5685. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5684. Don Jr.’s Investor Business Partner Abruptly Resigns From Fannie Mae Board

Conservative businessman Omeed Malik, a close Trump ally and business partner of Donald Trump Jr., has stepped down from the board of Fannie Mae.

The government-sponsored mortgage giant said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday that Malik resigned from the board of directors, effective Oct. 30. Malik is president of the venture capital firm 1789 Capital as well as founder of investment bank Farvahar Partners. Trump Jr. joined 1789 as a partner in November 2024.

Malik "brings extensive experience in financial services and capital markets as well as a blend of legal, entrepreneurial, and strategic leadership expertise," Fannie said in its last annual report in February. He was paid $114,222 last year, that filing shows.

As a member of the eight-member board, Malik has been a part of Fannie Mae as it has enlarged its balance sheet at the behest of President Donald Trump, who pushed the GSE to buy mortgage-backed securities in a bid to lower mortgage rates.

Trump has also floated the idea of ending the conservatorship of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, potentially setting the stage for a $30 billion IPO. But the Trump administration has said little of those plans in recent months as Americans grapple with inflation and rising housing costs.

Malik joined the board in April 2025. At the time, Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte, who chairs the board, posted to X that "Omeed brings great capital markets, legal and investment experience as we Make Fannie and Freddie Great Again!"

Fannie Mae reported $4.2 billion in net income in the third quarter. This year it has provided about $344 billion in liquidity to 295,000 homebuyers. The company's overall net worth has swelled from $47.4 billion in 2021 to $119.6 billion in the third quarter.

#5683. Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude

Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Electronic health record company athenahealth is opening up patient health records to outside AI assistants, starting with Anthropic’s Claude, through a new connection designed to give patients personalized answers based on their clinical data.

The new server solution, athenaPatient MCP, uses the Model Context Protocol to connect Claude directly with the athenaOne platform. Patients authenticate using their athenahealth patient portal credentials and decide what information Claude can access, according to the EHR company. Credentials are not shared with Claude.

Paul Brient, athenahealth's chief product and operations officer, said that information is encrypted in transit, patients control what information is shared, and they can revoke access at any time. "Once the connection is established and patients approve what types of data they would like to share, the rest is between Claude and the patient," he told Fierce Healthcare in an interview.

Brient noted that AI can meaningfully reduce complexity and help patients play a more active role in their care. "At its core, this is about helping patients get value from their own healthcare data," he noted.

Athenahealth is committed to responsible AI integration, company executives said.

Patients are turning to generative AI, like Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT, to interpret lab results, medication instructions and other medical information. More than a third of U.S. adults (34%) have used AI assistants for health-related purposes, including looking up symptoms to understanding a diagnosis, according to an August Pew Research Center survey. This trend reflects a growing expectation for immediate, conversational health guidance, but also introduces new governance challenges, athenahealth executives noted.

"Claude is the first connection we’ve enabled for athenaPatient MCP, but it's not intended to be the only one," Brient said. "Anthropic has been a strong launch collaborator because of its approach to responsible AI development. But our strategy isn't built around a specific AI model. The AI landscape is moving incredibly quickly, with new models and tools coming to market seemingly every week. We designed athenaPatient MCP with that reality in mind and built it on a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that has become an industry norm for AI interoperability."

Claude Pro and Max users in the U.S. can add the athenaPatient MCP connector within their Claude settings. Patients can then ask Claude questions about their health information using natural language. With a patient’s permission, Claude can reference information such as lab results, medications, vitals, health conditions, diagnostic reports, immunizations, visit history, allergies, procedures and care plans to generate personalized answers based on their clinical data, instead of generic or incomplete information, athenahealth executives said.

"Patients often have questions about their health records between visits, from what a lab result means to what to ask at their next appointment," Syed Mohiuddin, head of healthcare at Anthropic, said in a statement. "athenahealth is giving patients a way to bring their own records into Claude when they choose to, so they can explore those questions and feel more confident and prepared in conversations with their care team."

Athenahealth's EHR is a cloud-based, open platform, Brient noted, and the company's objective is to "create a secure way for patients to use their health information with the AI assistants they choose," he said.

The company plans to expand access to other models, but Brient did not provide any details about additional integrations.

The company built athenaPatient MCP to connect to general-purpose AI assistants rather than build those generative AI capabilities entirely within athenaPatient.

"It's not our job to decide which AI assistant patients should use. Patients are increasingly using AI tools in their daily lives, and I expect that trend to continue. If we've learned anything over the last few years, it's that people will gravitate toward the experiences that work best for them. Healthcare shouldn't be isolated from that reality," Brient said.

"At its core, this is about giving patients access to their health information in the places where they want them—safely, of course. Our patient-facing connector is consistent with our broader interoperability capabilities. Consumers increasingly expect their personal data to integrate into the digital tools they use. Healthcare shouldn't be an exception," he said.

Some providers have raised concerns that as patients increasingly use AI chatbots to interpret health records and lab results, it will drive an uptick in follow-up messages to physicians. Brient noted that giving patients an easier way to connect their health records to AI tools helps patients better understand the information their providers have given them and have more informed questions.

"One of the realities of healthcare is that patients often leave an appointment with more information than they can reasonably absorb in the moment. Lab results often arrive after the patient has seen their doctor. Questions come up after the visit. Medication instructions get forgotten. That's not a criticism of patients or clinicians. It's just reality," he said.

"When patients have a stronger understanding of their healthcare situation, conversations with their care teams tend to be more productive. From the clinician perspective, we were equally focused on what this should not do. We did not want to create additional work for clinicians. A recurring theme across our product strategy is reducing work while improving outcomes. The best healthcare technology helps patients become more engaged without creating more administrative burden for clinicians," Brient noted.

Athenahealth provides EHR software, revenue cycle management and patient engagement solutions to small and independent provider practices. A year ago, the company unveiled new AI features for ambulatory providers as part of a larger upgrade to an "AI-native" athenaOne platform. This summer, the company rolled out more than 80 new AI features for RCM operations on its AI-native athenaOne platform.

Athenahealth executives describe the launch of athenaPatient MCP and the connection to Claude as just the first step, suggesting a broader strategy of allowing patients to use AI tools with their health records.

"The immediate focus is helping patients securely access and understand their health information through the AI assistants they choose to use. Looking further ahead, I think it's reasonable to expect both the number of AI assistants and the capabilities available through them to expand. One of the reasons we're excited about MCP is that it creates a standardized way to provide context to AI systems. Context is what makes AI particularly useful. Without context, AI can provide general information. With context, it can provide a more detailed, personalized set of information and is less likely to lead you astray," Brient said.

Major EHR companies are moving forward with AI integrations to connect patient data with AI tools OpenAI's ChatGPT for Healthcare now integrates with Epic's EHR to enable authorized clinicians to access and summarize patient information from medical records within ChatGPT or directly in supported Epic workflows. That integration can now pull together clinical notes, lab results, medications and specialist documentation, the company said in a blog post.

Oracle’s AI-powered patient portal allows patients to chat directly with their electronic health record using a conversational interface built on OpenAI frontier models.

In healthcare, MCP creates a common framework for connecting AI agents to clinical systems and data.

"I think it's still early, but this is an important trend to watch," Brient said. "One of the challenges with AI is that intelligence without context isn't particularly useful. In healthcare, context must be accurate, permissioned, secure, and current. That's a much harder problem than simply connecting a chat to a data source."

What makes MCP interesting, he noted, is that it provides a framework for connecting AI systems with the context they need while preserving appropriate controls and governance.

"Whether MCP ultimately becomes the interoperability layer for AI in healthcare remains to be seen, but I think the demand for this type of interoperability is only going to increase. Patients and providers are already using AI. The question is whether healthcare data can participate in those experiences safely and effectively," he said, adding, "I feel good about where the industry is headed, and I believe standards like MCP can play an important role in getting us there. But we're still in the early innings, and much work remains. Our goal is straightforward: reduce friction, maintain trust, and help patients and providers benefit from advances in AI without compromising security or control."
