#5682. Opinion: I moved to Europe for free health care. I miss my patient portal

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Breland is a co-founder of The Neuro Studio.

Tuesday, at exactly 7 a.m., I arrived at my general practitioner’s office, in the basement level of his house, two blocks from mine in Mellieħa, Malta. There are six chairs in the waiting area. Ikea, I think. People note who got there first and go in, in turn. On his desk, there’s an ancient laptop with a big monitor running a vaguely Y2K version of Windows. He wears a digital Casio watch I remember my dad having in the 1980s. My American doctor’s office had a water feature.

My Malta doctor does bloodwork by appointment only, Tuesdays at 7 a.m. You tell him in advance what you need, and he has the tubes ready, hand-labeled with your resident number. The tubes are tracking the two diseases I brought with me. The number is what gets you into a socialized system that spends a quarter of what America costs per person and still has an average life expectancy of five more years. It’s not the Mediterranean diet doing the work. Malta has the highest obesity rates in adults in all of the E.U.

While I sat there, gauze pressed on the vein that just held the needle, he filled out a form for the lab, correcting an error with white-out tape. You can buy that down the street at the store that sells water shoes and postcards.

I left the United States for a variety of reasons, including that you can swim in the Potomac but shouldn’t. You can bask in the Mediterranean and should. But mostly, it was a calculation about health care. American medicine saved me, literally, more than once. My care was extraordinary, and it was also about to become extraordinarily unaffordable. I pay 38 euros a week here — about $2,300 a year — and it covers me and my medications, including the one that costs $80,000 per year in the U.S.

My medical resume is diverse. I’ve had multiple sclerosis since 2002. I had breast cancer. I have half a liver. I once broke my leg in three places — while standing still. In my adult life I have hit the catastrophic out-of-pocket maximum nearly every year.

Like most insured Americans, I had coverage through my employer, and later through my husband Brian’s employer, the federal government. My doctors were department heads at Georgetown and Johns Hopkins. The surgeon who repaired my leg did his residency at the Hospital for Special Surgery, the top-ranked orthopedic hospital in the country. I got him because he was on call. My post-mastectomy plastic surgeon had once chaired the board that certifies plastic surgeons. All of them. For the whole country.

Every visit was a $40 copay. Self-referral. My maximum out-of-pocket was $6,000. The plan cost $26,888 a year — Brian paid $9,988 and his employer paid the rest. We never thought about it.

Then came DOGE, which was clearing out the federal workforce in the name of preventing waste, fraud, and abuse. Brian worked for an Inspector General’s office that investigated and prosecuted … waste, fraud, and abuse.

He never got fired. But we didn’t want to live in the risk. He wanted to move into consulting, which meant buying insurance on the exchange.

I am an insurance company’s nightmare. Federal law currently says they have to take me. To be extra safe, we planned to go to New York, where Brian’s family lives, because preexisting conditions are written into state law.

The cheapest mid-level plan, including copays and deductibles, ran about $30,000 for the year for both of us. That was the 2026 number. Open enrollment for 2027 coverage runs Nov. 1 to Dec. 15. That’s a shorter timeframe than previous years, and marketplace premiums are up an average of 26% for 2026. United Healthcare is requesting a 52% increase for New York for 2027. Millions of Americans are running the numbers now.

Two incomes down to one. Our health care costs tripling from what we paid with Brian’s job. After a lot of thought and a single Excel spreadsheet, we decided our best option wasn’t New York after all. My mother, long dead, ended up being the deciding factor.

My mother left me an E.U. passport. That is not a financial plan or a policy proposal or anything I earned — it is an inheritance like my green eyes and forehead veins, and it is the only reason any of what follows was available to me. Most Americans with a condition like mine don’t have an escape hatch to the European Union. I did. And I had been claiming socialized medicine was ideal — the way! — for decades without ever having participated in it.

My social security contribution — that 38 euros a week — gives the entitlement.

Hospital stay in Malta? Free. Emergency helicopter rescue? Free. There is no prior authorization. No requirement to fail a cheaper drug before getting a better one. Nobody has sent me the letter I used to get every year from my U.S. insurer, announcing they would not cover my medication because they believed I had a secondary insurance policy I have never had. Every. Single. Year.

At least twice a year, my doctor would be on the phone yelling at an insurance company for denying coverage. There are people whose entire job it is to file those appeals. According to a 2025 AMA survey, U.S. doctors average 40 prior authorizations per week, and their practices spend 13 hours a week on them. Forty percent of doctors employ staffers just to deal with insurance companies. And about three-quarters of physicians report that denials have increased over the past five years.

To be honest, in Malta, I pay for medical care all the time. I just pay differently.

There’s a two-tiered medical system. Public and private. The care is guaranteed. Speed and convenience live wholly in the private tier.

I can walk into almost any pharmacy in Malta and see a GP operating privately that same day for 15 to 20 euros. A specialist is 70 euros. Always cash. Sometimes you get a receipt. An ultrasound — if you want it fast — is 120 euros. Mine was performed by a doctor specializing in breast cancer imaging. No tech. No radiologist to read it later. I got the report at the appointment.

Most specialists here see patients both publicly and privately, and many private appointments happen inside pharmacies. There are tiny offices tucked in the back or upstairs. My neurologist works in a hospital one day a week. The other four days he works in four different pharmacies. You pick the one closest to where you live or work or shop. When I asked him why the system works that way, he said, literally, “to make it convenient for the patients.” There is no lease, no waiting room, no receptionist, and no billing department because there is nothing to bill. You pay at the counter where the eye drops are.

In Attard, where I see him because it’s closest to my house, he works Tuesday mornings alongside a gynecologist, a nephrologist, and an ophthalmologist. The next day will be a different group. Malta has more than 200 licensed community pharmacies, dispensing medical care alongside prescriptions, sunscreen, nail polish remover, a surprisingly robust collection of perfumes, and subpar dental floss. I ship that in from the U.K.

When I needed an oncology checkup, I found Dr. Brincat, who ran the oncology department at Mater Dei Hospital for 17 years. I called a private clinic where he works now. They checked his schedule, called me back the next day, and gave me an appointment just two weeks out.

He scanned (visually, not electronically) more than 100 pages of my records. Other than the paper on his desk, there was a stethoscope. No computer. No iPad. No phone. He ordered a hormone panel to see whether I should switch from tamoxifen to an aromatase inhibitor — something my American oncologist had said we’d get to at some point. They were in agreement on the protocol.

He ordered an ultrasound, handwriting a referral on letterhead and sealing it in an envelope from his top desk drawer.

It feels like time traveling back to the ’80s. But I’ve never had a doctor who needed to prove I needed anything. And a bill? Never seen one.

The private tier is easy. The public tier is where my medical fluency in the U.S. didn’t translate. I have to plan for things I never considered before. Like the speed of mail.

Before Dr. Brincat, I tried to do it the correct way, or rather, the free one. My GP requested a referral, and I was told to watch the mail for an appointment slip. The time you are given is not negotiable. The time is the time. The slip should arrive in roughly two weeks following the request.

I waited. When I called, they said they were still looking for a time for me.

The horror story Americans tell about socialized medicine is the wait. If you need a hip — good luck, check back in three years.

A friend of mine recently went from hip pain to a bad X-ray to a new hip in under 10 weeks in America. She also has excellent insurance, which is the entire sentence. America is the fastest system for some of its people. For the uninsured, the wait is not a year or three. It is indefinite.

I wasn’t prepared for the Maltese system paperwork, emphasis on the paper. To get my medication free, the Pharmacy of Your Choice program required proof that I had paid into social security — because there is no centralized system that simply shows that … I have. Buy a printer/scanner. You will need it.

I scanned and sent my receipts. They replied:

Thank you for contacting the POYC Schedule V office. This is to acknowledge receipt of your email. We will reply to your email in due course.

I have four similar messages in a folder named “Bureaucracy Stuff.”

After three weeks of due course, I called. My form had been mailed, they said, and must have been lost. They would mail it again. I could expect it in 10 business days. I asked whether I could just come get it. They said yes, they were open until 1 p.m. It took me 32 minutes, door to door, in heavy traffic.

In America, there is paperwork to prove you deserve a drug or surgery or treatment because the insurance company doesn’t want to give it to you. In Malta, there’s paperwork because there are forms and they are still on paper.

I have not received reminder texts here. No confirmation calls. I think I have a dermatologist appointment next week. Am I sure? No. I will show up and hope.

I worry that if my cancer comes back, I won’t have what I would have had in the U.S. The doctors are good here. But the bench isn’t as deep.

There are more MS drugs available in America than here — but not the one developed for my subtype. Tolebrutinib, sold as Cenrifki, is the drug American patients lobbied hard for. The Food and Drug Administration rejected it over risk of severe liver injury and questions of efficacy. The European regulator approved it in June. It’s the first drug shown to reduce disability in non-relapsing secondary progressive MS, and I’m in that group, and there is nothing else.

But it won’t come to Malta soon. Just because E.U. approved it doesn’t mean it gets to Malta because there aren’t enough patients to warrant it. There are more people with MS in the United States — nearly a million — than there are people in my entire country.

I did learn recently that there is a portal for the public system. For the private system, I keep a folder on my phone of photographs of my doctors’ notes. One of them is a lonely piece of paper under a stethoscope.

I have never received a bill here. I have no idea what a day in the hospital costs.

My neurologist and I are discussing a minor surgery — one overnight stay — to implant a device that delivers medication directly to my spinal cord. He told me we won’t get to choose the size, even though I would want the smaller one.

“It’s free,” he said, “so we don’t get as much say.”

Mariska Breland is a co-founder of The Neuro Studio, which provides movement education for people with neurological conditions and training for the professionals who work with them.

#5681. CD38-Targeted Immuno-PET Tracer Can Detect Overlooked Multiple Myeloma

— "While no imaging modality is perfect, this adds a new tool," says researcher

A novel CD38-targeted immuno-PET tracer could help detect multiple myeloma in some patients with no signs of disease, according to results from a phase II trial.

While there was no overall difference in disease detection with CD38-targeted zirconium 89 (89Zr) deferoxamine (DFO)-daratumumab PET/CT versus standard-of-care fluorine 18 (18F)-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT (43% vs 47%, P=0.81), both scans identified multiple lesions not visible on the other, reported Gary A. Ulaner, MD, PhD, of the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, and colleagues in Radiology.

For example, multiple myeloma was demonstrated in 13% of patients only with 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab PET/CT and 17% of patients only with 18F-FDG PET/CT.

Moreover, the CD38-targeted immuno-PET tracer identified more sites of disease than standard imaging in 28% of patients, while 18F-FDG PET/CT identified more sites of disease in 22%. The two imaging approaches detected a similar amount of disease in the remaining patients.

"This study demonstrates that immuno-PET targeting CD38 can identify, localize, and quantify myeloma, which is overlooked by FDG PET in many patients," Ulaner told MedPage Today. "This allows oncologists to optimally stage, target, and treat disease."

"While no imaging modality is perfect, this adds a new tool for the care of patients with multiple myeloma," he added.

In a press release, co-author C. Ola Landgren, MD, PhD, of the Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, noted that "if we are going to cure multiple myeloma, we need two things. One, we need really effective medicines. Second, we need to be able to make sure there is no disease left behind after these treatments."

"We are developing new and better technology designed to see where the disease is and make sure we are not missing it," he said. "We show that you can successfully find much more disease. It's a more sensitive and more precise technology, and we have very strong proof of principle that it works and that it's meaningful."

In an editorial accompanying the study, Peter Choyke, MD, of the National Cancer Institute, observed that neither of the two agents detected more than half of the disease present in patients with histologically confirmed disease.

However, while those results may be "disappointing from a clinical perspective, there are several reasons for optimism," he wrote.

Choyke suggested that when combined with highly sensitive liquid biopsies, molecular imaging "might detect ... early disease that would otherwise be missed with conventional imaging and bone marrow biopsy."

In addition, he noted that 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab as a molecular imaging agent is based on daratumumab (Darzalex), which is an actual treatment for multiple myeloma, "so a positive scan implies the drug might be effective."

Ulaner and colleagues noted that while treatment for multiple myeloma has significantly improved over the past two decades, detection of multiple myeloma disease burden remains "suboptimal."

They pointed out that standard-of-care 18F-FDG PET/CT assessment is based on radiolabeled glucose uptake and has limited utility in patients with plasma cell disorders, since myeloma cells may have low glucose uptake. Thus, disease may be undetected with the standard imaging in 30% to 50% of patients with established bone lesions.

The idea behind immuno-PET imaging is that it integrates the target specificity of monoclonal antibodies like daratumumab with the sensitivity and quantitative power of PET, allowing for whole-body mapping of tumor and immune biomarkers.

This prospective, two-center trial was conducted between March 2022 and July 2025, and included 60 participants (median age 63 years, 53% women) who had previously pathologically proven CD38-positive multiple myeloma; had at least one tumor lesion visualized on CT, MRI, or 18F-FDG PET/CT performed within 90 days of protocol enrollment; had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group score of 0-2; and were planned for first-line or a new line of myeloma therapy.

Ulaner and team reported that there were no severe adverse events with 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab, while non-severe adverse events occurred in 5% of participants during non-radiolabeled daratumumab administration.

Brigham and Women's nurses set Nov. 12 date for open-ended strike" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Union nurses at Brigham and Women's Hospital are set to strike in the coming weeks after failed contract negotiations, in what could be the largest open-ended nurse strike in Massachusetts history.

Brigham and Women's Hospital said in a statement it received notice from the Massachusetts Nurses Association (MNA) on Nov. 1 about an open-ended strike beginning Thursday, Nov. 12 at 7 a.m.

"While we had hoped to avoid another strike, we are prepared to continue providing safe, high-quality care throughout any work stoppage, building on our experience and extensive contingency planning," the statement read. "We deeply value and respect our Brigham nurses and remain committed to reaching a fair and responsible agreement. Our latest offer provides market-leading compensation and competitive benefits while recognizing our responsibility to our patients, our entire workforce and the long-term financial sustainability of Brigham and Women’s Hospital."

Negotiations with MNA are set to resume Nov. 9, the hospital said.

MNA said in a statement negotiations will focus on "securing a fair contract that meets the needs of the nurses, their patients and the community members they serve." Nurses are seeking the following terms as part of a fair contract, per the union:

"We are ready to strike but are equally prepared to negotiate a fair contract that protects patient care, respects nurses, and averts the strike," said Kelly Morgan, chair of the union's bargaining committee for the hospital. “Brigham nurses are resolved to fight for as long as it takes for patient safety and the professional respect we deserve.”

Union nurses at Brigham and Women's Hospital voted to reject management's "last, best and final offer" on updated contracts, potentially steering the dispute back toward what could be the largest open-ended nurse strike in Massachusetts history.

The Massachusetts Nurses Association had previously scheduled the strike for Oct. 14, but postponed to give its members a chance to vote on the proposal from Mass General Brigham, the hospital's parent system. The union said it has requested to resume contract negotiations this week, with the hospital responding in its own public statement this it "is prepared to maintain uninterrupted care and respond to any steps the union may take."

MGB's rejected offer would have retained the hospital's existing nursing wage progression system of annual 5% step increases until 20 years tenure, with the addition of two additional 2.5% increases at the top of the prior structure. The union has said it is seeking limits on the use of temporary nurses, more affordable health insurance benefits and “a meaningful cost-of-living wage increase” that includes a differential for nurses floating between units.

“This vote shows the resolve of Brigham nurses, who are fighting for patient safety and for the professional respect we deserve," Kelly Morgan, chair of the union's bargaining committee for the hospital, said in a weekend release. "It’s [time for] MGB to return to the table ready to negotiate in good faith to reach a fair agreement that recognizes the value of Brigham nurses and the expertise they offer for the care of some of the region’s most complex patients every day.”

Brigham and Women's Hospital said it was "disappointed" by the rejection, and that its proposal "reflected the hospital’s commitment to investing in our nurses while supporting long-term sustainability, including meaningful compensation and benefit enhancements that kept Brigham nursing pay among the highest in the market."

Notably, the announcement of the member vote's outcome coincided with news that MGB has begun a new round of layoffs affecting both clinical and operational programs. The unspecified number of cuts reflect a financial need to further adjust operating MGB's structure even after roughly 1,500 people were laid off in 2024, the system said.

Nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have lifted their notice of an Oct. 14 strike after their union and Mass General Brigham management made progress toward a potential contract deal late Saturday night, the sides said in statements.

The 4,000-member open-ended strike would be the largest in state history if launched, and follows months of contract negotiations between the health system and the Massachusetts Nurses Association (see that coverage below).

A formal deal has yet to be struck, though the union said it agreed to call off its 10-day strike notice "given the complexity of the agreement and the impact of a potential strike on our nurses and the community." The proposal is being presented to members for a vote, which might yield a new 10-day notice if rejected.

Brigham and Women's Hospital, in a Sunday statement, said its "last, best and final offer ... reflects significant movement on several of the union's priorities while maintaining a responsible approach to supporting nurses, patients and the long-term strength of the hospital."

It added that the offer retains the hospital's existing nursing wage progression system of annual 5% step increases until 20 years tenure, with the addition of two additional 2.5% increases at the top of the prior structure. The withdrawn notice also saved the hospital from having to implement its contingency staffing plan of hiring temporary nurses.

"We are thankful the MNA has pulled its indefinite strike notice and will allow its members to vote on the hospital's final offer," the hospital said. The union's statement did not specify the timing of that vote.

Editor's note: On Oct. 2, the Massachusetts Nurses Association announced an Oct. 14, 7:00 a.m. start time for their strike if no deal is reached.

Nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have voted to authorize an open-ended, 4,000-member strike that could become the largest nurses’ strike in Massachusetts history.

The Massachusetts Nurses Association announced the 93% in favor vote that was held Thursday evening. No date has been set yet by the union, which is legally required to give employer Mass General Brigham (MGB) 10 days' notice.

“Brigham nurses have made clear that we are prepared to stay on strike for as long as it takes to win a contract that protects our patients and respects the nurses who care for them,” Kelly Morgan, a labor and delivery nurse and chair of the Brigham and Women’s Hospital MNA Bargaining Committee, said in the union’s announcement. “An open-ended strike is a serious step that will undoubtedly create a healthcare crisis in Massachusetts. MGB can prevent the strike by returning to the table and negotiating the contract our nurses need to keep providing world-class care.”

Contract negotiations between the sides have been ongoing since last November, with the prior agreement expiring on March 31. In July, the nurses (plus an additional 450 home care clinicians) conducted a one-day awareness strike that was also a record breaker for the state and the first at Brigham and Women’s, a flagship hospital and founding member of the nonprofit system.

Demonstrations have continued in the weeks since, including a rally held earlier this week outside of an MGB-hosted World Medical Innovation Forum, where bargaining members painted a contrast between executives’ conversations with investors on AI and the demands of their clinical workforce.

The hospital, in statements given to press, said “we remain committed to bargaining in good faith and have put forward a fair and responsible proposal that maintains Brigham nurses’ market-leading compensation, preserves meaningful wage growth and competitive benefits, and balances those investments with the long-term financial sustainability of our system,” the hospital said in a statement given to press.

The hospital has previously said it has found agreements with the union on several issues. However, the union has previously said that talks stalled in mid-August and reiterated Thursday that it still is seeking limits on the use of temporary nurses, more affordable health insurance benefits and “a meaningful cost-of-living wage increase” that includes a differential for nurses floating between units.

MGB is the largest private employer in Massachusetts with roughly 85,000 workers and $22.8 billion in annual revenue, making it among the country’s largest nonprofit health systems. Financial results released last month outlined a $15 million operating income (0.1% operating margin) across nine months of its ongoing fiscal year, up from a $44 million operating loss (-0.3% operating margin), though its nine-month bottom line including nonoperating gains like investment returns was $1.9 billion. Early last year saw the organization undertake the largest layoffs in its history, when it cut about 1,500 workers.

The union has pointed to MGB’s bottom line (nearly $2.4 billion across fiscal 2025), substantial total assets ($35.8 billion) and the compensation of executives (almost $9.2 million for CEO Anne Klibanski, M.D.) in its calls for stronger contracts.

Good morning from a round-the-clock elections team at STAT, where we’ve been closely monitoring Election Day results nationwide. Below is a newsletter full of sharp analysis on how the results (so far) will affect American health care — read on!

WASHINGTON — Republicans — who pushed sweeping, unprecedented health reforms, from Medicaid cuts to MAHA’s upheaval — had a terrible, no good, very bad election night on Tuesday.

Democrats gained control of both chambers of Congress, with shocking victories in deep red states like Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina: a sweeping, decisive result after many candidates ran on health-focused agendas.

The strong political signal is likely to be interpreted as, among other things, a rebuke of the GOP’s health reform agenda. That frustration and anger could be seen even among relatively new allies like the Make America Healthy Again movement, which attached itself to the Trump administration through health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Jeffrey Tucker, president and founder of the MAHA-aligned Brownstone Institute, told STAT that the GOP’s “failure to take its mandate seriously — to give people back their lives and liberties — has led to what looks like yet another populist revolt in a different form.”

“This loss tonight was well-deserved,” he said, echoing other MAHA leaders online.

Though non-health issues — gas prices, the cost of groceries, and the war in Iran — loomed large, broad voter support for congressional Democrats could be taken as a mandate for the party to take bigger swings on health care.

Democratic candidates who ran on trust in science and on their health credentials saw strong results, with the group 314 Action, which supports such candidates, calling the night a “STEM Wave.”

And some key MAHA-aligned candidates lost on Tuesday. Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), who was among the founding members of the MAHA Caucus, lost his race, as did MAHA champion Zach Lahn, who ran to be governor of Iowa.

The election, of course, will also have lasting impacts on America’s health policy. Democrats will now have powerful new tools to investigate the administration’s actions and push back on its agenda.

Late Tuesday night, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), a health policy leader in Congress, posted one word on X: “Subpoenas.”

In several closely watched races, candidates made health care affordability a key campaign plank, promising to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and fight the Medicaid cuts passed by Republicans as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill act in 2025.

In Ohio, physician Amy Acton won the state’s governorship after pledging to make health care a major focus in office. Acton, who led Ohio’s Covid-19 response, prioritized protecting the accessibility of Medicaid, forgiving medical debt, tackling surprise billing, and creating a new prescription drug plan to lower costs. Her opponent, billionaire biotech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy, frequently sought to turn the race into a referendum on the lockdowns and school closures that occurred during Acton’s pandemic-era tenure in state government.

In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship, becoming the first Black woman to occupy that position in any state. Bottoms also pushed for more aggressive health coverage for the state’s lowest earners. Georgia’s controversial Medicaid program, which partially expanded coverage to low-income adults if they proved they were working, expires at the end of the year. Bottoms promised to switch to full Medicaid expansion provided under the Affordable Care Act. She defeated Republican Rick Jackson, the wealthy founder of Jackson Healthcare, a large physician and nurse staffing company. — Sarah Todd and Bob Herman

A microbiologist. A doctor. A nuclear engineer. These are some of the Democrats who won seats in Congress last night.

Perhaps the most surprising was pediatrician Annie Andrews. Andrews won South Carolina’s open Senate seat, which had been held by Republican Lindsey Graham for 23 years before his death. She, along with Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed (more below on El-Sayed, who completed medical school but not residency), will be the the first Democrats with medical degrees in the Senate since 1969.

In her campaign ads, Andrews frequently wore her scrubs, and made walking back Trump’s health policies central to her campaign.

“My two decades as a physician have shown me in a thousand heartbreaking ways just how broken our health care system is,” her platform for reducing health care costs reads. Her platform included health care being a “right” and not a “privilege.” To that end, she said she will work to maintain access to vaccines and ensure rural hospitals do not close.

For a sense of how far Andrews has come, when our colleague Margaret Manto wrote about her last year, for NOTUS (now the Washington Sun), her race was considered a longshot. “This is not a path I ever envisioned for myself. I was perfectly happy in my role as a pediatrician,” she told Margaret at the time.

While not a doctor, Xavier Becerra, who served as health secretary in the Biden administration, cruised in his race to become California governor. From that perch, he could continue his focus on drug pricing, which has also been a priority for the state’s leaders.

On the other side, longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a prominent booster of federal support for academic research who criticized the Trump administration’s moves to reshape that system, lost her reelection campaign to Democrat Troy Jackson. — Anil Oza

He ran as a model MAHA candidate — an enemy of Big Agriculture, a friend of Kennedy.

And yet Republican Zach Lahn lost his race for the Iowa governorship, a crushing blow to the Make America Healthy Again movement. The MAHA PAC poured a million dollars into Lahn’s campaign and Kennedy enthusiastically backed him.

The loss may reflect the waning power of the MAHA movement, which has been on shaky ground over the last several months amid frustration by some members that the Trump administration was too slow on achieving real progress, including on pesticides. Lahn had promised to take down Big Agriculture, ban Covid-19 vaccines from the market, and tackle Iowa’s high cancer rate.

Sen. Roger Marshall (R) lost his reelection bid in Kansas. Marshall, a doctor, started the congressional MAHA Caucus. Although high prices for diesel and fertilizer were the initial drivers of discontent in the state, Marshall has spent the final two months of his campaign fending off reports of aggressive medical debt collection as an OB-GYN.

Marshall also faced an unusually well-suited Democratic contender, Adam Hamilton. Hamilton leads one of Kansas’ largest megachurches and has gained crossover appeal, including endorsements from two former Republican governors. – Chelsea Ciruzzo and John Wilkerson

Abdul El-Sayed’s win in a Michigan Senate race sets him up to be Democrats’ principal challenger to Kennedy. When I talked to him last week, he said he wants to lay the groundwork for a 2028 administration to rebuild the Department of Health and Human Services, but in the meantime he aims to hold Kennedy and Trump “accountable for all of the failures.”

While his race was one of the most closely watched of the cycle, largely because of Democrats’ angst about the direction of their party, many in academia and public health had hoped he could be a fighter for them. El-Sayed trained as a physician-scientist, doing research on health disparities and maternal health before becoming the head of Detroit’s public health department.

Through the race, he also amassed a huge platform that he will leverage to advocate for Medicare for All, as well as his vision for public health. We’ll have more to say later today, when my colleague Sarah Todd, who wrote about Acton’s gubernatorial campaign in Ohio, and I will have a breakdown of how doctors and scientists on the ballot fared. — Anil Oza

A new kind of medical clinic is surprising some patients with thousands in ER bills, STAT

#5678. UnitedHealthcare eliminates prior authorization requirements on 2K pediatric services

UnitedHealthcare eliminates prior authorization requirements on 2K pediatric services" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealthcare will eliminate the need for prior authorization on more than 2,000 codes for pediatric services beginning on Dec. 1, the company announced Monday.

Earlier this year, the insurance giant said it would ease prior auth requirements on an array of pediatric care, and now it's detailing the codes that will fall under that initiative. Services range from diagnostic imaging to cancer treatment to orthopedic care and more.

Examples include sleep studies, MRI scans, joint procedures, ear and tonsil procedures and some chemotherapy services, UHC said in an announcement.

The company said that it "chose to fast-track services that are widely considered in the medical community to be safe and effective," per the release. The changes will reduce prior authorization volume in pediatrics by nearly two-thirds, and apply across commercial, individual market and community plans where eligible under state law.

The changes aren't limited to services provided at pediatric facilities, UnitedHealthcare said.

“Every child deserves a health care experience centered on their needs,” said Tim Noel, CEO of UnitedHealthcare, in the announcement. “These changes will help make that experience simpler for children, their families and the physicians who care for them.”

UnitedHealthcare is among the insurers nationwide that signed on to a pledge in the summer of 2025 to ease the administrative burdens associated with prior authorization and embrace electronic submissions and decisions. Since then, the insurer has taken multiple steps to reduce the requirements on prior auth.

On Oct. 1, the company eliminated prior authorization on 1,700 services across its insurance lines. In May, UHC said it was aiming to eliminate 30% of prior auth requirements by the end of the year.

UnitedHealthcare is set to eliminate close to two-thirds of pediatric prior authorization requirements by the end of the year.

The insurance giant announced Friday morning that it will nix prior auth on an array of diagnostic tests, routine surgeries and specialty services, including cardiology, neurology, pulmonology and orthopedics.

UnitedHealth also said it will offer authorization waivers for certain procedures when they're performed at leading pediatric hospitals as a reflection of their "consistent use of well-established care practices." The insurer said that the facilities in this program represent a broad national network across medical and surgical specialties.

“Parents should be able to spend less time having to navigate the health system and more time focusing on their children as they get the care they need,” said Tim Noel, CEO of UnitedHealthcare, in the announcement.

“These changes are part of our broader efforts to simplify healthcare and allow families—and their doctors and nurses—to pursue routine care with far fewer administrative steps, while higher-risk procedures continue to undergo reviews," Noel added.

The company is undertaking a broad review of all pediatric prior authorizations to determine which can be rolled back while maintaining safety and quality. It said it plans to eliminate pre-approvals for some diagnostic imaging, sleep studies, routine outpatient tests and some surgical services and therapies that are approved consistently.

UnitedHealthcare said prior authorization will remain in place for services with high clinical complexity or variability, such as experimental treatments, or where it is required by regulations.

The company said the changes will take effect across its commercial and Medicaid plans.

The move is the latest from the company as it aims to reduce prior authorization requirements. For example, last month, UnitedHealth said it would exempt rural providers from most prior auth requirements.

The company has also made a push to reduce a wide swath of reauthorizations at its pharmacy benefit manager, Optum Rx.

#5676. Brain Health Linked With Longer Lifetime Estrogen Exposure

— Menopausal hormone therapy tied to lower cerebral small vessel disease burden, study shows

Women with higher lifetime estrogen exposure had less cerebrovascular pathology, a cohort study in Sweden showed.

A longer reproductive span was associated with 8% lower odds of having two or more signs of cerebral small vessel disease (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86-0.99), reported Anna Marseglia, PhD, of the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, and co-authors.

Menopausal hormone therapy was also linked with lower cerebral small vessel disease burden (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20-0.81) and with increasing white matter integrity (ß=0.28, 95% CI 0.06-0.50), Marseglia and colleagues wrote in Neurology.

Among APOE4 carriers only, menopausal hormone therapy was associated with greater cortical thickness in brain regions typically affected by Alzheimer's disease (β=0.38, 95% CI 0.01-0.76).

Women who used oral contraceptives earlier in life and menopausal hormone therapy later had the lowest small vessel disease burden (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.12-0.83) and the greatest white matter integrity (β=0.45, 95% CI 0.12-0.78), the researchers said.

"What was particularly striking was that the most favorable vascular brain health was observed among women who had used oral contraceptives during their reproductive years and later received menopausal hormone therapy. This suggests that hormonal factors acting across different stages of a woman's life may have cumulative associations with cerebrovascular health in older age," Marseglia said in a statement.

"While these findings do not establish cause and effect, they underscore the importance of considering women's reproductive and hormonal history when studying brain aging and dementia risk, not only in relation to Alzheimer's disease but also to vascular disease," she added.

The role of endogenous and exogenous estrogen exposure in brain health may be an opportunity to identify dementia mechanisms, observed Tracy Madsen, MD, PhD, of the University of Vermont in Burlington.

"The lifetime risk of dementia in U.S. women exceeds that of men, and recent projections suggest that by 2060, the number of incident dementia cases in women will surpass that of men by 233,000," Madsen wrote in an accompanying editorial.

The link between estrogen exposure and brain health has become more important with the FDA's recent removal of its black box warning from menopausal hormone therapy, Madsen pointed out. "Furthermore, the idea of reproductive lifespan and ovarian longevity as a potential modifiable target is a critical concept for women's health," she wrote.

Early research suggested that menopausal hormone therapy might protect against Alzheimer's and cardiovascular disease, but in 2003, the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study (WHIMS) reported that estrogen-plus-progestin formulations increased probable dementia risk in women ages 65 or older. The Women's Health Initiative trial also linked combined estrogen and progestin to higher breast cancer and heart disease risks, leading to black box warnings which the FDA removed in 2026.

Over time, the use of hormone replacement therapy in the U.S. declined among postmenopausal women from 26.9% in 1999 to 4.7% in 2020. The treatment is still considered controversial.

More recently, autopsy data and other research have linked estrogen-only menopausal hormone therapy with reduced Alzheimer's neuropathology and lower odds of a dementia diagnosis. A large U.K. Biobank study also suggested that starting hormone replacement therapy early was associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer's and dementia.

In their study, Marseglia and colleagues assessed 352 cognitively unimpaired women from the 1944 Gothenburg H70 birth cohort study who had brain MRI at age 70. Of these, 286 participated in a follow-up exam 5 years later.

The mean Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 29.2 at baseline, indicating normal cognitive function. About one-third (31%) of the cohort were APOE4 carriers.

Reproductive lifespan was calculated by subtracting the age at menarche from the age at menopause or oophorectomy. Study outcomes included cerebral small vessel disease, Alzheimer's-related cortical thickness, and white matter integrity. Small vessel disease burden was a composite score derived from white matter hyperintensities, lacunes, cerebral microbleeds, and perivascular spaces.

On average, women had a reproductive lifespan of 37.1 years. Most women (72.7%) reported using oral contraceptives; 60.8% reported using menopausal hormone therapy.

Longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and white matter trajectories over time, the researchers said. Use of menopausal hormone therapy was linked with fewer perivascular spaces and cerebral microbleeds, they added.

Hormone exposure was reported by participants and may be subject to recall bias and misclassification, Marseglia and co-authors acknowledged. The study lacked detailed information about oral contraceptive and hormone therapy use.

#5674. Zocdoc opens infrastructure to AI agents, launches partnership with Instinct

Zocdoc opens infrastructure to AI agents, launches partnership with Instinct" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As more patients turn to artificial intelligence agents to manage their healthcare, Zocdoc is opening its healthcare access infrastructure to streamline the process.

Beginning Oct. 28, agents can connect patients to care through a variety of channels—including MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, deep links and more.

Zocdoc Chief Strategy Officer Alex Doyne told Fierce Healthcare that AI agents are “becoming a new starting point for patients seeking healthcare.”

Doyne said traffic from AI agents on the platform has “at least doubled roughly every three weeks since July.”

“AI agents can help patients navigate their healthcare options and take action on their behalf, but they're only as reliable as the information and systems they can access,” Doyne said. “By connecting agents to Zocdoc's infrastructure, we can ensure they are booking the right appointments for patients.”

Zocdoc has over 175 scheduling integrations, with more than 10,000 insurance plans and 200,000 verified providers in its network, according to Doyne.

“Opening that infrastructure to agents means they now have access to a reliable booking experience,” Doyne said.

Doyne added that healthcare is “particularly challenging,” for AI agents since “so much of the information available online is fragmented, outdated, or inaccurate,” which can have “real consequences for patients who may already be struggling to access care.”

“That's why it's critical that agents have access to reliable provider and insurance information, accurate availability and infrastructure that ensures the booking is integrated with a provider’s calendar and will hold on the day,” Doyne said.

“We've established a two-way promise that sets clear expectations for Zocdoc and the agents connecting to our infrastructure,” Doyne said. “Zocdoc commits to welcoming agents that register and identify themselves, while agents are expected to obtain explicit patient consent before booking appointments and protect patient and provider data.”

The company also announced a partnership with AI personal assistant Instinct to let agents use Zocdoc’s healthcare access infrastructure to find vetted providers, verify insurance benefits and book appointments.

“Instinct is built to genuinely improve your life and handle important everyday tasks,” said Ben Schwerin, Instinct chief business officer, in a statement. “Since healthcare is more complicated than ordering groceries or booking travel, the stakes are higher. By partnering with Zocdoc, Instinct can navigate that complexity—so getting an appointment can be as simple as sending a text.”

Instinct will join Zocdoc’s growing Care Access Network, which also includes Google Gemini, Amazon Health AI, Yelp, Healthgrades and more.

Last month, Zocdoc acquired Sohar Health in its push to evolve beyond an appointment-booking marketplace into broader healthcare access infrastructure.

Sohar Health helps healthcare organizations simplify insurance workflows, and its APIs automate insurance discovery, eligibility and benefits verification, network status checks and cost estimates.

It marked the company's first acquisition in its nearly 20-year history, executives said.

#5673. Rhode Island Voters Back $120 Million Bond Measure To Support Affordable Housing

Rhode Island voters are projected to pass a ballot initiative to support increased housing through a massive bond issuance.

Rhode Island's Question 2 issues $120 million in general obligation bonds, which could then be used in various costs to increase the supply of affordable housing. The funding would go to pre-development work, new construction, property acquisition, and infrastructure improvements.

At 9 p.m. ET on Tuesday, an hour after polls closed, the measure had 61% support with 84% of the vote reported, according to the state's Board of Elections. The measure needs 50% support to pass.

Of the money from the bond issue, $25 million must go to increasing construction of for-sale homes and $10 million for public housing. The state expects construction on these projects to begin in 2028 and the new housing to come online from 2029 to 2032. That's according to the state's information on the ballot measure, which notes that the total cost of the bond will top out at around $192.5 million with interest.

The National Low Income Housing Coalition estimates that Rhode Island, with a population of about 1.1 million people, is short around 23,000 affordable rental homes for low-income renters. Around 30% the state's renters are considered extremely low income, with an average income of $31,970 for a household of four. According to NLIHC, renters need to make an annual household income of $70,617 to afford a two-bedroom rental home at HUD's fair market rent.

Many prospective buyers in Rhode Island are also being priced out.

Rhode Island's median listing price is $569,900, about $150,000 more than the median national listing price of $419,250.

Housing Works Rhode Island's 2026 Housing Fact Book found that purchasing a home in Rhode Island is out of reach for anyone making the median annual income and that housing costs continue to outpace wages.

Around a third of Rhode Island's homeowners are considered cost-burdened and spend more than 30% of their income on housing.

In the state's capital city, Providence, less than 4% of homes were considered affordable to middle-income buyers, showing a significant misalignment between available homes and local income level. In fact, Providence ranks among the most misaligned markets when it comes to incomes meeting the cost of housing, according to Realtor.com® research.

Former Gov. Dan McKee, who made housing reform a major focus of his administration, urged voters to support the bill. In September, he was defeated in the primary by Helena Foulkes, who is running against Republican gubernatorial candidate Aaron Guckian.

Guckian expressed opposition to the measure.

"Before we ask taxpayers to borrow another $120 million, plus interest, I think we owe them an accounting of the housing money we're already spending and what we're getting for it," Guckian wrote in an email to the Providence Journal.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5671. FTC issues warning letters over deceptive marketing as ACA enrollment opens

FTC issues warning letters over deceptive marketing as ACA enrollment opens" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Open enrollment season is getting underway, and the Federal Trade Commission sent warning letters to 25 companies that conduct marketing or generate sales leads for insurers.

The commission said in an announcement that the letters aim to put these companies on notice about deceptive or unfair marketing tactics that are likely unlawful. Activities in question include misrepresenting the benefits or limitations of a plan, or portraying a plan as comprehensive when it isn't.

In addition, FTC also warned against misrepresenting any costs associated with a plan or falsely telling consumers that a plan offers free rewards, cash offers or other incentives.

"Making healthcare more transparent and affordable is a top priority for the FTC," said Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, in the announcement.

"Americans experiencing rising healthcare costs should not also have to worry about whether a healthcare plan or program is what it claims to be," Mufarrige continued. "The FTC will remain focused on monitoring this market and will not hesitate to hold accountable companies that unlawfully market or advertise healthcare plans to consumers."

The FTC letters were largely sent to firms that market plans on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges, where open enrollment opened on Sunday, Nov. 1. Medicare is also in its annual enrollment period, which continues through Dec. 7, and late fall is when most employers begin plan selections for workers.

The agency does not allege wrongdoing in the warning letters, but instead suggests that the companies "conduct a thorough review of their advertisements to ensure they are complying with applicable laws and rules."

The letters include examples of previous enforcement actions against marketers in the ACA space, such as Innovative Partners and Top Healthcare Options Insurance Agency.

In the letters, the agency emphasizes that its staff will be closely watching for potential violations.

"FTC staff will continue to actively monitor this market for potentially deceptive or unfair acts or practices and will take enforcement action as warranted," the FTC wrote in the letter (PDF).

#5670. A Pediatrician, a Pastor, and a Paralympian Just Did Wonders for Kids’ Mental Health

— The midterm elections offer lessons in decency and difference

My son is 32. Early Wednesday morning he forwarded me a New York Times story about the new faces Tuesday's midterm elections sent to Washington and to statehouses.

He added a note: "Some themes for your next article, like the Knicks one. A message about being decent human beings. A message about how what makes us different brings us together." Then he quoted one line from the Times article: "There's a pediatrician, a pastor, a Paralympian and a former Navy helicopter pilot."

In June, I wrote that the Knicks' championship handed parents a teaching moment. My son was right: Tuesday handed us another.

Our kids and pediatric patients need the lesson. They have lived through a full campaign season. Attack ads. Comment sections. Adults yelling at screens. Before the last presidential election, 77% of American adults named the future of the nation a significant source of stress. Children absorb what we carry home. In the Trevor Project's 2024 national survey, 90% of LGBTQ+ young people said politics had hurt their well-being in the last year. Let's call that the un-teaching.

First, start with the line my son quoted. The pediatrician is Annie Andrews, MD, of South Carolina. She ran for the Senate on a platform focused on children's health after a 2025 measles outbreak sickened some 1,000 children in her state. Andrews, a pediatric hospitalist, saw harm to kids and asked for the job of stopping it.

The pastor is Adam Hamilton, who leads the largest United Methodist congregation in the country. In January he was a registered Republican. Now he is the first Democrat to win a New Hampshire Senate seat in Kansas since 1932. He campaigned on his faith and promised to work across the aisle.

The Paralympian is Josh Turek of Iowa. Two gold medals in wheelchair basketball. A working-class kid. A man who once voted for George W. Bush. He is headed to the Senate.

The helicopter pilot is Rebecca Bennett. She flew for the Navy, ran a healthcare business, and now heads to the House from New Jersey.

Then come the firsts. Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia will be the first Black woman ever elected governor in this country. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire will be the first openly gay man in the Senate; he told the Times he is living a life he could not have pictured as a boy. Abdul El-Sayed, MD, DPhil, of Michigan, a physician who ran Detroit's health department, will be the first Muslim senator. Melat Kiros, 29, becomes the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress. James Talarico, a former middle-school teacher who quotes Scripture in his stump speech, will be the youngest member of the Senate at 37.

Ask a child what these people share. Different faiths. Different bodies. Different races, ages, loves, hometowns. Each one walked into rooms full of strangers and asked for their trust. The strangers said yes. What makes each of us different brought them together.

Talk about Amy Acton, MD, MPH. A physician, Ohio's former health director, now its governor-elect. She has spoken openly about a traumatic childhood and sexual abuse at the hand of her stepfather. Late in the race, an ad from her opponent put Acton's estranged mother on camera to call her a liar. Acton held her ground. She said she told her story so other people might see a way out.

As a child psychiatrist, I treat children with histories like hers. Most of them believe the worst thing that happened to them is the truest thing about them. Let's tell these patients Acton's story.

Adolescents build an identity partly by borrowing one. They pick role models whose life stories connect to their own, and they gravitate toward role models who resemble them. For some kids that is a matter of life and death. LGBTQ+ youth who have an older LGBTQ+ role model report lower rates of considering and attempting suicide. In an earlier Trevor survey, more than 80% said positive public role models made them feel better about who they are. A gay teenager in Manchester watched a gay man win a New Hampshire Senate seat Tuesday night. A kid in a wheelchair in Des Moines watched a Paralympian win one in Iowa. That registers.

Difference, met up close, heals. Cross-group friendships rank among the strongest known antidotes to prejudice in childhood, and they support children's well-being. Civic life protects too. In a national study that followed more than 9,000 adolescents into adulthood, those who volunteered and voted went on to have better mental health and engage in fewer risky behaviors. Community engagement in adolescence predicted fewer depressive symptoms years later.

My son also pointed out another crucial point: Kids across the country just witnessed an incredible underdog story. Talarico and El-Sayed were up against hundreds of millions of dollars in opposition spending. Several of the winning candidates represent groups historically left out from Congress, including gays, Blacks, Hispanics, and women. There is something immensely powerful about marginalized candidates running campaigns built around taking care of their communities and defeating the wealthiest individuals in the country. It doesn't matter how powerful you are, compassion for others and belief in self is what can change the world. That's a story our young patients need to witness.

Of course, half of the country may have woken up disappointed Wednesday. But even for that half, the lesson holds. Hamilton was a Republican 10 months ago. Turek voted for Bush. A child can admire a person and still argue with the platform. Disagreement is healthy. Contempt is the toxin. After the last election, the head of the American Psychological Association warned that pulling away from people over politics can cost us the relationships we need most.

Decency. Service. Faith worn in the open. Grit in a wheelchair. Honesty about one's own pain. A hand across the aisle. Strangers saying yes to someone unlike themselves.

There's the message. Everyone in this country has a reason to bring it up this week, and a son or daughter or patient will be ready to hear it.

My son is 32. He still sends me lessons. That's how it's supposed to work. Don't let the moment pass.

#5668. LeanTaaS expands iQueue into ambient intelligence with LookDeep acquisition

LeanTaaS expands iQueue into ambient intelligence with LookDeep acquisition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Healthcare technology company LeanTaaS is expanding its iQueue platform beyond traditional hospital operations and capacity management into ambient intelligence, using computer vision to monitor patient rooms and turn signals into actions.

As part of this strategy, the company plans to launch iQueue for Virtual Care, using AI-powered patient-room monitoring to detect events such as fall risks, patient movement and other environmental signals, then route those insights into operational workflow.

The system is designed to turn events like an attempted bed exit into prioritized tasks rather than additional alarms. AI monitors rooms and surfaces events to a virtual observation team, which can assess the situation, remotely engage the patient or escalate to bedside staff when needed, Mohan Giridharadas, founder and CEO of LeanTaaS, told Fierce Healthcare in an interview.

Urgency and routing are based on the patient’s context and the health system’s established protocols. Human clinicians remain responsible for clinical decisions, Giridharadas said, while iQueue provides context, prioritizes events and helps route information to the appropriate care team.

The company’s software and services are being used by nearly 200 health systems in more than 1,200 hospitals, centers and clinics in the U.S.

To accelerate this strategy, LeanTaaS acquired LookDeep Health, its second acquisition in about two months following its purchase of care transition platform Aidin. The deal brings computer vision technology, an open platform approach and virtual care deployment experience into LeanTaaS.

LeanTaaS provided Fierce Healthcare with a first look at the acquisition news. Financial details of the deal were not disclosed.

Giridharadas said the company is building the "central nervous system of the hospital," and computer vision will be a key data source for this broader hospital operations platform.

"It is a move beyond retrospective dashboards toward continuous operational awareness and execution," Giridharadas told Fierce Healthcare.

"A great operational brain needs more signal[s], so [that] it can decide faster and decide better. Health systems generate hundreds of thousands of data points each day—but the vast majority of them are discarded after they have served their immediate purpose. The next frontier is building a robust and scalable approach to capture high-value signals from the physical care environment that may never reach the EHR, or may reach it too late to be useful. That includes whether a patient is alone, trying to stand or hasn't been out of bed in days, when a nurse was last in the room, and whether a room is ready for the next patient, from compatible cameras and in-room devices, and potentially other device-generated or workflow signals," Giridharadas said.

"The test is whether a signal is sufficiently accurate and timely, and whether it can be converted into a clear action for the care team. We intend to continuously expand the sources and uses of data from the entire end-to-end patient journey," he added.

Narinder Singh, former CEO and co-founder of LookDeep who joined LeanTaaS as senior vice president of ambient intelligence, said the technology can support stretched care teams by monitoring patients when clinicians can’t be present. "Nurses and physicians cannot be in every room at every moment, and too often technology has added to their work instead of taking it away. Ambient intelligence keeps watch when they can't be there, so staff finally feel the technology works for them, not the other way around," he said in a statement.

LeanTaaS acquired LookDeep rather than partner with a computer vision or virtual care company to integrate ambient intelligence technology deeply into the iQueue platform, executives said.

"We are building the central nervous system of healthcare operations—a highly functional nervous system must have audio and video sensory capabilities in order to be effective. This is why we needed to acquire the capability rather than rely on an arms-length partnership. We already had the intelligence that drives the car, 15 years of it. What we wanted was the best perception ever built for hospitals. Nobody confuses the cameras with the car, but there is no self-driving car without them," Giridharadas said.

LookDeep brings three capabilities to LeanTaaS' platform: peer-reviewed vision AI, an open technology platform that works with hospitals’ existing infrastructure and experience deploying virtual care. Its approach also focuses on using AI to ease care team capacity constraints rather than adding to clinicians’ workloads.

Health systems can build on compatible cameras and in-room devices already in place or deploy supported hardware as needed. This open approach helps preserve existing investments while creating a foundation for new capabilities, according to the company.

"The acquisition gives us the opportunity to make ambient intelligence a native part of iQueue and extend the technology across our broader portfolio. We also share a conviction that in something as complex as a hospital, before you can be smart, you must be open. Vendor-specific camera silos will not last as health systems demand greater interoperability," Giridharadas said, noting that a camera alone "does not generate an ROI." "The value comes when what it sees changes what happens next—earlier, with the right person acting. Nobody expects the barcode scanner to redefine the supply chain, yet no supply chain runs well without one."

The new virtual care offering includes three services: virtual observation for AI-assisted patient monitoring and escalation, virtual nursing to support admissions, rounding, patient education and discharge preparation, and virtual medicine to connect patients with remote physicians and specialists.

These offerings build on LookDeep’s experience deploying the technology in health systems. Across different deployments and operating models, reported results include a more than 70% reduction in fall rates, twice as much nursing contact, an 80% reduction in medication errors and threefold cost savings compared with traditional virtual sitting solutions, according to the companies.

Beyond virtual care, LeanTaaS plans to incorporate ambient intelligence into additional iQueue products and workflows to support capacity, patient flow and care coordination.

"We will bring the vision capability into all of our products beginning with inpatient flow and operating rooms and then moving on to infusion centers and other areas of the hospital," Giridharadas said.

The company aims to find areas in hospital patient care where important signals are either missed or received too late by current systems. "We will prioritize use cases where the signal is reliable, the response is well defined and the impact can be measured," he noted.

As adoption of AI in healthcare grows, LeanTaaS says its competitive advantage comes from a proprietary knowledge base built from more than 15 years of health system deployments. "We have accumulated an enormous knowledge base of thousands of corner cases that make operational improvement and change management difficult to accomplish. We have built a multi-layered knowledge architecture of tens of thousands of 'knowledge nodes' that enables us to deliver an enterprise-grade AI capability where the data and knowledge is tightly curated to the unique needs of each site at each customer rather than relying on generic recommendations from foundation LLM models," he said.

#5666. Samaritan Health Services, MultiCare Health System close merger

Samaritan Health Services, MultiCare Health System close merger" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

After months of securing the necessary regulatory approvals, Samaritan Health Services officially joined up with MultiCare Health System at the top of November to create an 18-hospital, $7.5 billion nonprofit health system.

The Northwestern organizations' deal, announced last year, directs $700 million from MultiCare into care services, workforce development, facility improvements and technology investments across Samaritan facilities over the coming decade. Those investments and other "longer-term" decisions will be informed by local community needs and perspectives, with decisions headed by "a locally led regional strategic planning process," they said in this week's announcement.

“MultiCare brings expertise and resources that will help us meet the changing healthcare needs of our region and support our clinicians and employees in their work every day," Marty Cahill, Samaritan's president and CEO, who has also taken on the roles of senior vice president and chief executive of MultiCare's Oregon Coast to Cascades Region, said in the announcement.

Samaritan comprises five hospitals in western Oregon, and will also remain locally led under its new parent organization, officials have said throughout the merger process. Its addition represented a geographic market expansion for the 13-hospital MultiCare.

Samaritan Health Services and MultiCare Health System have cleared all the regulatory bars necessary to complete their merger, which will cross the finish line on Nov. 1.

The nonprofits' affiliation would create an 18-hospital system with more than $7.5 billion in revenue—and give MultiCare an acute-care foothold in Oregon. Announced in 2025, it also includes a $700 million, 10-year commitment from MultiCare to invest in Samaritan's facilities, workforce and care access points.

On Monday, the pair said that all public agencies that were reviewing their deal "have either approved the transaction or announced their intent to do so." Some of these, such as the approval from the Oregon Health Authority (see below), would bring additional conditions on areas such as the reinvestment of operating margins into local care.

“We look forward to investing in the future of healthcare across Samaritan’s service area and advancing our vision to be the Pacific Northwest’s highest-value system of health,” Bill Robertson, CEO of MultiCare, said in a statement. “Together, we can build on the strengths of both organizations and invest in the future of healthcare for the people who depend on us.”

A phased integration process will begin on Nov. 1, with the organizations reassuring patients and health plan members that the process wouldn't interrupt services or coverage. Samaritan is also slated to retain its name, local leadership and community-based governance, they reaffirmed.

The Oregon Health Authority (OHA) approved a deal on Monday that would merge the nonprofits MultiCare Health System and Samaritan Health Services.

State regulators said the OHA's Health Care Market Oversight (HCMO) program reviewed how the proposed merger would affect Samaritan's facilities and its impact on Oregon citizens' access to affordable and equitable healthcare.

HCMO approved the deal provided it meets established conditions (PDF), including requiring MultiCare to follow its financial commitment of investing $700 million towards Samaritan and posting a public-facing version of the commitment on Samaritan's website. Other conditions involve reinvestment of Samaritan's operating margins into local communities and a requirement to maintain existing services.

The proposal to form a $7.5 billion, 18-hospital system still has to face review from other state programs prior to moving forward.

OHA's Coordinated Care Organization (CCO) Form A review is analyzing the deal's potential impact on InterCommunity Health Network's financial stability and ability to serve state Medicaid recipients. Moreover, the state Department of Consumer and Business Services (DCBS) is reviewing the financial and overall impact of changing control of Samaritan commercial health plans.

Samaritan President and CEO Marty Cahill said in a statement that the approval is "an important step forward for the communities we serve."

"Our affiliation with MultiCare will provide additional resources to invest in our workforce, facilities, technology and services—and help make it easier for people to receive high-quality care close to home," Cahill said.

The nonprofits will continue to operate as independent organizations until the transaction closes, and executives say they are working toward an Oct. 1 closing.

The boards of nonprofits MultiCare Health System and Samaritan Health Services have approved an affiliation they expect to consummate in mid-2026.

The arrangement would bring Samaritan, which runs five community hospitals as well as health plans and clinics in Oregon’s Benton, Lincoln and Linn counties, under the 13-hospital MultiCare—a new geographic foothold for the Tacoma, Washington-based organization.

“MultiCare and Samaritan are closely aligned in our mission, vision and values, making us ideal partners as we strengthen our networks across our service regions,” MultiCare CEO Bill Robertson said in the announcement. “It will be our privilege to be a part of the communities Samaritan serves, and we look forward to working together to support and advance health care in Oregon.”

The systems said there are no immediate changes for Samaritans’ patients, plan members or employees as the two sides move through the affiliation process.

Once the deal is finalized, Samaritan will remain “locally governed and community-based” but receive new resources from MultiCare that will expand services, update its operations and ensure sustainable care in its Oregon communities, according to the announcement.

More specifically, the deal includes a 10-year investment commitment focused on modernizing Samaritan’s facilities, expanding the flagship Good Samaritan Regional Medical Center’s inpatient capacity, adopting new technologies including telehealth capabilities and growing primary and specialty care. MultiCare’s behavioral health will also expand into Samaritan’s service area along the mid-Willamette Valley and central coast.

These changes will together increase care quality and access while helping to lower the cost of care, the organizations said.

“This affiliation represents an important step in securing the future of nonprofit health care in our region,” Marty Cahill, president and CEO of Samaritan, said in the announcement. “Our commitment has always been to remain a community-based, mission-driven organization, and this partnership strengthens that promise for decades to come. […] We are excited and honored to become MultiCare’s first health system in Oregon and to bring the benefits of MultiCare’s expertise home to the communities we serve.”

The parties said they will sign a formal affiliation agreement “in the coming weeks.”

MultiCare Health System employs more than 28,000 people across its 13 hospitals. It has 300-plus care locations in Washington, Idaho and Oregon, though no hospitals in the latter. The system reported $5.9 billion of total operating revenue but a $116.5 million operating loss (-2% operating margin) in 2024, a nearly $70 million improvement over the prior year.

Samaritan Health Services operates more than 80 physician clinics and multiple health insurance plans, serving 110,000 people, as well as its five community hospitals. In 2024, the nonprofit reported more than $1.7 billion of revenue but a $93.6 million operating loss (-0.5% operating loss).
