#5657. Measles update: New York reports first measles-associated death; US nears 5,000 confirmed cases

Measles update: New York reports first measles-associated death; US nears 5,000 confirmed cases" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease."

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to New York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they said.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

#5655. Investigating RFK Jr., Fixing Surprise Billing Law May Be on Agenda for New Congress

— Reversing or delaying Medicaid cuts could also be a possibility, experts suggest

Changes to laws on surprise billing and price transparency as well as investigations of HHS officials could be on the menu when the Democratic-controlled Congress assumes office next year, analysts say.

"We're heartened to see a number of people elected who are likely to be public health champions," Bruce Mirken, communications co-chair at Defend Public Health, said in a phone call.

"[Sen.-elect] Abdul El-Sayed, MD, talks a lot like we do, and there are a number of other people who got elected" such as Reps.-elect Richard Pan, MD, (D-Calif.) and Mitchell Berman, RN (D-Wisc.), he said. "So there will be a lot of voices in this next Congress who will speak up for public health in a way that hasn't been happening enough in the last 2 years."

Among possible actions to be taken by the new Democratic-controlled Congress, "one is a complete and thorough investigation and airing of [HHS Secretary] Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s record of malfeasance and disinformation, which we think should lead to articles of impeachment," he said. "This guy's guilty of public health malpractice and Congress needs to assert its authority ... and start the process of removing Mr. Kennedy."

Reasserting authority over health spending should be another top priority, Mirken said. "This administration and HHS played a lot of games with money Congress appropriated. Congress needs to dig in quickly and [fix the] damage done to disease monitoring and tracking, food safety, and health research."

Tom Miller, JD, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, took a more cautious approach. "Tuesday's sweeping election results will trigger the usual post-mandate cross pressures for congressional Democrats: the urge to get some things done differently versus the strong temptation for factions to overstate and overreach their mandate to settle scores, address grievances, and pursue boundary-stretching changes not supported by the voters who just threw another set of rascals out," he said in an email. "All of this will be challenged further by the calendar pressures of starting the 2028 presidential campaign ... this week!"

"Although healthcare usually ranked in the top two or three issues most of concern to voters, it's far from clear what those voters really want (other than the generic wish for more care at lower prices)," Miller said. "Developing a list of priority targets and feasible reforms will remain challenging for the new leaders of Congress. In the meantime, competing demands on the calendar, and the limited attention span of both voters and officeholders, will make substantive legislating more aspirational than successful."

He did offer a few possibilities for action, however. "Expect few large reforms or rollbacks of recent Trump administration policy changes, but some adjustments at the margins. Some limited consensus may be available for adjustments to the flaws of the No Surprises Act and targeted shots at common villains of the moment in the health sector (hospitals, drugmakers, insurers), but expect more rhetoric than reality in what changes from current law."

Other health cost initiatives may also come under the new Congress's radar, said healthcare consultant Thomas Campanella, professor emeritus of health economics at Baldwin Wallace University in Cleveland, in an email. These include initiatives such as site-neutral hospital payments, "stricter vertical and horizontal anti-trust enforcement of hospital systems, addressing 340B abuses, and stricter enforcement of user-friendly price and ideally quality transparency," he said. "Also, there is bipartisan support for enhanced investment in primary care and rural healthcare."

Medicaid is another possible area of action, according to Edwin Park, JD, research professor at Georgetown University's Center for Children and Families in Washington. For example, the House and Senate could try to repeal the Medicaid and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefit cuts that were included in the reconciliation bill passed by Congress last summer, "and if that's not successful they may attempt to delay some of those cuts," Park said in a phone interview. There are also provisions of the Medicaid program that are expiring next year -- such as money to pay Disproportionate Share Hospitals -- that Congress will need to deal with by year's end, he added.

Park also said he expected more scrutiny of actions taken by CMS. That includes how the agency is implementing Medicaid cuts included in the reconciliation bill -- also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill.

"There have been a number of occurrences where CMS has gone well beyond what [the bill] requires, whether in [the interim final rule] for work reporting requirements ... or guidance related to financing Medicaid waivers," he said. In such cases, "CMS is going way beyond what is required. Similarly, there is little information on how prices are obtained or what drugs are subject to rebates. There is a lot of talk about how great [these deals] are but no transparency about what they actually do."

The analysts all acknowledged that many reforms have little hope of being enacted since Democrats don't have a veto-proof majority in the Senate. However, Mirken said a veto override isn't beyond the realm of possibility in today's political climate. "It's worth trying and people need to see [that] this new Congress is trying to fix the damage."

In June 2025, insurers nationwide—including Humana—agreed to take steps to reform prior authorization, including supporting electronic prior authorizations.

#5653. Medicare Part D premiums projected to rise 50% in 2027 without plan switching: KFF

Medicare Part D premiums projected to rise 50% in 2027 without plan switching: KFF" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Medicare beneficiaries who remain in their current stand-alone Part D drug plans could face sharply higher premiums in 2027 if they don’t switch to lower-cost plans during open enrollment, according to a KFF analysis.

The average monthly premium for stand-alone prescription drug plans, or PDPs, is projected to rise 50%, from $34 in 2026 to $51 in 2027, if current enrollees remain in the same plans, according to the analysis from KFF, an independent source for health policy research, polling and news.

The increase would widen the gap between stand-alone drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans that include prescription drug coverage. KFF projects that drug coverage through Medicare Advantage plans that offer Part D coverage, or MA-PDs, will average $9 a month in 2027, compared with $51 for PDPs. The average PDP premium would rise by $17, compared with an increase of less than $2 for MA-PDs.

For Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage, the average beneficiary has 28 Medicare Advantage prescription drug plans (MA-PDs) and 9 stand-alone prescription drug plans (PDPs) to choose from, with varying costs associated with these different options. KFF analysts examined premiums and cost-sharing requirements for Part D coverage in 2027 and how these costs have changed over time, based on Medicare plan landscape and benefits data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

The $51 figure assumes current PDP enrollees remain in their existing plans. The actual average premium could be lower as beneficiaries switch to less expensive plans during open enrollment and new beneficiaries select coverage.

CMS projected a much smaller increase in the national average Part D premium, from $35 to $36. KFF noted that CMS, which based its estimate on September 2026 enrollment, did not explain its calculation methodology.

Among PDP enrollees who do not receive low-income subsidies, 76%, or 10.4 million people, would pay higher premiums if they keep their current plans. About 2.4 million would see their monthly premiums increase by more than $50.

That's a sharp increase from 2026, when only 38,000 enrollees faced monthly premium increases exceeding $50, according to KFF. The Trump administration’s decision to discontinue the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration after 2026 ended the additional premium subsidies that were provided to PDP sponsors and the cap on the maximum allowable monthly PDP premium increase, which was set at $50 for 2026, according to KFF analysts.

Another 4.1 million beneficiaries without low-income subsidies are enrolled in zero-premium PDPs this year, but no zero-premium PDPs will be available in 2027.

“With some plans increasing premiums substantially, the stakes are higher this year for people with Medicare stand-alone drug coverage if they sit on the sidelines during open enrollment,” Juliette Cubanski, a vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said in a statement. “There are relatively low-premium PDP options, but people facing large premium increases need to take action if they want to avoid paying significantly more.”

According to KFF's analysis, if PDP enrollees who are not receiving Part D Low-Income Subsidies (LIS) keep their current plan in 2027, more than half (55%), or 7.5 million people, will pay premiums of less than $20 per month, but nearly 30%, or 3.9 million people, will pay at least $100 per month.

Average monthly premiums for the eight national PDPs are projected to range from around $6 to $204 in 2027. Among national PDPs, the two lowest-premium plans are Centene’s Wellcare Value Script Rx, an enhanced PDP with an average premium of $6.50 for 2027, up from $5.80 in 2026,  and Wellcare Classic, a basic PDP with an average premium of $10.90 for 2027, up from $8.60 in 2026, according to the analysis. The national PDPs with the highest average monthly premiums are United’s AARP Medicare Rx Preferred at $204.50, up from $126.00 in 2026, and Humana Premier Rx Plan at $137.40, up from $119.60 in 2026.

The analysis also finds that most Part D enrollees will face a deductible of several hundred dollars for drug coverage in 2027, including 85% of MA-PD enrollees, up from 80% in 2026, and virtually all PDP enrollees, 99.8%, up from 96% in 2026, based on current enrollment. The average Part D deductible in 2027 will be $643 for PDP enrollees, up from $540 in 2026,  and $489 for MA-PD enrollees, rising from $360 in 2026. The standard Part D deductible in 2027 is $700, up from $615 in 2026.

Most Part D enrollees will also face coinsurance rather than fixed copayments for preferred-brand and non-preferred drugs, potentially making their out-of-pocket costs less predictable. Virtually all PDP enrollees will face median coinsurance of 25% for preferred brands and 35% for non-preferred drugs, according to KFF.

#5652. Democrats Regain House and Senate in Midterms Defined by Affordability Concerns

Democrats rode affordability concerns to major wins on Tuesday night, retaking control of the House and Senate and flipping multiple districts.

Democrats flipped Senate seats in Texas, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina, and South Carolina and picked up a swath of seats in the House to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press projections. They've spent the year hammering Republicans on affordability and housing costs.

In the 2026 elections, voters decided all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats, and numerous housing-related measures. Both Democrats and Republicans have listed priorities to improve housing affordability in coming years.

"Tonight’s Democratic sweep shuffles control of the legislative branch, but the economic impact, which is fundamental for the U.S. housing market, is far less clear," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel. "Democrats have a clear mandate to focus on pocketbook issues, but whether they can translate that into a legislative agenda that delivers on that mandate remains to be seen."

Housing issues have been a dominant note in 2026, as Americans struggle with affordability. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hit its highest level in three years last month before dipping back to 7.24% last week, according to Fannie Mae. The national average gas price is $4.14 a gallon compared to $3.03 a year ago, according to AAA. President Donald Trump has pledged to focus on affordability issues.

"President Trump has been laser-focused on making housing more affordable," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Realtor.com in a statement on Tuesday morning.

Ingle noted that Trump in his second term had signed an executive order prohibiting large Wall Street firms from purchasing single-family homes, directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to purchase $200 billion in mortgage bonds that helped drive rates to four-year lows, and "cut unnecessary red tape at a historic pace to boost supply, speed construction, and lower costs."

"The President will not stop fighting until the American Dream of homeownership is within reach for every American, which is why he continues to sign bold new executive orders and calls on Congress to pass further legislation," he said.

Congress passed a bipartisan housing package aimed at making it easier to build homes, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, this summer. But it will take years for some of those changes to take effect in the market. And lawmakers expect states and local governments to implement some changes.

The Trump administration, meantime, has undertaken other changes such as encouraging more innovation in the homebuilding sector and reducing rules for some housing, like manufactured homes. It's also sought to limit the impact of institutional investors in the housing market.

"I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump posted on X late Tuesday, as major news outlets projected Democrats would take control of the House after flipping a half-dozen seats. Trump later told The New York Times he would accept the results of the election.

The economist Krimmel says that one "wild card" to keep an eye on is how the election outcome affects Trump's war with Iran.

"Many Democrats have been vocal critics of the conflict, which has sparked inflationary oil supply shortages," he says. "A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates. However, a lot of uncertainty remains. Wanting the conflict to end and finding terms that work for all involved are two different things."

Democrats marked the evening with several key wins in both the House and the Senate.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews flipped the Senate seat formerly held by Republican Lindsey Graham. Andrews beat Graham's sister, Darlene Graham, who had been picked by Trump.

And Democrat James Talarico flipped a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat in almost a century to be elected to the Senate.

Democrats had several early victories. Democratic former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper flipped the state's Senate seat, replacing Republican Thom Tillis, who chairs the Senate's Financial Institutions and Consumer Protection Subcommittee. Democrat Jamie Ager also flipped a North Carolina House district.

"We knew that the chaos and corruption in Washington were hurting our people," Cooper said in a speech. "Today, you said, 'This has to stop.'"

Pennsylvania saw three formerly Republican seats picked up by Democrats Janelle Stelson, Paige Cognetti, and Bob Brooks. They ousted incumbents Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan Jr., and Scott Perry.

In New Jersey, Tom Kean Jr. lost reelection after an extended absence fueled national headlines. Meanwhile, in Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown returned to Congress after campaigning heavily against incumbent Jon Husted, attacking the Republication over his prior support of data centers.

"Politics should never, ever be about two private clubs who are more interested in beating up each other than they are in solving problems," said Josh Turek, who flipped a Senate seat in Iowa for Democrats.

On Truth Social, Trump posted a photo of a red hat with the word "veto." He has repeatedly criticized Democrats this year saying their policies drive up housing and other costs.

Trump told Fox News late on Tuesday night that he would not shy away from using presidential vetoes to block "crazy" measures advanced by Democrats in Congress.

"I have the power of veto, and the power of veto, you know, it's impervious," the president said.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, who won reelection in Louisiana, defended Republicans' economic actions in remarks before midnight. He said Americans would "suffer" if Democrats use control of Congress to enact "retribution" over the next two years.

"From the first day of this election we knew that to keep the House and sustain the majority, we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history," Johnson said. "It's very, very difficult to overcome."

But Johnson said an agenda of "common sense" would lead Republicans to take back the House in 2028.

"Republicans have much more work to do," he said. "The new Congress doesn't change that at all."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5651. CVS Health plans to split pharmacy business from Aetna, Caremark

CVS Health plans to split pharmacy business from Aetna, Caremark" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The healthcare giant announced Wednesday morning that it would divide its business units into two companies. The first houses its retail pharmacies and Health 100 technology businesses, and will operate as CVS Pharmacy. The second includes Aetna, Caremark, Oak Street Health and Signify Health and will be referred to as CVS Health on an interim basis.

CVS said in the announcement that it expects the separation to be completed in the first half of 2028, subject to closing conditions, and until then, it will continue to operate jointly. The move will reverse CVS' historic acquisition of Aetna for $69 billion in 2018.

Current CVS CEO David Joyner will become chief executive of the new CVS Health, while Prem Shah, group president of CVS Health, will become the CEO of the new CVS Pharmacy unit.

The company said that the decision "follows a comprehensive strategic review" by its board of directors.

Joyner said during the company's earnings call Wednesday morning that the shift comes "from a position of strength" after multiple years of hard work at CVS to shift its strategic approach and drive improvement. That includes significant investments in technology across the enterprise, and an overhaul of its leadership team to drive needed change.

He said that the "environment around us is constantly changing" as the company pushes toward this new strategy.

"We can take this strategic action today because of our tremendous progress since 2024," Joyner said.

"We will be better positioned to address this changing environment as two strong independent healthcare leaders," he continued. "Following a thoughtful and deliberate strategic review by the board and senior management, we have a structure and plan that are built to win and represent the best path to create value over the long term."

During this process, the team has identified significant opportunities for greater integration between Aetna and Caremark and has leaned on those to support key strategic initiatives, like advancing value-based care, Joyner noted. However, the pharmacy business has generally "operated behind a firewall."

"It has always been an arm's length negotiation and structure, which again, just reinforces the fact that there are integration opportunities, but nothing that we cannot solve for with a commercial agreement," Joyner said.

While there are clear synergies that exist between the pharmacies and Caremark, those commercial deals can maintain what's working, he added.

"We don't need the integration in an operating structure," Joyner said. "We need to make sure that we're aligned around where we believe that there can be value creation and make sure that there's an appropriate commercial agreement in place to support that."

CVS' strategy over the past several years has been built on four key principles: delivering on best-in-class execution, rethinking the consumer experience, becoming a go-to partner and harnessing capabilities across the company.

Following the split, both companies will continue to lean on these concepts, CVS said. Each individual entity will also benefit from a more focused strategy and the ability to adapt more nimbly to its own unique goals and strategic needs.

The future CVS Pharmacy will continue to identify ways to expand the reach of its pharmacists and identify further partnerships across the healthcare spectrum, while CVS Health will adapt in new ways to serve its clients, the company said.

Joyner said the company will continue to be transparent about its progress during the separation process.

Shares in the company were up 3% pre-market as of about 7:30 a.m. ET. CVS also reported its Q3 earnings on Wednesday, posting $2.2 billion in profit and $108.4 billion in revenue for the quarter.

Joyner said on the earnings call that post-split, investors will own shares in both companies.

Its platform processes over 8.5 billion healthcare payment transactions annually, representing more than $3 trillion in gross claims, according to CEO Matt Hawkins. Hawkins told investors and analysts during the Q3 earnings call that the quarter “reflects strong progress,” on three strategic priorities of “driving broader adoption of the Waystar platform, extending our reach through partners and integrations, and advancing AI and innovation.”

Large health care organizations increasingly look to Waystar to support more of the revenue cycle through a single connected platform, he said on the call. "Within our large client cohort, which we define as clients generating more than $100,000 in LTM revenue, the average client now uses approximately five Waystar product modules. With over 30 modules across six product families, we see significant opportunity to continue driving broader platform adoption within these relationships," he said.

Hawkins added that the company “secured the largest new client win in Waystar’s history” during Q3.

“In a competitive process, a major East Coast health system representing approximately $7 billion in annual net patient revenue selected Waystar's full platform across patient access, mid-cycle, and back-end revenue cycle operations,” he said. “The organization plans to replace more than 20 separate vendors with Waystar as it simplifies its technology infrastructure and streamlines operations.”

Moreover, Hawkins said the company is expanding its reach with “strategic channel relationships,” with an emphasis on the ambulatory market—noting an expanded partnership with a leading physical therapy practice management system that expands Waystar’s reach to “nearly 4,000 providers across more than 2,500 sites, representing approximately 17 million claims annually.”

“Decisions like these reflect the trust we've built with channel partners, the breadth of our platform, and our ability to deliver real ROI,” Hawkins said.

Alpana Wegner, who took over as Waystar’s chief financial officer in August, said that large client relationships “now represent approximately 75% of revenue,” adding the company is seeing momentum across growth in number of clients, strong bookings and implementation backlog expansion.

But larger, broader platform implementations have longer revenue conversion times, which can extend to 12 to 18 months, Wegner noted. This creates a longer period between booking and recognized revenue. The company reported that the backlog of larger deals, those in excess of $100,000 in annual sales, was up more than 50% year-over-year.

In response to a question from an analyst about the disconnect between bookings and revenue growth, Hawkins said, "We are seeing strong demand. We're not seeing a change in the competitive environment or our win rates, and we're pleased with that," adding that the company sees a "long-term double-digit opportunity to drive revenue."

For its full-year outlook, Waystar management forecasted revenue of $1.277 billion to $1.287 billion, with a midpoint of $1.282 billion. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to be between $543 million and $549 million for fiscal 2026.

The company expects slower, near-term revenue growth, forecasting fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $323 million, representing growth of about 6%.

Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote in an analyst note that Waystar delivered strong results on both the top and bottom line. "We continue to expect solid organic growth going forward. While investor focus may turn to the very modest (0.2%) reduction in sales guidance, we believe strong profitability, solid bookings performance, and robust free cash flows will continue to lead the stock higher over time; we maintain our Outperform rating," he wrote.

Daniels wrote that Waystar remains a "category leader in end-to-end RCM software... leveraging its competitive position and scale advantages to enhance the platform with innovations that drive client value. Moreover, we believe innovation momentum is driving an uptick in pipeline activity, size, and bookings performance, highlighted by a continuation of strong win rates and an uptick in larger deal sizes."

Daniels also noted that concerns over AI risks and "end-market noise," such as weaker healthcare volumes and Medicaid and ACA exchange lives moving to uninsured status, are "overblown."

Waystar is positioned to capitalize on the AI-enabled transformation of RCM via stronger pricing, an expanding total addressable market and increased value-add for clients, he said. "We continue to view the sales model as highly recurring (and visible) and do not anticipate any major AI-related competitive disruption as providers continue to turn toward trusted and fully integrated partners for RCM solutions," Daniels wrote.

#5647. What Democratic control of Congress means for healthcare in 2027

What Democratic control of Congress means for healthcare in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Tuesday’s forecast-busting blue wave puts wind in the sails of Democrats who have promised a stark departure from Trump-era healthcare policy—though whether or not the shifts will be incremental or seismic hinges on intra-party debates and the president’s veto.

As of noon Wednesday, Democrats had flipped seven seats in the Senate and 21 in the House, setting the party up for comfortable majorities as unexpected battleground races continue to be tallied.

Healthcare issues were a major talking point through many midterm election campaigns. In battleground Senate races, for instance, Democrats spent $65 million on ads primarily focused on healthcare, more than twice that of their next-most prominent topic. Healthcare was overall the second-most prominent issue featured in ads (as measured by spend) across the two parties, behind a push on taxation topics from Republicans.

And within those ads: promises to deliver lower costs, greater coverage and federal oversight, starting Jan. 1, 2027.

The immediate legislative impact will be seen in the bills new chamber leaders bring to the floor.

A health policy agenda circulated in September by a working group under Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.)—the House’s current minority leader and likely speaker in the next Congress—outlined immediate, “First 100 Hours” goals that include repeal of the Medicaid coverage and funding cuts of 2025’s H.R. 1 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) as well as restoration of enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits that expired at the top of 2026 and vastly increased marketplace plan premiums.

Other 100-hours priorities outlined in the document include medical debt protections, removal of visa program fees for healthcare workers, an end to an AI prior authorization program in Traditional Medicare, restoration of withheld National Institutes of Health funding, a block on immigration enforcement operations in hospitals and guaranteed no-cost coverage of recommended vaccines regardless of changes in federal recommendations.

Additionally, the new majorities would install key Democratic policy heads to congressional committees responsible for advancing healthcare legislation and conducting oversight into government and private sector conduct. Among those new chairs would be Vermont’s Bernie Sanders, a vocal opponent of corporate interests in healthcare and the country’s chief Medicare for All advocate, who would chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee; and Oregon’s Ron Wyden, who as Finance Committee ranking member recently pursued oversight of Medicaid stakeholders, endorsed Sanders’ Medicare for All bill, led calls to hold “Big Insurance” accountable for administrative roadblocks to care and summarized his midterms reaction with a single word: “Subpoenas.”

Underpinning the party’s legislative leaders are a slew of new-to-office healthcare advocates. Several of those elected to Congress have backgrounds as physicians or other COVID-era public health experience. Among the standouts are Ohio Governor-elect Amy Acton, a pediatrician who was director of the state’s Department of Health and resigned early in the pandemic in protest of state leadership; and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and Detroit’s former health director, who has made progressive health policy goals like Medicare for All a cornerstone of his campaign.

For the public and the healthcare industry, the key question is how Democrats will pursue their healthcare agenda under a divided government and lame-duck president.

Molly Turco, who covers healthcare policy at TD Cowen Washington Research Group, wrote in a Wednesday policy note that “with Trump in the [White House], passage of major reforms are very unlikely and even medium-sized policies, like rollbacks of Medicaid [state-directed payment] cuts or restoring ACA subsidies, are an uphill battle. But the midterm results and catalysts like the debt ceiling give Ds leverage.”

Consultants at BRG, in a media roundtable late last week, generally agreed with the veto hurdle, but noted that a stymied Congress still has room to write and pass bills that could become new policy in a future majority, as was the case with Medicaid work requirements pushed by Republicans during the end of the Biden administration but ultimately codified last year.

There is still an avenue for dealmaking between the parties, analysts and advisors noted, such as on areas with general bipartisan agreement (think this year’s pharmacy benefit manager reforms, or other major pain points like physician pay or surprise billing arbitration reform) as part of must-pass spending packages slated for this December and the coming years. The president, for his part, told outlets late Tuesday night that he intends to work with Democrats to pass bills he believes will benefit the country.

PricewaterhouseCoopers, in a Wednesday policy note, said “targeted bipartisan legislation is most likely to move. Look for action on cybersecurity, AI, price transparency, modernizing drug development and prior authorization processes. Regardless of congressional gridlock, continued regulatory implementation will shape near-term business and compliance requirements.”

Turco’s note predicts a dual messaging strategy for congressional Democrats on affordability and accountability, with the latter involving “an aggressive corporate investigation and hearings strategy.”

The TD Cowen analyst also questioned whether Democrats’ midterm over-performance and gains by progressive candidates will embolden the party to pursue and campaign on “bold” healthcare reforms like Medicare for All ahead of 2028.

Wyden’s recent endorsement of Sanders’ reform bill “is a powerful signal that even long-tenured moderates are under pressure to have a vision that reimagines [healthcare],” Turco wrote, though “many other D members are worried about blowback from M4A support that has almost no chance of being a viable policy. These members are vocal about their concerns and want to work on more realistic policies like restoring the ACA and Medicaid, building on IRA negotiations, reducing premiums/ deductibles for employer-based coverage, adding more benefits to Medicare, etc.”

Investment banking firm William Blair’s equity research team, in an election day brief, noted that Democratic governorships bring immediate impact to the healthcare industry as states make strategic decisions on how to implement, or offset, the provisions of H.R. 1.

The limited avenues for swiftly rolling back that sweeping bill mean that industry players, including Medicare Advantage plans and margin-strapped hospitals, should begin preparing for its financial headwinds, consultants and health systems heads have said. But that doesn’t mean Democrats’ strong night has dashed all hopes for rollbacks or other tweaks to ease the pain.

“While the election has changed who controls Congress, it doesn't change the financial challenges hospitals will face in 2027,” Chris Van Gorder, president and CEO of nonprofit integrated health system Scripps Health, said in a statement reacting to midterm election results. “Democrats won't have the votes to simply reverse major federal health care cuts over a presidential veto. But Congress is far from powerless. Lawmakers can use their oversight and budget authority to press for changes in how those cuts are carried out, protect critical health care funding where possible and work across party lines to ease the growing financial pressures on hospitals and impact on patients."

Even if political gridlock takes hold, Tuesday’s results ensure that affordability will be center stage in Washington, analysts said, especially as consumers’ cost pressures will likely persist well through the 2028 election cycle.

“Even where legislation stalls, don’t dismiss the headlines,” PwC advised healthcare executives. “Democratic hearings, investigations and proposed bills offer insight into the policies taking shape for 2028, while growing pressure around affordability continues to push the healthcare market toward consumer expectations. Executives who look beyond near-term political conflict, plan for multiple policy scenarios and adapt to evolving consumer demands will be better positioned for potential healthcare reform after 2028.”

On the virtual care front, ATA Action, the advocacy-focused affiliate of the American Telemedicine Association, said the election presents an opportunity to build on strong bipartisan support for telehealth and virtual care at the federal and state levels. The group plans to continue working across party lines to make Medicare telehealth policies permanent, expand digital health access and remove regulatory barriers to virtual care, Kyle Zebley, CEO of the ATA and Executive Director of ATA Action, said in a statement.

#5645. Your blood could reveal inflammatory bowel disease 10 years before diagnosis

Scientists have identified hidden changes in the immune system that can appear up to 10 years before a person is diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The findings, presented at UEG Week 2026, suggest that certain antibody patterns in the blood could eventually help doctors identify people at risk of developing the condition and even predict how severe their disease might become.

Inflammatory bowel disease refers to a group of long-term disorders, including Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), that cause persistent inflammation in the digestive tract. These conditions develop when the immune system responds abnormally, contributing to inflammation and damage in the intestines.

Scientists increasingly believe that IBD begins developing years before it is officially diagnosed. However, the immune system changes that take place during this early, largely hidden period have remained poorly understood.

Tracking Immune Changes a Decade Before Diagnosis

To investigate what happens before IBD is diagnosed, researchers examined 2,000 blood serum samples collected from 500 people. The participants included 200 who eventually developed Crohn's disease, 200 who developed ulcerative colitis, and 100 healthy individuals of comparable age and sex.

Blood samples were available from the time of diagnosis and from approximately two, four, and 10 years earlier. This allowed the researchers to look backward through a decade of immune activity and identify changes that emerged before the diseases were recognized.

The team analyzed antibody reactions to approximately 357,000 antigens associated with bacteria, viruses, food, and the immune system itself. Antigens are substances that the immune system can recognize and respond to, while antibodies are proteins produced by the immune system that help identify specific targets.

Across all 2,000 samples, the researchers detected 123,980 unique antibodies.

A striking pattern emerged. People who later developed Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis had significantly less antibody diversity than healthy participants, meaning their immune systems showed a narrower range of antibody responses. Distinctive changes could be detected in both diseases as far back as 10 years before diagnosis.

Different Blood Signals Reveal Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis

The researchers also found that Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis were associated with different immune signatures.

Among people who later developed Crohn's disease, antibody responses to herpesviruses and bacterial flagellin were elevated. Flagellin is a protein that forms part of the tail-like structures some bacteria use to move.

These elevated responses were especially noticeable in individuals who eventually developed complicated Crohn's disease or disease affecting the ileum, the final section of the small intestine.

At the same time, antibody responses to encapsulated bacteria gradually decreased as diagnosis approached. These bacteria are surrounded by protective outer coatings that can help them evade immune defenses.

People who later developed ulcerative colitis showed a somewhat different pattern. Their antibody responses to herpesviruses and autoantigens increased, while responses to encapsulated pathogens declined. Autoantigens are components of the body's own tissues that can mistakenly become targets of an immune response.

Together, these findings suggest that the immune system undergoes measurable changes many years before inflammatory bowel disease is diagnosed.

AI Identifies Hidden Disease Risk Years in Advance

The researchers then used machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence that identifies patterns in complex data, to determine whether these antibody signatures could distinguish people who would eventually develop IBD from healthy individuals.

Using blood antibody patterns from up to 10 years before diagnosis, the models distinguished future Crohn's disease cases from healthy controls with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.90. For ulcerative colitis, the corresponding value was 0.84.

AUC is a measure of how well a model distinguishes between two groups. A score of 0.5 indicates performance equivalent to chance, while 1.0 represents perfect discrimination.

The researchers also discovered that antibody patterns could help distinguish people who would develop complicated Crohn's disease from those whose disease would remain less complicated. This distinction was possible approximately 10 years before diagnosis, with an AUC of 0.85.

These findings raise the possibility that blood antibody testing could eventually help identify not only who is at increased risk of IBD, but also which patients may need more intensive treatment.

Commenting on the findings, lead author Dr. Arno Bourgonje said: "It is fascinating to see that complicated CD at diagnosis is associated with a distinct antibody profile years before the first clinical symptoms and is not simply the consequence of disease progression after diagnosis. Finding these patterns so early points to the potential of antibody profiling to support earlier risk detection, distinguish between disease subtypes and help identify patients who may benefit from more intensive therapy as early as possible."

Could a Blood Test Detect Gut Disease 10 Years Early?

Although the results offer compelling evidence that IBD has a detectable early immune signature, the researchers emphasize that the findings are not yet ready for use in routine medical screening.

The study establishes an important proof of principle, but additional research is necessary to determine whether these antibody patterns can reliably predict disease in broader populations.

Researchers must also establish whether antibody testing provides meaningful benefits beyond existing genetic information, clinical assessments, and other blood-based measurements. Any potential screening test would need to be accurate, affordable, reproducible, and ultimately shown to improve patient outcomes.

"The next priority is to validate these signatures in independent, more diverse and prospectively followed populations," concluded Dr. Bourgonje. "We also need to determine their added value alongside genetic, clinical and other blood-based markers, translate the findings into a reproducible and affordable targeted assay and, ultimately, demonstrate that using such a test actually leads to better clinical outcomes."

If future studies confirm these results, blood-based immune profiling could offer doctors a new way to recognize inflammatory bowel disease risk years before diagnosis, distinguish between disease subtypes, and identify patients who might benefit from earlier intervention.

#5644. Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?

A small device that delivers gentle electrical pulses through the ear could offer a new approach to treating stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home.

Although the treatment did not significantly lower blood pressure compared with a placebo device across all participants, researchers observed encouraging results in patients with more severe hypertension. The findings suggest that stimulating nerves in the ear could eventually help certain people whose blood pressure remains elevated despite taking medication.

The results come from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension, a journal of the American Heart Association. Researchers emphasize that larger studies are needed to determine whether the approach can provide meaningful benefits and which patients might respond best.

How Ear Nerve Stimulation Could Lower Blood Pressure

The experimental treatment uses a technique called transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), which aims to influence the autonomic nervous system. This network of nerves automatically controls essential bodily functions, including heart rate, digestion, and blood pressure.

By delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear, researchers hope to influence the body's natural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure without requiring an invasive procedure.

The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, uses two small clips positioned on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage located just in front of the ear canal. These clips deliver gentle electrical stimulation, allowing patients to administer the treatment themselves without visiting a clinic.

Clinical Trial Tests the Device in 63 Patients

The clinical trial, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), enrolled 63 people with uncontrolled hypertension. All participants were already taking at least one medication to lower their blood pressure, but their readings remained above recommended levels.

Researchers randomly divided the participants into two groups. One received active nerve stimulation, while the other used a sham device designed to serve as a comparison. This approach helped investigators assess whether the electrical stimulation produced benefits beyond those associated with using the device itself.

Participants used their assigned devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks. For the following 10 weeks, they reduced their sessions to once per week.

The results showed that the treatment was safe and generally comfortable for participants. Most also followed the prescribed schedule, suggesting that the technology could be practical for regular use at home.

However, when researchers compared blood pressure changes across the entire study population, they found no statistically significant difference between patients receiving active stimulation and those using the sham device.

Promising Results in Patients With Severe Hypertension

Despite the lack of a significant overall benefit, the researchers identified a potentially important finding among participants who entered the trial with more severe hypertension.

A prespecified subgroup analysis, meaning the researchers had planned this comparison before examining the results, revealed a greater reduction in blood pressure among these patients when they received active nerve stimulation rather than the sham treatment.

This finding raises the possibility that the technique may work better for people with particularly difficult-to-control blood pressure. However, the trial was relatively small, and the subgroup results require confirmation in larger studies before any conclusions can be drawn about its effectiveness.

Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said:

"This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham.

"As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension."

A Potential New Option for Hard-to-Control Blood Pressure

High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular disease and increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. It places additional strain on blood vessels and the heart, potentially causing serious damage over time.

Although medications help many patients manage their condition, a substantial number continue to have blood pressure readings above recommended targets even while receiving treatment.

This ongoing challenge has encouraged scientists to explore additional approaches that could complement existing therapies.

Ear nerve stimulation is one such possibility. Because the device is small, does not require surgery, and can be used at home, it could offer a convenient option if future research establishes that it reliably lowers blood pressure in certain patients.

For now, the findings represent an early step rather than proof of an effective new treatment. The researchers say larger clinical trials will be essential to confirm the encouraging results in patients with severe hypertension and identify which groups, if any, could benefit most from this approach.

#5643. CommonSpirit Health signs definitive agreement to sell 3 more N.D. hospitals to Altru Health System

CommonSpirit Health signs definitive agreement to sell 3 more N.D. hospitals to Altru Health System" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

CommonSpirit Health has locked in a deal to sell three hospitals to Altru Health System, rural North Dakota nonprofit.

The deal is contingent on regulatory review and other customary closing conditions, but expected to close in early 2027. The pair's new definitive agreement, announced Wednesday, follows 10 months of due diligence following a letter of intent unveiled near the top of the year (see that story below). Financial details were not disclosed.

The to-be-sold facilities are CHI St. Alexius Health Bismarck, a multispecialty acute care medical center in the state’s capital, and two smaller critical access hospitals, CHI St. Alexius Health Turtle Lake and CHI St. Alexius Health Garrison.

They would join Altru's flagship acute care hospital, a critical access hospital it also purchased from CommonSpirit in March, a trauma center, a specialty hospital and 20 practices spread across the northern part of the state.

The organizations said there are no changes to patient care or day-to-day operations related to the deal. The hospitals will maintain their Catholic identity and mission.

"Through our work together over the years, we’ve developed tremendous confidence in Altru’s commitment to high-quality, compassionate care," Tim Bricker, president of CommonSpirit Health's Central Region, said in reference to prior partnerships with the  We believe Altru is the right partner to build on St. Alexius’ proud legacy, honor its Catholic mission and continue serving patients and families for generations to come.”

CommonSpirit is in the midst of a sweeping operational overhaul as it looks to bolster its financial performance ahead of imminent Medicaid cuts. Those efforts have opened the $42.4 billion system to a string of hospital divestitures, including its four handoffs to Altru as well as the sale of a four-hospital Ohio system to UPMC in September.

CommonSpirit Health and Altru Health System are considering a deal to transfer three North Dakota hospitals to the latter, the organizations announced Thursday.

The pair’s signed letter of intent outlines plans to evaluate a potential deal for the facilities, a process they said would run “the next several months” before a potential definitive agreement might be struck.

In the balance are CHI St. Alexius Health Bismarck, a multispecialty acute care medical center in the state’s capital, and two smaller critical access hospitals, CHI St. Alexius Health Turtle Lake and CHI St. Alexius Health Garrison. All three are Catholic facilities within CommonSpirit’s regional healthcare system CHI St. Alexius Health.

Potential financial terms of any deal for the hospitals were not disclosed, nor were any details on whether other assets tied to the hospitals, such as clinics, would be included.

“This is a natural next step in exploring how we can continue to support strong, sustainable healthcare for the region,” Tim Bricker, president of CommonSpirit Health’s central region, which includes CHI St. Alexius Health, said in the announcement.

CommonSpirit is a $40 billion nonprofit that counted 137 hospitals in two dozen states. It’s in the midst of an operating performance turnaround initiative and, at this month’s J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference, teased “a couple” of portfolio divestitures to be announced in the next quarter as part of the effort.

Grand Forks, North Dakota-based Altru Health System is a smaller nonprofit, with just over $700 million of revenue in 2024 from its sole acute care hospital, a specialty hospital and 20 practice locations in northeast North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. It opened a new $500 million hospital in January 2025.

The news comes hot on the heels of another deal between the systems for ownership of CHI St. Alexius Health Devils Lake, another critical access hospital. That handoff was unveiled in December and is set to close March 1.

Both deals have been described as a boon for rural communities and an opportunity for Altru to better coordinate its local care.

“Altru has a long history of serving communities across North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, and our organizations share a deep respect for the people we serve and the responsibility that comes with delivering local healthcare,” Todd Forkel, CEO of Altru, said in the announcement. “We look forward to working more closely with CommonSpirit to strengthen access to care for patients and families well into the future.”

#5640. Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment

Scientists have uncovered new details about how pancreatic cancer constantly changes its genetic makeup, allowing it to become more aggressive, spread throughout the body, and resist treatment. By examining nearly half a million individual cancer cells, researchers identified genetic changes that could reveal new ways to fight one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

The study, conducted by scientists at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center, focused on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, a particularly difficult cancer to treat. Nearly 85 percent of patients die within five years of being diagnosed.

Although researchers have already linked more than half a dozen genes to the disease, much remains unknown about how pancreatic cancer develops and adapts. By examining tumor cells individually rather than studying them in large groups, the team gained a clearer understanding of how different populations of cancer cells change their DNA as the disease progresses.

How Pancreatic Cancer Evolves To Escape Treatment

The researchers discovered that pancreatic tumors contain a variety of distinct cell populations known as clones. Each clone consists of cancer cells with similar genetic characteristics, but their behavior can differ dramatically.

Some clones develop changes that help them withstand cancer treatments, while others become better equipped to invade surrounding tissues and spread to other parts of the body. These findings suggest that the cancer's ability to continually reorganize its genetic material plays a central role in both treatment resistance and metastasis.

Previous studies generally divided pancreatic cancer cells into two main categories: classical (less aggressive) and basal (more aggressive). However, because those studies examined large collections of cells together, scientists could not fully explain how cancer cells move from one category to the other.

The latest findings help explain this process. Genetic changes occurring within individual tumors allow cancer cells to shift between these two states, potentially making the disease more dangerous as it develops.

Scientists Identify a Gene That Could Make Pancreatic Cancer Less Aggressive

Published on October 13 in Nature Genetics, the study identified several genetic changes associated with pancreatic cancer progression. One particularly important finding involved MYC, a gene that showed heightened activity in some of the most aggressive cancer cell populations.

In additional laboratory experiments, the researchers blocked MYC activity in aggressive basal pancreatic cancer cells. Remarkably, the cells shifted back toward the less aggressive classical state.

The change also made the cancer cells more exposed to immune cells, suggesting they could become easier for the immune system to recognize and attack. Although further research is needed, the results point to MYC as a promising target for future pancreatic cancer treatments.

"Our study provides the most granular view to date of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, revealing how ongoing genetic reshaping drives tumor evolution over the course of disease," said study lead investigator Despoina Kalfakakou, PhD, a postdoctoral research fellow at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and Perlmutter Cancer Center. "These findings suggest that targeting the mechanisms underlying tumor evolution, including MYC, may help restrain the cancer's rapid progression."

"Our research also suggests that single-cell clonal analysis offers a better approach to understanding complex cancers, like pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, as it develops over time, by mapping how tumors evolve and adapt at each stage of disease progression," said study co-senior investigator Aristotelis Tsirigos, PhD, a professor in the Departments of Medicine and Pathology at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a member of Perlmutter Cancer Center.

"More broadly, our study results highlight the critical role of clonal diversity, genetic plasticity, and interactions with the tumor's microenvironment in shaping human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma biology," said Dr. Tsirigos, who is also co-director of the Division of Precision Medicine and director of NYU Langone's Applied Bioinformatics Laboratories.

Why Pancreatic Cancer Can Evade the Immune System

The investigation also provided important clues about pancreatic cancer's ability to hide from the immune system, a characteristic that may help explain why the disease often responds poorly to immunotherapy.

Researchers discovered that certain cancer cell clones showed increased activity of the TIGIT gene, which is associated with proteins that help tumors escape immune detection.

At the same time, these clones exhibited reduced activity of the PD1 gene. This combination may help explain why immunotherapies designed to target PD1 have shown limited effectiveness against pancreatic cancer.

Understanding these differences between cancer cell populations could help scientists develop treatments that interfere with the specific mechanisms tumors use to avoid immune attack.

According to Dr. Tsirigos, clinical trials investigating drugs that inhibit MYC or TIGIT are already underway for pancreatic ductal carcinoma and other cancers. He said the latest findings underscore the need for larger studies examining the different states cancer cells can adopt and how treatments might be tailored to target them.

Nearly Half a Million Cancer Cells Reveal Hidden Tumor Diversity

To investigate how pancreatic cancer changes over time, the scientists examined gene activity (using transcriptomics) in 443,451 individual cells collected from 62 tumors belonging to 56 men and women diagnosed with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

Six of these patients also provided tumor samples both before and after chemotherapy, allowing researchers to examine changes associated with treatment.

Unlike traditional approaches that measure changes in gene activity across large groups of cells, the new analysis examined individual cells. This provided a much more detailed picture of the different cancer cell populations living within the same tumor.

The results showed that individual tumors contained approximately two to 11 distinct clones, consisting of varying combinations of classical and basal cancer cells.

By tracing the genetic origins of these clones and comparing patterns of gene activity, the researchers connected differences in DNA copy numbers with the types of cells present in each tumor.

This approach allowed them to identify which genes, including MYC and TIGIT, were particularly active at different points during cancer progression.

Together, the findings provide a more detailed understanding of how pancreatic tumors evolve, resist treatment, and spread. They also suggest that interfering with the genetic mechanisms driving these changes could offer new opportunities to combat a disease that remains exceptionally difficult to treat.

The research was supported by the Sky Foundation and National Institutes of Health grants P30CA016087 and R01CA245005.

In addition to Drs. Kalfakakou and Tsirigos, the NYU Langone research team included Daniel Cameron, MS; Emily Kawaler, PhD; Ziaohong Jing, PhD; Cristina H. Hajdu, MD; Dylan Tamayo, MS; Yoona Shim; Amanda Ackermann, MD, PhD; Daniel Weissinger; Rosmel Hernandez, PhD; Matthew Beier, MD; Dacia Dimartino, PhD; Peter Meyn; Kalina Rice, MS; Shanmugapriya Selvaraj, MS; Cynthia A. Loomis, MD, PhD; Adriana Heguy, PhD; Amanda W. Lund, PhD; and Igor Dolgalev, PhD.

Additional contributors from Oregon Health and Science University were co-investigators Motoyuki Tsuda, MD, PhD; Hayley Zimny; and Rosalie Sears, PhD.

Researchers from the University of California San Diego included Lidong Wang, PhD; Qi Su, PhD; Sungsik Kim, PhD; Hannah Carter, PhD; Theodore Welling, MD; and co-senior study investigator Diane Simeone, MD.

Materials provided by NYU Langone Health / NYU Grossman School of Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5638. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5637. Popular cannabis sleep gummies may have a hidden dark side

Cannabinol (CBN) has become a popular ingredient in sleep supplements, often promoted as a natural, gentle way to relax and get a better night's rest. However, new research from the University of Connecticut suggests that this widely available cannabis compound may have risks that consumers should know about.

Scientists found that repeated exposure to CBN caused mice to develop signs of physical dependence. The findings, published in the November issue of the journal Drug and Alcohol Dependence, raise questions about the safety of using CBN regularly, particularly over long periods.

"CBN is everywhere right now. Gummies, tinctures, capsules, and it's marketed as a safe, herbal sleep supplement," says Steven Kinsey, professor in UConn's Elisabeth DeLuca School of Nursing. "Our findings suggest consumers should be aware repeated use may carry risks."

Popular Sleep Aid Shows Effects Similar to THC

CBN is a naturally occurring compound in cannabis, along with THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) and CBD (cannabidiol). Although CBN is generally considered less psychoactive than THC, the researchers discovered that it affects some of the same biological systems and can produce several key signs associated with drug dependence.

In the experiments, mice received CBN twice a day for three consecutive days. As treatment continued, the animals became less responsive to the compound, indicating that they had developed tolerance. When CBN was withdrawn, the mice also displayed physical symptoms resembling withdrawal, including head twitching and paw fluttering. These movements are comparable to the shaking that people can experience during drug withdrawal.

Another experiment revealed a surprising connection between CBN and THC. Mice previously trained to recognize and respond to THC's psychoactive effects reacted similarly when given CBN. This suggests that the two compounds produce overlapping subjective effects, at least in mice.

Together, the results indicate that CBN, despite its reputation as a milder cannabis compound, interacts with some of the same receptor systems that contribute to THC dependence.

Scientists Raise Concerns About CBN Sleep Supplements

The findings are particularly relevant because CBN products have become increasingly common, even though scientists still have limited information about their long-term effects.

The lead author of the study, Olivia Vanegas '26 Ph.D., notes "The marketing of minor cannabinoids is pretty wild right now. There are so many therapeutic claims about these drugs, but we really don't know much about their potential risks, especially with repeated use."

CBN is now widely promoted as a sleep aid, yet important questions remain unanswered. Researchers do not fully understand how CBN affects sleep quality or whether taking it repeatedly at doses commonly found in supplements could lead to addiction in humans.

There is also a historical reason for caution. Over the past century, several medications initially promoted as helpful sleep treatments were eventually found to carry serious risks of dependence and habit formation.

Potential Benefits Come With Unanswered Safety Questions

The researchers also identified potentially useful properties of CBN. The compound demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects, including at lower doses that did not produce psychoactive effects.

However, the experiments revealed another possible concern. During a simulated bacterial challenge, CBN reduced the body's ability to defend itself. This weakening of immune protection could make it easier for an infection to develop, similar to how bacteria can enter through a cut on the foot and cause illness.

These findings suggest that CBN may have medical applications, but scientists need a clearer understanding of its benefits, potential side effects, and appropriate doses before determining how it can be used safely.

Importantly, the experiments were conducted in mice, so the findings do not establish that CBN causes dependence or withdrawal in people. Additional studies are needed to understand how the compound affects humans, especially when taken frequently, at higher doses, or over extended periods.

"CBN may still have therapeutic value," he says. "But until we know more about dosing and long-term effects, the message for consumers is simple: buyer beware."

#5636. Chutes & Ladders—UHC names individual MA leader; HATCo CEO steps down

Chutes & Ladders—UHC names individual MA leader; HATCo CEO steps down" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Welcome to this week's Chutes & Ladders, our roundup of hirings, firings and retirings throughout the industry. Please submit the good news—or the bad—from your shop, and we will feature it here each week.

> UnitedHealthcare has named Suha Assi as CEO of individual Medicare Advantage, per a LinkedIn post.

Assi previously spent nearly a decade as executive director for Medicare and Retirement in Tennessee, and she previously held roles based in the state for Cigna. She wrote in the post that the "relationships with our teams, providers and communities have shaped how I think about this business and, most importantly, the people we serve."

"As I step into this national role, I’m excited about what’s ahead for Medicare Advantage," she wrote. "I look forward to working alongside teams and provider partners across the country to modernize how we work together, strengthen relationships, and find new ways to deliver for our members."

> Daryl Tol, president and CEO of General Catalyst's Health Assurance Transformation Company (HATCo) is stepping down from the role, the venture capital firm's CEO Hemant Taneja shared Tuesday.

Tol had been with the firm for about four and a half years in the wake of his time as president and CEO of AdventHealth's Central Florida Division. During that time he headed HATCo's partner and advisory network—helping grow it to nearly 40 providers, payers and other portfolio companies—and took the company's top spot partway through 2025. Of note, he helped HATCo close its acquisition of regional health system Summa Health and served as its interim CEO for much of the past year until the appointment of Jennifer Eslinger last month.

Tol is being succeeded by Reva Nohria, a founding member of the HATCo team who has been with General Catalyst since 2018. Taneja, in his announcement, said her work at both organizations has encompassed investment, company creation and strategic partnership, and that she will continue as an investor at the venture capital firm alongside her new appointment.

Tol will be supporting a smooth leadership transition and stay on in an advisory role, a representative of General Catalyst told Fierce Healthcare.

> Jennifer Shuford, M.D., is leaving her post as deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Nov. 12, just four months after joining, according to a Washington Post report that was confirmed by the agency on Tuesday.

The agency told press in a statement that Shuford was departing "to spend more time with family." Her appointment was announced by President Donald Trump in April, and she joined in June.

Shuford, an infectious disease specialist came to the federal stage from a role as commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services, and before that served as the state's chief epidemiologist. Notably, she had been credited for heading Texas' response to a measles outbreak last year. Her departure comes as the CDC clashes with state health departments and other public health leaders over its response to a growing national measles outbreak.

Satish Pillai, M.D., is slated to fill the role in the interim as the agency seeks a replacement, the CDC said.

> Johns Hopkins Health Sysem CEO Kevin Sowers is set to retire at the end of 2027.

Sowers has served as president and CEO of the Johns Hopkins system since 2018. He also previously spent more than 32 years as a leader within the Duke University Health System, including eight as CEO of Duke University Hospital.

The early announcement of his retirement plans gives Johns Hopkins significant time to conduct a search for a successor, with Theodore DeWeese, dean of the medical faculty and CEO of Johns Hopkins Medicine, leading the charge. Sowers will become a strategic adviser to Johns Hopkins to support the transition, the health system said.

"When I joined Johns Hopkins Medicine in 2018, I made a commitment to the organization and to myself to give 10 years of everything I had to this extraordinary place—to the talented, dedicated people who work here, and the people and communities we serve. And I intend to keep that commitment," Sowers said in a video message.

> Calley Means, a prominent senior advisory to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. closely aligned with the Make America Healthy Again Movement, resigned from his role on Thursday.

The resignation was reported by the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by Means on social media.

Media reports from the past several months described Means' frustrations seeing MAHA policy priorities delayed or blunted by others in the administration, with the journal citing sources describing him as "disillusioned." Still, his time advising the secretary notched several wins for the movement including overhauled dietary guidelines, steps toward greater food ingredient transparency and loosened restrictions on psychedelics as potential medical treatments.

Means wrote in his confirmation post that he still holds "tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy" in their battles against "the entrenched, dark forces in D.C. that profit from Americans getting sick."

"More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past two years than any time in history—and I know this movement is just getting started," he wrote.
